World.title: As Chavez and Maduro images disappear, is Venezuela entering a new chapter?
World.content:
Caracas, Venezuela – In a small square in central Caracas, Victor Rodriguez pauses at a giant mural of a figure draped in teal green. It’s the man he credits with giving him the opportunity to become an artist: former President Hugo Chavez.

Rodriguez, who paints under the name Forastero, helped create the image for the late Venezuelan leader's birthday on July 28. He says Chavez opened up new spaces for art and culture, giving artists from poorer neighbourhoods opportunities they never had before.

But today, Forastero is dismayed. He worries about the future of such art.

“Chavez represents revolution. He is anti-imperialist,” Forastero told Al Jazeera. “But now Chavez murals are disappearing.”

In recent months, Caracas has seen a transformation. Monumental images of Chavez and other figures linked to his political movement, chavismo, used to be common.

But now, graffiti, murals and billboards are being painted over or taken down. The Palace of Justice, once flanked by twin portraits of Chavez and the 19th-century revolutionary Simon Bolivar, has seen both images covered up.

In their place, there are new blue banners, emblazoned with the slogan "Venezuela renace" or "Venezuela reborn".

The changes come as Venezuela undergoes a period of political change after nearly three decades of chavista rule.

Since the United States launched a military operation to abduct and imprison then-President Nicolas Maduro in January, the country has been under intense pressure to reimagine its socialist government.

For some Venezuelans, the cosmetic changes are happening faster than any substantial ones. Some don’t want any changes at all.

Forastero sees maintaining his murals as a way of pushing back against the US influence in his government. “Now, painting Chavez is resistance," he said.

World.title: What are the five pros and cons of artificial intelligence?
World.content:
AI creates new opportunities in programming and automation, but experts warn of the spread of harmful content and risks to early-career workers.

Share What are the five pros and cons of artificial intelligence? on social media

Artificial intelligence has rapidly become a tool used by hundreds of millions of people, but tech leaders are sounding alarms against the rapid advancement of AI that is being seen as a threat to humanity.

AI systems can now generate text and images, write computer code, and perform complex analyses that once required a significant amount of time and human input.

Supporters argue these tools could raise productivity and create new kinds of work.

However, their rapid development has also raised concerns about job losses, the spread of misinformation, and the resources needed to power AI infrastructure. Researchers have also warned that regulation and safeguards are struggling to keep pace with the technology.

“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, whose company created AI tool Claude, said on Saturday. “Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain.”

So, what are the pros and cons of artificial intelligence, and where is this rapidly growing technology headed?

Boosts productivity and makes tasks easier

One of the obvious benefits of AI is its ability to help people complete some tasks more quickly.

AI tools are already being used for education, writing and editing text, gathering information, and computer programming.

Almost one billion people use AI for a wide range of tasks, according to the 2026 International AI Safety Report published by the United Kingdom’s government.

The report found that the most frequent queries by users on AI giant OpenAI’s ChatGPT platform involved practical guidance on editing or generating text, researching medical health, and searching for information.



There is also evidence of significant productivity gains in particular tasks. In September 2025, the Bank for International Settlements found generative AI had “productivity gains of between 10 and 65 percent, and efficiency gains of roughly 20 to 50 percent in time savings”.

Gains were particularly evident in industries such as “coding, consulting tasks and professional writing”, it added.

Indian technology company Wipro, for example, said its use of AI had freed up capacity equivalent to 20,000 employees, who were reassigned to other roles.

Creates new opportunities and skills

While AI is certainly bound to eliminate or transform some jobs, it is also spurring the creation of others.

Demand is increasing for skills that include machine-learning programming and chatbot development. Software developers are also increasingly using AI to produce code before checking and debugging the results.

The changes mean workers may increasingly need to learn how to use AI alongside traditional professional skills.

Wipro Chief Technology Officer Sandhya Arun said the company was training more than 100,000 employees in advanced AI skills as it shifts towards what it calls a “human-AI operating model”.

Threatens jobs

AI’s groundbreaking ability to automate work is also one of the biggest risks to society, experts say.

While no concrete data exists, some 60 percent of jobs in advanced economies and 40 percent in emerging economies could be vulnerable to AI, depending on how employers and workers adopt the technology, the 2026 International AI Safety Report warned.

Earlier this year, a slew of tech giants announced cuts amid growing reliance on and shifts towards AI.

Amazon slashed 16,000 jobs in a second wave of layoffs at the e-commerce giant in three months, while social media site Pinterest announced it would cut 780 jobs as the company reallocated resources amid increased investment in AI.

There are also concerns about people starting their careers.

Stephen Clare, lead writer of the 2026 International AI Safety Report, said there is “suggestive evidence” that early-career workers in occupations highly exposed to AI may be finding it harder to get jobs.

Can be misused and spread harmful content

Generative AI – which creates content based on existing data – can create convincing text, voices, images and videos, capabilities that can also be exploited.

AI-generated deepfakes have been used to scam people, and AI systems have also been used in cyberattacks.

Deepfake technology has been used to impersonate senior US officials and corporate executives.



Criminals can use synthetic voices and videos to make people reveal sensitive information, providing access to computer systems, and transferring money.

Uses significant energy and resources

AI technology depends on physical data centres filled with powerful computer chips, which require large amounts of electricity and cooling.

The expansion of data centres is raising questions about electricity supply and whether governments have enough infrastructure to support large AI projects.

For example, a proposed data centre in the US state of Utah would use more electricity than the entire state.

Beyond electricity, environmental activists in the United States are ringing the alarm over the enormous amounts of water needed to cool down servers at data centres at a time when parts of the country are experiencing droughts.

Some residents living near US data centres have also complained of the constant hum they emit. A Gallup poll conducted in March suggested that 71 percent of Americans oppose establishing AI data centres in their areas.

The concerns around data centres extend beyond just the US and the developed world.

In Kenya, a proposed $1bn data centre involving Microsoft and Emirati technology company G42 has drawn considerable attention.

Kenyan President William Ruto highlighted the scale of the centre’s energy demands, warning that the infrastructure of that size would require substantial additional power generation.

World.title: Iran Finds Escalation Is Fruitful Path to Leverage in War With U.S.
World.content:
The routes to export oil out of the Middle East are diminishing. The price of energy is soaring. And Iran’s neighbors could be about to endorse some measure of its authority over the Strait of Hormuz.

In the past week, Iran and its allies have used military escalation to upend any minimal sense of stability in the region, most dramatically in Yemen. That is shifting the momentum in Iran’s war with the United States to its advantage.

The shift may not be decisive. The Islamic republic remains under immense economic pressure, with the ongoing U.S. naval blockade of its southern ports and escalating rounds of sanctions cutting it off from the world.

And yet, a series of attacks in recent days by Iran and its allies have expanded the scope of the conflict. That, analysts said, may have given Tehran greater leverage, at least at this moment.

World.title: Russia hits Ukrainian train shortly after Boris Johnson and top European officials leave station
World.content:
A Russian drone has hit a train near the Ukraine-Poland border shortly after former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson and top European security officials had passed through.

No casualties were reported after the strike at Yahodyn, which hit the train's engine. All the passengers had been evacuated, Ukrainian authorities said.

Johnson and other European national security advisers, including the UK's Jonathan Powell, had passed along the same line on a different train on their way back from a conference in Kyiv.

Russia said it had struck "railway infrastructure" in western Ukraine, but Ukraine's state railway company Ukrzaliznytsia said that "quite possibly, the target of this drone could have been the diplomatic train".

In a statement, it said the train "had left the station earlier than expected because of the timetable change... due to constant threats of Russian strikes".

It also said that an evacuation order for passengers on the hit train had been given "just 15 minutes" before the strike by a Russian jet-propelled drone.

The railway authority also said former CIA chief David Petraeus had been on board another train at Yahodyn station at the time of the drone strike.

Both Ukrainian and Polish authorities said the Russian drone had struck 2km from the Polish border.

Former Swedish Prime Minister Carl Bildt, who had also attended the conference in Kyiv, told the BBC passengers on board his train had been told to prepare for evacuation before subsequently being allowed to continue their journey.

"On the train I was on we received order to prepare evacuation after it had stopped. But after a number of minutes we were informed that it was clear and we could proceed," he said.

That train then safely arrived at Poland's border station in Dorohusk.

Some reports have suggested Bildt was on the same train as Johnson, but the former UK prime minister has not confirmed any details.

Johnson wrote on X: "I don't know what warped logic drove Putin to blow up a stationary Ukrainian locomotive on the Polish border this morning.

He said this was "the kind of random and senseless attack Ukrainians are enduring every day - even on civilian railways".

Johnson also said Russian President Vladimir Putin "has been responsible for the deaths of 1,700 staff of Ukrzaliznytsia", urging Kyiv's allies to urgently provide Ukrainians "the air defences they need".

Ukraine has made repeated pleas to its allies - particularly the US - to provide more interceptors to defend against daily Russian attacks that increasingly use fast-moving ballistic missiles and jet-propelled drones.

World.title: Trump downplays AI risks after dire expert warnings and calls to slow development down
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has downplayed risks posed by artificial intelligence following days of dire warnings by experts.

"You have a lot of very negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn't be bringing it up and they're bringing up things that won't happen," Trump said during a visit to Ireland.

One of the warnings came from a former Anthropic researcher who said "there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future" if the current pace of development continued.

On Saturday, top industry bosses agreed and called for a slow-down. Trump did not directly address the idea, but said: "We're leading China on AI... and, frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins."

Trump spoke on the same day AI researcher Jacob Coxon - who quit Anthropic a few days ago - told the BBC staff who were developing the systems were "genuinely frightened" for the future of humanity.

Coxon â who has also worked at OpenAI â welcomed the idea of a slowdown but said it would need to be co-ordinated with China.

On Saturday, Elon Musk, owner of xAI, and Sam Altman of OpenAI, backed a warning from the head of Anthropic Dario Amodei that the pace of development should be slowed "to reduce the risk that something goes seriously wrong".

The Anthropic CEO said any slowdown would have to be limited to avoid allowing China to pull ahead.

The issues surrounding AI have prompted fierce debate - and present a dilemma for many world leaders.

On one hand, the sector is seen as huge opportunity to boost economic growth and a way to improve outdated digital systems and ways of working.

But there have also been a number of incidents where AI appears to have gone seriously wrong.

In August OpenAI said it had slowed down training some of its most advanced AI models to improve security.

The ChatGPT-maker said it was adding new measures after its AI agents bypassed safeguards and hacked the tech start-up Hugging Face.

And the same month it was disclosed two of the world's most powerful AI tools created fake human profiles to try and trick people in attempted cyber-attacks.

The UK's AI Security Institute (AISI) said in the most serious case, Anthropic's Mythos AI tried to gain access to a service by sending private messages, having set up fake accounts mimicking real people - then hid the evidence.

World.title: Six dead, 130 missing after Indonesian ferry capsizes in Java Sea
World.content:
Six people have died and 107 have been rescued from a capsized Indonesian passenger ferry in the Java Sea, authorities have said.

Another 130 people are still missing after contact was lost with the Virgo Transport8 ship, as it encountered bad weather.

The ferry was travelling from Surabaya to the South Kalimantan city of Banjarmasin and was last reported to be about 150km (93 miles) south of Banjarmasin around 02:00 on Sunday (18:00 GMT on Saturday).

Ships and a helicopter have been deployed to the scene, with 280 personnel taking part in a search and rescue operation. All vessels in the area of the Java Sea have been alerted to report any signs of passengers.

World.title: Turkish police detain dozens in raids on gay bars and homes of LGBTQ+ activists
World.content:
Police in Turkey have detained 47 people in a series of raids on gay bars and the homes of LGBTQ+ activists, officials say.

Raids took place in 12 provinces over the weekend as part of a campaign dubbed "My Family is Safe" that the Turkish government says has been designed to protect family values.

One of the targets of the operation was LGBTQ+ association Kaos GL.

Same-sex marriage is not recognised in Turkey, with growing pressure on gay couples. Human rights groups in Turkey have accused the government of using the campaign to target the LGBTQ+ community.

Officers detained 26 people and seized drugs, digital equipment, smuggled alcohol and a firearm during the raids, according to the Istanbul chief prosecutor's office.

In a separate statement, the Ankara chief prosecutor's office said another 21 people had been detained as part of an investigation into Kaos GL.

The organisation said 50 activists had been detained, more than 10 taken after police raids on their homes.

It said that authorities had blocked several websites and social media accounts linked to LGBTQ+ organisations.

According to the group, authorities have accused Kaos GL of making "obscenity" in online posts that are available to children and had demanded the shutting down of the Kaos GL X account, as well as those of around 15 other LGBTQ+ organisations.

Same-sex relations are not an offence in Turkey but homophobia is common, with President Recep Tayyip Erdogan describing LGBTQ people as "perverts" responsible for the falling birth rate.

As part of "My Family is Safe", Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek says legal proceedings have been started against more than 160 people and a number of organisations and companies across the country.

Gurlek did not say how many people had been taken into custody, but said the raids came in the context of the "Decade of the Family" campaign.

However, the Turkish Human Rights Association says the Turkish government has been using the campaign to target the LGBTQ+ community in recent years.

"The real name of this operation is not 'My Family is Safe'; it is state-led discrimination, politics of fear and the dismantling of civil society," the organisation said on X.

World.title: Iran war reshapes Brics ties but also exposes divisions
World.content:
This weekend, some of the most powerful people in the world gathered in Delhi around a vast circular table.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced that together, the leaders next to him should increasingly become "rule-shapers", not "rule-takers".

Among those listening were members of the Brics group, including Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian, Abu Dhabi's Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan and South African President Cyril Ramaphosa.

These are hardly natural allies. They have histories of border disputes and even military confrontations.

India and China engaged in a deadly clash along their disputed border in 2020. Iran and the UAE have been on opposing ends of the war in the Middle East, with Tehran launching missiles and drones at its fellow Brics member as the conflict sent shockwaves across global economies.

The fact that India was able to gather these leaders together in person is a feat in and of itself and testament to its diplomatic reach. The weekend also provided a platform for countries to reassess their relationships in light of the Iran war.

But agreeing on what a new global order should look like and achieving clear, tangible outcomes was a much harder task, and that tension ran through this weekend's summit.

World.title: Trump doubles down on united Ireland comments on day two of visit
World.content:
President Donald Trump has doubled down on his support for a united Ireland.

He's on day two of a visit, which he is spending at Trump International Golf Links in Doonbeg, County Clare, for the Irish Open.

On Saturday, Trump told reporters he would love to see a united Ireland while at a meeting with the Taoiseach (Irish PM) MicheÃ¡l Martin in Dublin.

Speaking on Sunday at his Doonbeg golf resort, he said it would be natural to put Ireland and Northern Ireland "together".

He spoke to reporters after watching the tournament leader Irish golfer Shane Lowry tee off.

He described what he said about a united Ireland as "a fairly routine comment".

World.title: Legendary Canadian boxer George Chuvalo dies aged 89
World.content:
"George Chuvalo was a heavyweight boxing legend, a family friend and a Canadian icon," Ontario Premier Doug Ford wrote on social media.

"My thoughts are with all of George's family and loved ones as we mourn his passing."

After retiring from professional boxing in 1978, Chuvalo travelled the country as a public speaker advocating for anti-drug education and mental health awareness.

Chuvalo lost three sons and his wife to drug overdoses and suicide, he has said.

"I'd like to think if you're ever tempted with the idea of doing drugs, or you ever flirt with doing drugs, I hope you think of me, George Chuvalo, and what drugs did to my family," he once said, according to a CBC Radio report in 1998.

In retirement, Chuvalo also dipped his toes in acting, appearing in the 1998 comedy film Dirty Work and alongside Jeff Goldblum in the 1986 horror film The Fly.

He also served as a guest commentator for major boxing matches and co-hosted a TV boxing program called Greatest Knockouts with his friend and fellow fighter Charles "Spider" Jones.

Chuvalo is survived by his eldest son Mitch, daughter Vanessa, grandchildren, and second wife Joanne.

He died on Saturday, his birthday, said Sully's Boxing Gym.

World.title: US congressman swims to safety after his plane is forced to land on a lake
World.content:
Wisconsin Congressman Tom Tiffany has said he sustained minor injuries after a plane he was on landed on a lake, forcing him and the pilot to swim to safety.

Tiffany, the state's Republican nominee for governor, was travelling in a small plane on Saturday night when the aircraft encountered a mechanical issue, forcing the pilot to make an emergency landing in Lake Wausau, the county sheriff's office said.

Tiffany said he and the pilot called 911 once they landed.

"As the plane began to submerge, we exited the aircraft and swam to a shallow area, where we waited until emergency responders reached us by boat," Tiffany wrote on social media. The pilot also sustained minor injuries.

Tiffany was coming home from a dinner in La Crosse County when the plane suddenly lost power as it approached Wausau Downtown Airport, he said on Sunday.

Authorities received a 911 report of a plane crash on the lake at 20:49 local time (02:49 BST), the Marathon County Sheriff's office said in a press release. The pair managed to get out of the plane and to shallow water where a Wausau Fire Department airboat rescued them about 15 minutes later, at 21:05 local time, according to the sheriff's office.

The office said Tiffany and the pilot were the only two people on board the Beechcraft K35 - a single-engine plane, also known as a Bonanza, that can carry up to five people.

"God was watching over us tonight, and I am incredibly grateful to be here in the hospital with my wife, Chris, by my side," Tiffany said. "An experience like this reminds you just how precious life is."

He received a small cut over his right eye in the incident, his campaign said.

The cause of the mechanical issue was not immediately clear, and the sheriff's office said the Federal Aviation Administration and the National Transportation Safety Board will investigate the incident.

The plane remains in the lake as emergency crews work to remove it, the office added.

World.title: Two savage Kano murders, 45 years apart, By Festus Adedayo
World.content:
Last Wednesday, popular political commentator, Ibrahim Khalil (aka Dan Shagamu) was brutally murdered in Kumbotso, Kano. He had his throat slit. Known for his scathing Hausa posts on Facebook and TikTok, Khalil was a fierce critic of the APC-led government, President Bola Tinubu and the military. Kano Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf also frequently drew his ire, as he hit him hard with his spatula. The influencer constantly called out economic hardship, northern insecurity, and alleged army atrocities against Fulanis. Condemning his murder, Amnesty International Nigeria highlighted the growing threats facing government critics.

This tragedy mirrors the July 10, 1981 murder of 35-year-old Dr. Bala Mohammed in Kano. It was a defining political hit of the Second Republic. Decades apart, both killings point to a persistent menace: political thugs acting as ruthless enforcers for the ruling class, leaving a long-standing trail of violence, blood, and broken institutions across Nigeria.

Forty five years before Dan Shagamu, Dr Mohammed was equally mercilessly murdered in same Kano. Often dubbed the Kano “July 10 Rampage,” Mohammed’s brutal killing remains one of Second Republic Nigeria’s most terrifying and defining political killings. The masterminds of that dark day were political thugs — the very same dangerous, rampaging breed that disrupted the peace of Benue State last week and who likely killed Dan Shagamu. Like swarming wasps defending a rotten nest, political enforcers have long served as the blunt force instrument of Nigerian statecraft, leaving behind a trail of ashes, blood, and broken institutions.

Dr Mohammed was murdered in a lethal convergence of traditional feudal allegiance, party rivalry, and federal-state power struggles. His killing illustrated the horrific mechanics of state-tolerated violence inflicted upon political oppositions. At the time, Bala served as the Special Adviser on Political Affairs to Alhaji Abubakar Rimi, the radical leftist People’s Redemption Party (PRP) governor of Kano State.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Though the next general elections were still two years away, political upheavals had already seized Kano by the throat, in preparation for the 1983 polls. President Shehu Shagari’s ruling party at the center, the National Party of Nigeria, (NPN) which operated as an opposition party in Kano State, was in an intense, desperate campaign to capture the state’s massive voting population. On the streets of Kano, violent rhetoric and inciting epigrams became as cheap and ubiquitous as tuwo masara.

The immediate flashpoint for this political explosion was Governor Rimi’s growing friction with the Emir of Kano, Alhaji Ado Bayero. In early July 1981, Rimi issued an official query to the revered monarch, demanding explanations for acts the state administration classified as official insubordination.

The NPN, frantically seeking an inroad into Kano’s vast electorate, seized upon the query to confront the Rimi administration head-on. Mobilising royalists, traditionalists, and a broad coalition of political opponents, the NPN framed the query as a sacrilegious assault, a direct attempt to humiliate the traditional aristocracy of the Kano Emirate system. They preached to the populace that Rimi’s ultimate agenda was the deposition of the Emir.

In this carefully crafted narrative, the NPN singled out Dr Bala Mohammed. The brilliant leftist intellectual in Rimi’s cabinet was woven in as the master strategist and primary author behind the query. He was also seen as architect of the administration’s broader anti-feudal policies and a rumoured upcoming government white paper targeting traditional privileges.

Thus, on Friday, 10 July, 1981, immediately following Jumaat prayers, a premeditated anarchy erupted across Kano. Political mobs and armed thugs, moving with the directionless fury of ojúoró and òsíbàtà — the floating water lettuce and lilies of Nigerian rivers — meandered through the ancient city. Before Kano could blink an eye, coordinated violence enveloped the metropolis. Armed with cutlasses, daggers, and arson weapons, the mobs operated under the guise of defending the throne against aróbafín — those who displayed contempt and insolence toward royal authority.

State institutions perceived to be offering the PRP ruling party government of Rimi backing received the first deadly salvo. Kano State House of Assembly, government ministries, Radio Kano, and offices of The Triumph newspaper were torched.

Then, like an invading army of locusts, the political mob matched towards the GRA home of Dr Bala Mohammed. The egghead was right inside his official residence. Pronto, the mob decorated the house in a hieroglyphics of gasoline. They also cut off his escape routes, trapping Dr Mohammed within. He was then treated to a session of machetes and dagger blades, like butchers do on meats at the abattoir. Done with this nicely decorated but deep severe wounds on Bala, which gushed fresh blood from the orifices of their mouths, the mob then set the scholar’s residence on fire. By then, he had been mercilessly tattooed with matchete wounds, his life hanging on a cliff. Gradually, like a weaver builds a tapestry, the fine scholar was incinerated alive, alongside tonnes of his documents and research materials. After the mob’s dispersal, Dr Mohammed’s charred remains were retrieved amid the smouldering ruins.

Public outrage over the carnage eventually forced President Shagari to momentarily stub out his Benson & Hedges cigarette. He then instituted an inquiry, a Judicial Commission headed by Justice EA Fernandez. Its charge was to investigate the rampage.

The commission’s findings were damning: it confirmed that state security forces were directly complicit in the tragedy. The Nigeria Police Force, led by Inspector-General Sunday Adewusi and controlled by the NPN-led federal executive, stood by idly while rioters rampaged across the city for hours. Justice Fernandez concluded that the police purposefully allowed the mob free rein.

By the time the violence subsided, an estimated 34 people had been killed, with Dr Bala Mohammed as the primary high-profile target. Millions of Naira in public and private property lay in ruins. Yet, despite the commission’s clear findings, the masterminds and political instigators were never held criminally accountable. Just as the identity(ies) of killers of Dan Shagamu may never be unraveled. This failure to punish perpetrators has established a dangerous precedent of impunity for state-sponsored political violence in Nigeria.

I recount this long, dark chapter of political assassination – and this recent one – to emphasise a fundamental truth of human conflict. As the classic Yoruba proverb warns:“Ìbèrè ogun l’àá mò, ẹnìkan kìí mọ ìparí è — We only know the beginning of a war; no one can predict how it will end. This proverb serves as a solemn warning against the unpredictable, destructive, and uncontrollable nature of political violence that has become the face of Nigerian politics.

During the First Republic, the Western Region witnessed the rise of violent political thugs called enforcers. They were shawled in the deceptive title of Májêkóbàjé (Do not allow things to deteriorate). Ironically, under their watch, public order deteriorated completely as political arson, popularly known as Operation Wetie, turned homes and public buildings into smouldering ash.

Across Nigeria’s distinct socio-linguistic landscape, various terms exist to describe these political enforcers: In Lagos, they are historically referred to as Òráìsà (derived from their servile chant, “Alright, Sir!”) and modern Agbèròs. In the North, they are known as Yan Daba and nationwide, are colloquially termed “Kill and Go.”

In the North, the ruling Northern People’s Congress (NPC) systematically suppressed political rivals like Aminu Kano’s NEPU and Joseph Tarka’s UMBC. The NPC deployed the Native Authority police and Yan Daba enforcers to crush internal dissent — a sharp contrast to South Africa’s uMkhonto weSizwe, which was formed to fight state apartheid rather than fellow citizens. Ultimately, politicians unleashed forces of violence that spiraled out of control and destroyed Nigeria’s First Republic. This widespread breakdown of law and order provided the military with its primary justification for the bloody 15 January, 1966 coup d’état.

This brings us to recent events surrounding Peter Obi, the presidential candidate of the NDC. You may not like Mr Peter Obi; you may even despise his political guts or campaign methods. But during his recent visit to Benue State, Nigeria stood on the precipice of tragedy once again, something of the Bala Muhammed hue. When hired political thugs blocked Obi’s passage into Benue, the nation narrowly avoided a catastrophe akin to the 1981 Kano massacre. Had Obi’s security detail or supporters chosen to return fire, the resulting escalation could have ignited widespread civil unrest across the region.

The thugs who waylaid Peter Obi in Benue and those who murdered Bala Mohammed 45 years ago are direct political descendants. They belong to the class of “flies who death don’t scare,” a clan my people dub “esin ò k’okú.” Their actions represent a lineage of political violence that has plagued Nigeria for about seven decades.

Whatever reason took Peter Obi to Benue State was irrelevant under the law, provided his mission was lawful. Yet, as his convoy proceeded, suspected political thugs, armed with weapons, intercepted his path along the Boko Road near the Air Force Base. The mob blocked the highway, pursued vehicles in his entourage, and pelted his convoy with stones. Sensing danger, his team attempted to escape the ambush. This incident marked the second time Obi was forcibly prevented from moving freely within Benue State. In April 2025, the state governor, Reverend Father Hyacinth Alia, similarly barred Obi from accessing internally displaced persons (IDP) camps in the state, citing official security and protocol concerns.

Of course, political demagogues queued around the ugly behind of tyranny. Such treatment was necessary for a political wayfarer like Obi, they chorused.

Long before today’s street enforcers were born, their political predecessors patrolled electoral corridors with unearned impunity. Nigeria’s post-colonial political architecture was constructed around a violent doctrine: that power in Nigeria is rarely persuaded through debate; it must be violently extracted.

Ever since the exit of the British colonial administration on 1 October, 1960, the weaponry of political intimidation — cutlasses, clubs, stones, and firearms — has remained intertwined with the Nigerian electoral process. The nation has increasingly normalised an environment where the political thug functions as an essential operative, echoing the themes of Wole Soyinka’s 1995 satire, The Beatification of Area Boy. Set against a backdrop of urban decay and systemic failure, Soyinka’s work highlighted a moral inversion where street miscreants were elevated into political power-brokers. “Area boys” — euphemism for street thugs, extortionists and miscreants — got elevated, becoming Lagos society’s moral compass. They taught society the way to go, in contrast to the predatory military and political ruling class.

Today, political thugs dictate the boundaries of public engagement. They enforce the harsh reality of the Yoruba proverb — brute physical size does not open the door; only the person with the key can — “Gìdìgbà ò sí’lèkùn, àfi ẹni t’ó ní kókóró”. In modern Nigerian politics, physical force and control of armed groups have become the effective keys to political power. The entity that commands the most ruthless enforcers often secures control of the state apparatus. The road to 2027 may have been defined. No other horoscope but thuggery will predict the rainbow of elections. He who controls political thugs will hold the ace, the key to the Government House or Aso Rock Villa.

This institutionalisation of thuggery is clearly visible in the evolution of the National Union of Road Transport Workers (NURTW). Transport unions in Nigeria were not always bastions of political violence. In the early 20th century, transport organisations served as vital economic drivers and civic advocates. Industry prestige grew around 1917 when John Holt and the Miller Brothers entered the trade from the Ejinrin lagoon market (celebrated in Ebenezer Obey’s classic lyric, “b’ókòkan ò r’Ejìnrìn, egbegbèrún è á lo“). In Ibadan, Salami Agbaje dominated motor transport so effectively that the colonial government closed its Southern Nigeria transport service; his fleet later joined the 1937 general motor strike.

By the Second Republic, Lagos transport shifted dramatically as municipal buses gave way to private dáńfó and armed union factions seized motor parks from local councils. This shift accelerated during the political war between the NPN federal government and Governor Lateef Jakande’s UPN. To undercut UPN dominance, the NPN empowered Adebayo Ogundare, aka Bayo Success, to violently capture key transit hubs. Ogundare secured control, becoming the Oshodi branch chairman and a formidable power broker until his 2002 death. Today, MC Oluomo is the President and Lagos APC’s Bayo Success.

In contemporary era, union leaders have increasingly functioned as political warlords. In exchange for enforcing voter suppression in opposition strongholds, state actors frequently grant them access to lucrative park revenue collection and informal immunity from prosecution. Consequently, the street enforcer has evolved from an informal park collector into a core component of the electoral machinery, often operating with greater authority than formal law enforcement agencies.

The long-term danger of this system is that the weapons distributed during election cycles do not vanish once results are declared. The political enforcer of an election season frequently turns to armed robbery, cult violence, or kidnapping during the off-cycle years. By weaponising poverty for short-term political gain, the political elite has constructed a violent system that ultimately threatens public security across all socio-economic classes. Because they chose the route of weaponising poverty in elections, Nigerian political elite are building an unsustainable Frankenstein’s monster whose terrorism will know no tribe or class.

The Benue State government’s attempt to distance itself from the recent obstruction of Peter Obi, by questioning why he did not seek prior administrative clearance, fails to address the underlying issue of political intolerance. When state administrations rely on informal enforcers to restrict the movement of opposition figures, they weaken the rule of law and invite further instability.

To break the cycle of what appeared harmlessly in Benue last week, we must begin the process of demilitarising elections, strip political enforcement structures of state protection and get those thugs prosecuted, including their political sponsors. Nigeria must dismantle the structures that enable state-sanctioned political violence. As the Yoruba proverb cautions, it is when the Iroko tree is a young sapling that we must uproot it; once it matures into a giant, it demands sacrifices from the entire community.

By now, Hyacinth Alia’s recruiters of political thugs should be answering police questions. What Alia wanted was to keep Benue’s political temperature frozen, while continuing to institutionalise thugs for state capture. Just as it was done in the First Republic. If the Nigerian state fails to hold recruiters and enforcers of political violence accountable, its politics will continue to degenerate into a contest of brute force, mirrored by the killing of Dan Shagamu. Soon, we will arrive at an intersection where public policy is dictated not by debate or democratic consensus, but by the power of the armed mob.

Festus Adedayo is an Ibadan-based journalist.

World.title: As new academic session begins, schools in Nigeria-Benin border communities remain closed
World.content:
On Monday, 14 September, many basic schools in Nigeria and neighbouring Benin are expected to reopen for a new academic session.

But for thousands of children living in vulnerable communities along the two countries’ northern borders, the new school year is beginning under a cloud of fear.

In Benin, schools in 10 northern communes remained closed at the start of the academic year due to concerns about possible terrorist attacks, according to education authorities. Pupils in the affected communities were instead directed to schools in areas considered safer.

The authorities did not disclose the number of schools affected. Parents of some pupils confirmed the relocation to AFP, while Benin’s government spokesperson, Wilfried Houngbedj, earlier announced the decision. Education authorities said the affected areas were facing security concerns linked to armed groups operating near the country’s borders with Burkina Faso and Niger.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

In Nigeria, the story is the same. More than 20 communities around the vast Kainji forest corridors stretching through Niger and Kwara states, and sharing borders with Benin, have also come under growing security pressure.

Schools in these areas have been targeted by terrorist groups. Mukadas Dindey, a zonal education officer in Borgu LGA, Niger State, told PREMIUM TIMES that virtually all schools in terrorised villages have been closed down since 2025.

He said only schools in the garrison towns of Wawa and New Bussa will resume academic activities on 14 September. An official at the Niger State Ministry of Education corroborated him.

“All those schools will remain closed for security reasons,” the official, who asked not to be named because he was not authorised to speak with the press on the matter, said. “If any community feels it is safe to reopen their school, they will write a letter through their local government chairman to the Ministry of Homeland Security.”

The official added that the homeland security ministry will then notify security agencies to assess whether the school is safe to reopen, in line with the federal government’s safe school initiative.

An expanding landscape

The development offers a glimpse into how the expansion of armed groups across the Sahel is increasingly affecting basic services in communities far from the region’s traditional conflict theatres.

An analysis by the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED) found that violent events involving jihadist groups across Benin’s Alibori and Borgou departments, Niger’s Dosso region, and Nigeria’s Sokoto, Kebbi, Niger and Kwara states increased by 86 per cent in 2025 compared with 2024. Associated fatalities increased by 262 per cent over the same period.

ACLED said the expansion of groups linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State has entered a new phase, with the borderlands becoming a growing theatre of jihadists’ activity. The data hub linked the development to limited state presence, weak border controls and declining regional security cooperation.

The Kainji axis, in particular, has recorded a series of deadly attacks in recent months.

In October 2025, this newspaper reported that Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), an al-Qaeda franchise in the Sahel, claimed its first attack in Nigeria, further blurring the security landscape in the Kainji axis, where multiple armed groups, including Boko Haram, Ansaru, bandits and Lakurawa, co-exist.

Nigeria’s Defence Minister, Christopher Musa, has also acknowledged the changing security environment along the frontier.

In July, Mr Musa said Nigeria was increasing military cooperation with Benin and Niger and creating another military sector to cover the tri-border area.

He said the al-Qaeda-linked JNIM was seeking to exploit routes through Benin into Nigeria.

“We’re opening another sector to cover the border between Nigeria, Benin Republic and Niger,” Mr Musa, a retired general, had said.

He said the arrangement would give Nigerian forces greater freedom to operate in the area.

Unending terror

Both jihadist groups and bandits continue to wreak terror, causing an escalating humanitarian crisis across borders.

A few days after a Boko Haram franchise led by Mallam Sadiku freed captives taken from Kwara (Woro and Nuku) and Niger (Konkoso, Pissa, Kasuwan Daji and other villages), about 600 Muslim worshippers, including children and women, were abducted at Dekara and surrounding villages.

The attack was blamed on Lakurawa, but that attribution is difficult to independently verify given the presence of multiple armed groups in the area.

For residents, however, the distinctions between jihadists, bandits and other armed groups often become less important when violence disrupts everyday life.

Shuaibu Ba, a displaced resident of Dekara, said it is hard to tell which group is which.

“I believe they are all partners and are determined to chase us away from our ancestral homes.”

Mr Ba lamented that schools, farms, markets and roads have become difficult to access. According to him, teachers are also targeted.

Education under threat

After the deadly November 2025 attack on St Mary’s Catholic School in Papiri, where more than 300 students were kidnapped, more schools have been targeted.

In June, terrorists set Dekera Central Primary School ablaze weeks after forcing the villagers to pay a N10 million levy.

“Days after they burnt the school, they came back to the community and kidnapped the headmaster,” Mr Ba narrated. “They took him to the forest and slaughtered him.”

Data compiled and analysed by PREMIUM TIMES show that mass school abductions have already spread well beyond the Northeast and Northwest, becoming a recurring national security problem.

Within President Bola Tinubu’s first three years in office, Nigeria recorded 13 mass school kidnapping incidents involving 674 students and staff, compared with three incidents involving at least 120 victims during the first three years of former President Muhammadu Buhari’s administration.

That represents a 333 per cent increase in the number of incidents and a 462 per cent increase in the number of victims.

The data also show how the geography of the crisis has changed.

Under Buhari, school abductions expanded from the insurgency-ravaged Northeast into the Northwest, where heavily armed bandit groups began targeting schools on a large scale. Under Tinubu, the threat has continued to spread southwards.

World.title: Police deny report of officers’ deaths in checkpoint crash
World.content:
The police in Akwa Ibom State have denied reports that police officers were killed in a car accident at a checkpoint in Ibesikpo-Asutan Local Government Area.

The police said no police officer was killed or injured in the incident, which occurred on Wednesday, at Ikot Obio Odongo along the Aka-Nung Udoe Road.

The police spokesperson in the state, Timfon John, stated this in a statement sent to PREMIUM TIMES on Saturday.

The clarification followed the circulation of a video on social media claiming that police officers had lost their lives in the crash.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

In the video, a woman can be heard saying, “Everywhere the police are mounting roadblocks,” while another person said, “Roadblocks using tyres had been banned.”

The video showed a silver-coloured vehicle with severe damage to its bonnet, with passers-by gathered around the scene near Nung Udoe Roundabout.

“Happening now in Ibesikpo Asutan Local Government Area, Nung Udoe to be precise, police officers nearly lost their lives,” a Facebook user, Etido Precious, wrote on the social media site.

She added that the driver involved was a lawyer, while questioning the use of roadblocks.

Police account of crash

According to Ms John, a stop-and-search operation was underway at the checkpoint at about 1:40 p.m. when a minibus driven by a man identified as Anietie was stopped.

The police said the minibus was stationary when a Lexus car, allegedly travelling at speed from behind, crashed into it.

“The command categorically states that the claim is false. No police officer lost his or her life, and no police personnel were injured in the incident,” the statement said.

Both vehicles were subsequently taken to a police station for investigation and documentation, according to the command.

The police urged residents to disregard the claim of deaths and avoid circulating unverified information capable of causing panic.

World.title: Nigeria’s fastest man Kanyinsola Ajayi reflects on breakthrough 2026 season
World.content:
Nigeria’s sprint sensation, Kanyinsola Ajayi, has described his 2026 campaign as a season of growth, major victories, and valuable lessons after ending his breakthrough year with a narrow fourth-place finish at the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest.

Ajayi clocked 9.93 seconds in the men’s 100-metre final, the same official time as American Ronnie Baker, who was awarded bronze after the photo finish. Kenny Bednarek won gold in 9.85, while Oblique Seville took silver in 9.90.

Despite missing the podium by just 0.004 seconds, Ajayi, speaking to Making of Champions in Budapest, was satisfied with how he fought through a demanding season.

“It was a good fight. I put in all my effort, I put in my best.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The Nigerian admitted his start was not perfect, but he was proud of his effort.

“I didn’t get my block clearance, but that was a little bit decent. I tried my best. I’m going to take it like that.”

NCAA success set the tone

Ajayi began the season by completing a sprint double at the NCAA Championships, winning the indoor 60m title in 6.45 seconds before claiming the outdoor 100m crown in Eugene.

He clocked a wind-assisted 9.72 seconds (+2.2m/s) in the outdoor final. Although the mark was not legal for record purposes, it underlined his rapid progression.

For Ajayi, the NCAA triumph was one of the biggest highlights of his year.

“Winning the NCAA was the best, also the London Diamond League”

Breaking Fasuba’s Record

The NCAA success was followed by another historic achievement when Ajayi ran 9.84 seconds to break Olusoji Fasuba’s Nigerian 100m record of 9.85.

He subsequently equalled the mark several times and recorded two major victories over reigning world champion Oblique Seville; first at the Prefontaine Classic in Eugene and again at the London Diamond League. Ajayi also broke and then twice equalled the Nigerian record during the season.

The London victory stood out for him.

“The second was the London Diamond League. That was the best.”

Commonwealth Bronze

Ajayi entered the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow as one of the favourites following his victories over Seville.

Cameroon’s Emmanuel Eseme won gold in a Games record 9.83 seconds, Australia’s Lachlan Kennedy took silver in 9.85, while Ajayi finished third in 9.90 to claim bronze.

Although the medal made him Nigeria’s first men’s 100m Commonwealth Games medallist in 20 years, Ajayi had arrived in Glasgow targeting gold.

The experience, however, gave him another taste of the pressure of major championship competition.

New life as professional

After three seasons at Auburn University, Ajayi left collegiate athletics and turned professional, signing a partnership with Adidas in August.

The transition has also exposed him to a new lifestyle, particularly the demands of travelling from one competition to another.

“It’s the first time I’m travelling around the world. It’s so funny, travelling around the world, getting to see people.”

From NCAA competition to the Diamond League, Commonwealth Games and ultimately Budapest, Ajayi repeatedly raced against some of the world’s best sprinters, and he believes those experiences have accelerated his development.

“They helped me a lot, coming from the NCAA, going into the Diamond League, Commonwealth, coming back to the circuit again.”

Budapest Heartbreak

Ajayi reached the 100-metre final in Budapest after running 10.00 seconds in his semifinal before producing 9.93 in the final.

The result left him fourth, just 0.004 seconds behind Baker, but it also marked his 17th sub-10-second performance of the season, underlining the remarkable consistency of his campaign.

The 100-metre field itself featured the reigning world, African, and Commonwealth champions, the European champion, and the reigning NCAA champion.

Ajayi also finished as the fastest African in the final and earned $25,000 for fourth place.

Follow the plan

With the season finally over, Ajayi’s immediate priority is recovery. He believes discipline and sticking to his programme were central to getting through such a long campaign.

“If you follow the plan, if you keep your plan, everything is just going to work out for you.”

Now, he wants to return home, rest and enjoy some time away from competition before turning his attention to 2027.

“Right now I’m going back home to rest, enjoy myself.”

Ajayi eyes the 200m

The Nigerian has also hinted at a potentially exciting change to his programme, revealing that he is considering taking the 200m more seriously.

Ajayi already has a personal best of 20.93 seconds, but some have questioned whether he can become a genuine two-event sprinter.

He is confident those doubts will eventually disappear.

“Many people are doubting, like I can’t run the 200, but yeah, those who don’t see this yet, they’re going to be surprised, I promise.”

Season that changed everything

Ajayi’s 2026 campaign was about far more than his fourth-place finish in Budapest.

He became an NCAA champion, a Nigerian record-holder, and an Adidas professional; defeated the world champion twice; won Commonwealth bronze; and established himself as a consistent sub-10-second sprinter on the global circuit.

He also made history by reaching the podium at the Diamond League Final in Brussels.

Budapest may have ended with disappointment, but missing bronze by four thousandths of a second only reinforced how close Ajayi now is to the very top.

The inaugural Ultimate Championship featured a record $10 million prize fund, with $150,000 available to individual event winners.

Now comes the next challenge: recovering, resetting and finding another level in 2027.

And if Ajayi follows through with his plans for the 200m, Nigeria could have an even more versatile sprint star to watch in the next Olympic cycle.

World.title: Pressure mounts on Sanwo-Olu to reinstate dismissed LASU lecturers, seven years after
World.content:
Seven years after the dismissal of five lecturers at Lagos State University (LASU), there are renewed calls for the state government to reinstate them.

The lecturers, leaders of the Academic Staff Union of Universities (ASUU) in the school, Isaac Oyewumi (chairperson), Adebowale Adeyemi-Suenu (vice-chairperson), Anthony Dansu (secretary), Adeolu Oluwaseyi Oyekan (assistant secretary), and Oluwakemi Aboderin-Shonibare (treasurer), were dismissed during the university governing council’s 122nd meeting on 12 September 2019.

Dubbed ‘LASU Five,’ they were accused of unauthorised removal and dissemination of confidential documents.

However, despite a recommendation by the university’s governing council to reinstate the sacked lecturers, the state government and the university have yet to reinstate them.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Renewed call

The lecturers, in a statement on Saturday, described the waiting period and their dismissal as unjust and renewed their call to the state government to reinstate them unconditionally.

Speaking for the sacked lecturers, Mr Dansu said they carry no bitterness or regret. He said they remain committed to fairness, the truth and justice.

“Some disappointed (in some cases, the least expected persons); others, sent by God, appeared and gave even more than desired support. Such is the mystery of the journey; where men withdraw, Providence sometimes speaks,” he said.

Mr Dansu noted that he is certain that the case “will end in praise.”

“Seven years is not the end of a story. Sometimes, it is merely the silence before the final chapter.”

Refusal to reinstate the lecturers

In February 2022, the David Sunmoni-led Governing Council of the university reinstated the lecturers after an Appeal Committee headed by the Deputy Vice-Chancellor, Adenike Boyo, cleared the lecturers of all offences and recommended their reinstatement.

But in a strange move, 48 hours after the council approved its appeal committee’s recommendation, the same governing council ruled to put the recall of the lecturers on hold.

Over the past seven years, the affected lecturers and various professional associations have staged demonstrations in Lagos to demand their reinstatement. In a 2025 appeal to Lagos State Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu, the Concerned Sons and Daughters of Ikoga-Zebbe Kingdom in Badagry urged him to intervene and “lift the embargo his government placed on the implementation of the decision of the LASU Governing Council on 23 February 2022.”

“…To the effect that our illustrious son Tony Dansu, and other four ASUU-LASU officials that were wrongfully and illegally dismissed from the services of the university in 2017 and 2019 be reinstated unconditionally,” the statement said.

World.title: StarTimes’ Hello Mr Right returns for Season 4
World.content:
Television host Bukunmi Adeaga-Ilori, popularly known as KieKie, and reality TV personality Nelson Enwerem, known as Prince Nelson, will return as hosts of Hello Mr Right as the StarTimes dating reality show introduces new twists in its fourth season.

KieKie will host the programme for a third consecutive season, while Prince Nelson returns as co-host for a second season.

The new season will introduce AI-assisted matchmaking and a role-reversal format in which women take charge of selecting their potential partners.

The season opens with an audition episode on 26 September on ST Nollywood Plus. It will be rebroadcast on 1 October, ahead of the main show’s premiere on 3 October.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Women take charge

The new format, dubbed “The Switch”, reverses the show’s traditional setup, where several women compete for the attention of one man.

“Usually, we would have the girls on the stand and the man in the centre, but this year we have the men on the stand as well, with the woman deciding who she wants from among them,” KieKie said.

Series director Jide Ali said 12 men would compete for one woman under the new format.

“The usual format is that 12 women are vying for one Mr Right, but we reversed it so that 12 men compete for one Miss Right,” he said.

The programme will also deploy AI to assess contestants’ profiles and suggest potential matches.

“We also have an AI segment that matches contestants based on their profiles. AI uses its own assessment to match the lady it considers most compatible with the profile of Mr Right,” Ali explained.

Ali described the new season in one word as “Lambacious.”

Different cast, new dynamics

Prince Nelson said the new contestants bring a different dynamic to the programme.

“The people we have this year, I believe, are more interesting than the people I saw last season,” he said, describing them as outspoken and genuine.

Series producer Rotimi Babalogbon said the casting process was broadened to accommodate contestants from different professions, age groups, backgrounds and body types.

“This season has exceeded my expectations in every aspect,” Babalogbon said.

He said some relationships formed during filming appeared promising, with at least two couples showing potential to continue their relationships after the programme.

KieKie calls for authenticity

Despite the introduction of AI and other format changes, KieKie said contestants would still need honesty and authenticity to build meaningful relationships.

“I just think it’s about being genuine and being real, being authentic, because relationships are one very quick way to expose your flaws,” she said.

“A long-lasting relationship has a lot to do with being honest, and of course, it starts with love,” she added.

StarTimes Marketing Director Oke Umurhohwo said the programme was designed to reflect dating and relationship experiences from a Nigerian perspective.

“Relationships, dating, and the search for companionship are universal experiences, but we wanted something that reflects them through a distinctly Nigerian lens,” Mr Umurhohwo said.

He said the new season would also use social media content and audience engagement to extend conversations around the programme.

“The objective is to make Hello Mr Right more than something people watch. We want it to become something they talk about,” he said.

World.title: One killed, others feared trapped as hotel building collapses in Enugu
World.content:
At least one person was confirmed dead in Enugu State on Sunday after a four-storey hotel building under construction partially collapsed.

The incident, PREMIUM TIMES gathered, occurred at about 5 a.m. at the Independence Layout area.

Apart from the deceased victim, some other people were feared trapped in the rubble.

Speaking with reporters at the scene, Uche Anya, the chairman of the Enugu Capital Territory Development Agency (ECTDA), said four people trapped in the rubble were rescued. In contrast, one other person died in the incident.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“This property collapsed in the early hours of the morning. We arrived here around 6 a.m. When we arrived, we met one of the securitymen, who said that six people were sleeping in the unfinished property, but one of them was not around when the incident occurred.

“So, the government emergency services arrived, and we started rescue operations. Four people, right now, are in the hospital receiving treatment as we speak,” he said.

Mr Anya, a lawyer, said the property owner secured approval to build the structure in 2021.

The chairman, however, said the ECDTA recently sealed the facility after the developer failed to comply with building codes.

“When I led the team that inspected here, we found out that there were serious integrity issues and non-compliance with their 2021 approval.

“I issued the first ‘stop work order,’ which, due to the violation, resulted in our sealing the place over the last six months.

“So, I think within the last 30 to 40 days, the representative of the owner, whom they say lives abroad, has been interfacing with us to remedy the situation,” he recalled.

“This is the process that we are still trying to interface on, and it came down.”

Representative arrested

Mr Anya said he had handed the representative over to the police in Enugu State to assist in the ongoing investigation into the incident

“I have handed the representative to the police, not necessarily for detention, but to help with the investigation. But this is really a very unfortunate situation,” he said.

Fire chief speaks

Also speaking to reporters, the Director of the Enugu State Fire Service, Okwudiri Oha, praised officials of various agencies who assisted in the rescue operation.

“As a rescue officer, what we did was to ask the security man how many people were here. He said that there were supposed to be six. One person had left before it happened.

“So, we were able at that initial time to rescue four persons. Out of the four, two sustained minor injuries and they were all rushed to a health facility for proper checks,” Mr Oha said.

The Information Officer of the National Emergency Management Agency, Ezeani Nnanyelugo, confirmed the number of victims and noted that the situation could have been worse if not for the state government’s earlier sealing of the site.

On her part, the Executive Secretary of the State Emergency Authority, Chinasa Mbah, said that while only five persons were reportedly present at the time of the incident, the entire wreckage would be cut through and excavated to ensure that no one was left behind.

“We are going to excavate everything because you can see the machines that the government brought. We will excavate everything to ensure no survivor or body is left,” she said.

World.title: NDLEA seizes tonnes of cannabis, other drugs in seven states
World.content:
The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) has seized large quantities of cannabis and other illicit drugs in separate operations across seven states, the agency said on Sunday.

The NDLEA’s Director of Media and Advocacy, Femi Babafemi, explained in a statement shared with PREMIUM TIMES on Sunday that the operations took place in Kano, Plateau, Edo, Ondo, Kaduna, Bayelsa and Delta states.

In Edo, the agency noted that its operatives destroyed 4,832.56kg of cannabis, also known as skunk, found on farms in Usen, Igwe-Oke and Ogboha forests.

The farms were in Ovia South West, Owan East and Owan West Local Government Areas. A 39-year-old man, Sunday Segun, was arrested during the operation on Friday.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

In Bayelsa, four people were arrested at Ovom in Yenagoa after 110 bags of cannabis weighing 876kg were recovered, the agency said.

They were identified as Godwoman Gboriye, 70; Motombo Silver, 44; Pere Andrew, 39; and Keme Andrew, 43.

In Kano, operatives raided a location in Sabon Gari and arrested 20-year-old Saidu Adamu with 785,000 capsules of Pregabalin weighing 669.425kg.

Another suspect, Habibu Sabitu, 28, was arrested after NDLEA officers stopped his vehicle along the Zaria-Kano-Hadejia road.

The agency said 1,700 tablets of diazepam were found hidden inside loaves of bread in the vehicle.

In Plateau State, operatives recovered 157,100 capsules of tramadol from Chinedu Uzor, 51, at Katako Market in Jos.

In Ondo State, NDLEA operatives acting on intelligence raided a residence along Oke-Iya, Ijoka Road, Akure, on Wednesday and found 186kg of cannabis in the boot of a Toyota Avalon.

The agency identified the suspect as 58-year-old Paul Ogbuwala and alleged that he was preparing to transport the consignment to Jos for distribution.

In Kaduna, operatives arrested Hannah Michael at Gonin Gora with 369.6kg of cannabis.

Drugs hidden in speakers

In Delta State, separate operations in Ughelli and Asaba led to the recovery of pentazocine injections, codeine syrup, tramadol, diazepam, flunitrazepam, also known as Hypnox, and MDMA, commonly called Molly.

Some of the drugs were hidden inside music speakers, the agency said. Two suspects, Emeka Oji and Chukwuebuka Anedi, were arrested.

The latest seizures come amid a series of major drug interceptions reported by the agency in recent weeks. Last week, the NDLEA stated that it seized 966,200 tablets of Tramadol worth more than N1.1 billion at the Lagos airport.

Also, the agency intercepted 2,145kg of cannabis concealed in a fuel tanker in Ondo State.

During the week, NDLEA stated that its commands carried out drug-abuse sensitisation programmes in schools, worship centres, workplaces and communities.

NDLEA Chairman, Buba Marwa, commended the operatives involved in the operations.

He directed them to keep up efforts to disrupt drug trafficking routes and cannabis cultivation.

He also urged the agency’s formations to maintain surveillance of trafficking routes through airports, seaports, land borders and cannabis-growing areas.

World.title: 2027: Free, fair or not, we’re ready for anything  -  ADC
World.content:
ADC National Publicity Secretary, Bolaji Abdullahi

The African Democratic Congress (ADC) has said it is prepared for any outcome ahead of the 2027 general election, insisting that it is confident of defeating the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) if the election is free and fair.

ADC National Publicity Secretary, Bolaji Abdullahi, stated this during an interview on the Naija Unfiltered Podcast, while responding to whether the opposition party could realistically defeat the incumbent despite the multiplicity of opposition groups.

Abdullahi said the party had no doubt about its chances at the polls but expressed concern over the credibility of the electoral process.

“Yes, we believe so. In a free and fair election, we have no doubt in my mind that we win this election,” he said.

The ADC spokesman said the party was prepared to protect its votes, alleging that the APC would seek to manipulate the 2027 election.

“The challenge is: Will there be a fair and fair election. We are ready for that. We are ready for anything,” Abdullahi said.

He added, “If you are dealing with these APC people, you have to be ready for anything quickly because we know that they want to steal the election. We will police our vote.”

Abdullahi also cited a recent comment attributed to the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike, about the outcome of the Osun State governorship election.

According to him, Wike’s suggestion that he would have delivered Osun for the APC if he were in the state raised questions about the minister and his party’s intention to influence electoral outcomes.

“What does that mean? That regardless of what the Osun people think, you have a way to deliver it. That’s confession,” he said.

The ADC spokesman further alleged that the ruling party had resorted to threats because it had lost the support of Nigerians.

He said, “We know Nigerians have abandoned them. They know Nigerians have abandoned them, and that’s why they are threatening everybody.”

Abdullahi said the ADC was therefore preparing for the 2027 election with the expectation that its supporters and votes would need to be protected throughout the electoral process.

World.title: Yamal shines with brace as Barcelona beat Levante 4-2 to stay perfect
World.content:
Barcelona’s Spanish forward #10 Lamine Yamal celebrates with Barcelona’s Brazilian forward #11 Raphinha and Barcelona’s Spanish midfielder #16 Rodrigo scoring his team’s third goal from the penalty spot during the Spanish league football match between Levante UD and FC Barcelona at Ciutat de Valencia Stadium in Valencia on September 13, 2026. (Photo by JOSE JORDAN / AFP)

Lamine Yamal struck twice to help Barcelona to an exciting 4-2 win at Levante on Sunday in La Liga, extending the Catalans’ perfect start to the season.

Hansi Flick’s side reestablished their three point lead over Real Madrid at the top of the table, after Los Blancos beat Rayo Vallecano on Saturday.

Xavi Espart opened the scoring for the champions in Valencia with Yamal netting the second and then scoring a penalty early in the second half.

Barca may have a 100 percent record so far from their five games but their defensive frailties were exposed as Ivan Romero and Roger Brugue pulled Levante back into the game in the final stages.

Substitute Karim Adeyemi made the game safe for Barca in stoppage time with a stunning solo goal, breaking through at pace and beating Mathew Ryan.

Flick warned Barcelona’s players to keep their focus ahead of the game, lest their sparkling form start to fade, and the Catalans came flying out of the blocks at the Cituat de Valencia stadium.

The visitors took the lead in the fifth minute, with Levante barely touching the ball before Barca defender Espart found the net.

Barca cut through the middle of Levante’s team too easily and the 19-year-old finished from the edge of the box with the help of a slight deflection.

It was Espart’s first goal for the club, with the young midfielder brought into the first team this season by Flick and deployed at left-back.

Levante responded with a spell of concerted pressure and Barca were fortunate to maintain their advantage.

Petar Ratkov could not get a proper shot away when well placed and Barca goalkeeper Joan Garcia saved well from Brugue.

Levante soon came to regret those spurned chances when Raphinha created Barca’s second for teenage star Yamal.

The Brazilian rounded goalkeeper Ryan and squared for Yamal to smash into the empty net in the 19th minute.

Between the afternoon summer heat and some heavy tackles, the pace of the game slowed.

– Paying the penalty –

Yamal claimed his second goal soon after the restart, winning and then converting a penalty.

The Spain winger was hacked down by Aissa Mandi and powered the resulting spot kick past Ryan for his seventh goal in four games across all competitions.

Levante could have pulled one back but Andreas Christensen cleared Romero’s bobbling shot off the line.

The striker did get on the scoresheet when Espart gave the ball away with a loose pass towards Christensen, and Romero nipped in to strike.

Levante fans roared when Brugue capitalised on a Marc Bernal error, with Garcia saving his first shot but the striker able to nudge home the rebound.

However, former Borussia Dortmund winger Adeyemi ended the hosts’ dreams of a point with a dynamic burst through the defence and then a cool finish to match.

Barcelona host promoted side Racing Santander on Wednesday, while Levante welcome Athletic Bilbao.

Earlier on Sunday, Celta Vigo were held to a 1-1 home draw by Malaga. Later, Diego Simeone’s Atletico Madrid visit Real Sociedad and Getafe face Deportivo La Coruna.
