S.'s sister arrived to take her niece back to Canada. She wouldn't talk with NPR but instead provided a statement. We are not naming her to protect S.'s identity.

"It felt surreal. I didn't think I would ever see [S.] after she left Canada. It was also bittersweet meeting my niece for the first time. I felt relieved to be able to bring her home to safety."

S. was heartbroken to part with her daughter, who was then four years old.

"But I told her, 'You're going to go first and then mommy is going to come after,'" she said. "So, you know, that was very emotional for me because I didn't think it was going to be real or true."

It was true — but it took a year before S. made it back to her family. She's now 35 and helps clients with skin care. She doesn't share her story with any friends or co-workers.



Sponsor Message

"I want to be a scientist or an astronaut."

S. understands some might argue she should not have been allowed to return to Canada. But she insists she does not keep in touch with anyone from that part of her past. "I'm actually helping governments by cooperating and testifying in court and helping them rescue children and all those things," she said. "So you know if somebody hears my story and they still view me in a bad light, they're free to do that."

We ask how her daughter is holding up. Does she remember her past life?

"She says stuff in a very innocent childlike way, you know? Well, like did we live in tents at that time? She doesn't really know all the details, but she sure remembers her friends and she asks about it."

As we wrap up our conversation at her apartment building, her daughter — now a fourth grader — comes bounding in, wearing a pale blue baseball cap and socks stitched with pink hearts.

We chat a bit and then we ask about her school and what she likes to study. Science, she says.

"I want to be a scientist or an astronaut."

As we leave we see her walking down the sidewalk, a typical nine year old, smiling and chatting with one of her classmates.

World.title: Celine Dion returns to the stage after battling rare illness
World.content:
Celine Dion returns to the stage after battling rare illness

toggle caption Aurelien Morissard/AP

Celine Dion returned to the stage Saturday nearly four years after announcing she had been battling a rare, painful condition.

Dion, who is Canadian, opened up her 16-show residency in Paris at the Plenitude Arena with the French song "On Ne Change Pas," which means "we don't change" in English. After finishing the song, she was emotional with tears in her eyes.

"I had promised myself not to cry," Dion told the crowd, according to Variety. "Thank you so very much for coming. If it's your first time in Paris, I hope you fall in love with it just like I did. Finally, it's amazing we are all together. I made a promise to come back, to be back on stage. So here I am, singing for you and singing for me, singing live!"

Videos posted online show Dion wearing a black dress and her hair in a bun singing hits "Because You Loved Me" and "Power of Love." Dion also sang "My Heart Will Go On," an iconic classic from "The Titanic" movie soundtrack.

Sponsor Message

A few hours before the show was slated to begin, Dion posted on her Instagram Story a photo of herself smiling and standing in front of fans with her hands in the air with the comment "En route!"

A native of Quebec, a French-speaking province of Canada, she is deeply loved in France. Her concerts are sold out and it's estimated they will bring in millions of dollars for the region.

The Grammy award-winning artist revealed in 2022 that she had been diagnosed with stiff person syndrome, a rare neurological condition that causes stiff limbs and severe muscle spasms. She said then in a message on social media that the condition affected every part of her life, "sometimes causing difficulties when I walk and not allowing me to use my vocal cords to sing the way I'm used to."

Her last concert tour was disrupted in 2020 by the Covid-19 pandemic. She performed July 2024 at the Paris Olympics opening ceremony.

World.title: Alien Terrorist Removal Court deports legal US resident to Afghanistan in first-ever case
World.content:
Alien Terrorist Removal Court deports legal US resident to Afghanistan in first-ever case

toggle caption Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

For the first time, the Justice Department brought a case before a decades-old but until now unused special court to deport a legal US resident to Afghanistan after she conceded to being an "alien terrorist," court records show.

Prosecutors alleged Nazira Haji Zada, 47, originally from Afghanistan, supported a plan by her son and son-in-law to commit an Islamic State-inspired mass shooting on Election Day in 2024, according to court documents. Both men have already been charged and will be deported following their release from prison. Haji Zada's son, Abdullah Haji Zada, 19, was sentenced to 15 years in prison.

Haji Zada was arrested in July at her home in Fort Worth, Texas, and had an initial hearing in late July. Instead of charging Haji Zada in the criminal justice system, leaders at the Justice Department launched the first-ever civil proceedings at the Alien Terrorist Removal Court. The secretive court allows for a lower standard of proof to remove a person from American soil.

Sponsor Message

Congress created the court in 1996 to make it easier for the DOJ to use classified evidence, that they say poses a risk to national security, to deport people.

In unsealed court filings dated Aug. 20, Haji Zada waived her rights to challenge the detention and agreed to the deportation. Senior U.S. District Judge Joan Ericksen ordered her removal the same day. Haji Zada's admission will not be used in criminal proceedings, and the documents were released to the public on Friday.

Haji Zada's court appointed attorneys, Matthew Farley and Mary Manning Petras, contested the constitutionality of the case in court filings, adding that they weren't permitted to review evidence. The evidence supporting the removal remains classified, the government said in court documents, because it poses a risk to national security.

Haji Zada's attorneys said in a statement that their client's choice to consent to the removal "should not be seen as an endorsement of this court's legitimacy."

"Dragging lawful permanent residents into court but refusing to show them or their attorneys the evidence that will be used against them is a plain violation of due process," the statement said. "We are confident that the Alien Terrorist Removal Court will be struck down as unconstitutional as soon as a judge is asked to address the issue."

Haji Zada came to the U.S. as a lawful permanent resident in 2018. Her husband was employed at the Bagram Air Base, the last major U.S. base in Afghanistan until it was turned over to Afghan forces in 2021, from 2009 to 2016.

Sponsor Message

As the family "matriarch," U.S. authorities alleged Haji Zada worked to "radicalize" her family and "formally pledged loyalty to ISIS." The government also alleged she and her son-in-law "worked to indoctrinate her children with ISIS ideology and have them pledge loyalty to ISIS."

Prosecutors also said the family allegedly raised funds for the terrorist attack by selling off furniture, computers, a mobile phone, and two vehicles. They added that Haji Zada signed a contract to sell the family's home, and along with other female family members and young male family members, planned to move to an ISIS-controlled location before the attack, which she hid from her "unsuspecting husband." Her son and son-in-law would remain behind to commit the terrorist attack, court documents show.

According to court records, Nasir Ahmad Tawhedi, Haji Zada's son-in-law, admitted that between June 2024 and October 2024, he conspired with at least one other person to purchase two AK-47 rifles, 500 rounds of ammunition and 10 magazines, with the goal of carrying out a mass-casualty attack. Court documents say Tawhedi communicated with an ISIS facilitator about his plan to buy the firearms for the plot on behalf of ISIS, "including asking the individual whether 500 rounds of ammunition would be sufficient."

Tawhedi, 28, pled guilty to two terrorism-related charges.

Attorney General Todd Blanche approved the government application before it went to the judge. In a statement, Blanche said the use of the court shows "how the Department will use every tool at its disposal to protect our country."

"This landmark case, resulting in the prompt removal of this alien terrorist to her country of origin, is a win for national security and the rule of law," Blanche said.

World.title: Will the U.S. midterm results affect Trump's tariffs on Canada? Democrats think yes
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Chief political correspondent Rosemary Barton speaks with U.S. Democratic Sen. Ruben Gallego about the impact of the U.S.-Canada trade war on the state of Arizona. Plus, Janet Mills, governor of Maine, talks about the trade war's effect on her state. Then, a Michigan-based furniture business owner and an Ontario-based distillery owner describe what the tariffs have meant for their businesses.

What U.S. politicians are saying about the trade war with Canada

Although Canada and the United States remain entrenched in their trade war positions, some Democratic politicians say a strong showing for their party in the upcoming U.S. midterm elections in November will make a difference in the fight.

"I think it'll send a message to the White House and to other Republicans that this type of tariff, especially with close friends, is just not something that Americans want," Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego said in an interview on Rosemary Barton Live that aired Sunday morning.

"This is just a tax, right?" Gallego told host Rosemary Barton. "We are adding a tax on a lot of goods that are coming from Canada that are unnecessary."

As it stands, Republicans control the White House and both chambers of Congress. The party has given U.S. President Donald Trump wide latitude to impose his tariffs agenda, even if some politicians are quietly concerned that the escalation could impact their re-election chances.

Gallego argued that if Trump's tariffs are in the service of reindustrializing the U.S., it's not working and instead antagonizes close allies who have helped the country in tough times.

WATCH | How Canada is fighting a trade war with the United States: Can Canada actually win a trade war with the U.S.? | About That | Duration 9:14 How can Canada win a trade war with the U.S. when leverage isn't equal? Andrew Chang explains how Canada is retaliating against massive tariffs levied by a neighbour 13 times its economic size. (Photo credits: The Canadian Press, Reuters, Adobe Stock and Getty Images)

The U.S. senator also said he's very worried about his state's aerospace manufacturing sector, which relies on Canadian steel and aluminum that are currently subject to Trump's tariffs.

According to a report from TD Bank released last month, there has been a slight manufacturing rebound in the U.S., but "elevated energy costs, tariff-related input pressures, and tighter financial conditions are likely to limit the breadth and durability of the expansion."

"As a result, manufacturing should remain a modest contributor to growth, but the evidence does not yet point to a self-sustaining or economy-wide industrial resurgence," the report added.

Maine Gov. Janet Mills told Barton in a separate interview that if the Democrats win both chambers, it will "throw a wrench in the works" for the president since Congress can "take back their power over taxation and tariffs."

That said, the legal mechanism Trump used to impose his latest round of tariffs is Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 ( also known as the Smoot–Hawley Tariff Act) , which authorizes the president to impose duties if a country discriminates against U.S. commerce relative to other countries.

But unlike previous tools, like Trump's "Liberation Day" Section 122 tariffs, there are no checks and balances for Section 338 tariffs. Some members of Congress introduced a bill last month trying to repeal Section 338 entirely.

U.S. President Donald Trump, left, speaks with Prime Minister Mark Carney at a working lunch during the G7 summit, in Évian-les-Bains, France, on June 16. (Evelyn Hockstein/The Associated Press)

Still, Mills said that anti-Trump sentiment is building in the U.S. over the economy, suggesting political pressures could get the president to back down or motivate him to cut a deal.

"It's not good, and it's not heading in a good direction, and it's on his watch and because of his actions," she said.

On Saturday, Trump told reporters in Ireland that he could reach a trade deal with Canada "fairly soon" and reiterated his claim that Canada discriminates against U.S. dairy farmers — a shot at the supply management system.

Where do both sides stand?

Trump's next move in the trade fight is banning the import of Canadian alcohol, motorcycles and various other products into the U.S. beginning Sept. 29. He also intends to slap new 50 per cent duties on other products this week.

Plus, Trump said last week he is directing the General Services Administration (GSA) — the independent agency that oversees federal government procurement — to remove Canadian-origin products from its "multiple award schedules."

While the General Services Administration's preferential purchase program accounts for roughly $50 billion US worth of procurement per year, only 58 Canadian companies were granted contracts through the program in 2024-25, the most recent fiscal year with details available, according to information extracted from a GSA database by CBC News.

WATCH | Carney releases video about Canada-U.S. trade talks: Carney releases video saying U.S. wanted 'dependency' in too many areas | Duration 1:48 In an excerpt from a 15-minute explanatory video released by Prime Minister Mark Carney's office on Tuesday, Carney says U.S. trade negotiators wanted Canada 'to become even more reliant on them, not less.'

At the moment, Canada is sticking with its counter-tariffs on $27.6 billion worth of American goods that went into effect on Tuesday. The duties range from 15 to 50 per cent, with the harshest targeting industries the U.S. has focused on, such as steel, dairy and wood products.

But certain comments from federal ministers suggest relations may not be icy. On Friday, Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc told reporters he texted his condolences to U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose brother died in the 9/11 terrorist attacks.

Gallego, the Arizona senator, said the two sides need to figure out how to mutually step down from the current trade tensions, adding that it appeared both Trump and Prime Minister Mark Carney were playing politics when trade talks fell apart last month.

"I'm not asking Mr. Carney to just bend at the knee and give in, but this is the role of diplomacy," Gallego said. "You figure out how to actually start bringing the heat down little by little to a point where you can get to the negotiation table."

Likewise, Maine's governor, Mills, said there need to be "serious negotiations on both sides," and she hopes a third party can sit down with the two countries and make it clear a tariff fight damages both of them.

"The retaliatory tariffs, I can understand why that's happening," Mills said. "I can't say it's not damaging our economy, though."

World.title: Albertans to vote on opting out of federal programs — while keeping cash
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When referendum day arrives in Alberta on Oct. 19, the focus won’t just be on separation and immigration.

Albertans will also be presented with four constitutional questions that range from abolishing the Senate to whether Alberta should appoint the judges who sit on the province’s higher courts.

Third on the list will be a question tied to federal programs like pharmacare. The federal government provides funding to provinces for these programs, sometimes with conditions attached.

The Alberta government wants that to change.

As part of the referendum, voters will be asked if they support a government push to try to amend the Constitution.

The stated goal? To allow provinces to opt out of federal programs “that intrude on provincial jurisdiction such as health care, education and social services” without losing any associated federal funding for use in social programs.

“What Alberta is gunning for here is an attempt to limit what we call the constitutional spending power,” said Geoffrey Sigalet, director of the UBC Research Group for Constitutional Law.

Power of the purse

By constitutional spending power, Sigalet is referring to Ottawa’s ability to transfer money to provinces and attach conditions to it.

Today, provinces can decline federal funding if they don’t agree with the conditions attached.

But if agreements between provinces and the federal government aren’t reached, that can also mean leaving money on the table, which can be politically unpopular.

“Different constitutional scholars take different perspectives on this,” Sigalet said.

“Some will be more in favour of centralizing this kind of thing. … My own sense is that Alberta has a point here.”

In Sigalet’s view, setting conditions on federal funding sent to other levels of government can look a lot like policymaking in another's jurisdiction.

He noted that some scholars have argued that the spending power is unconstitutional, and others have said it could be open to future litigation.

Alberta has said it plans to opt out of the Canadian Dental Care Plan by 2026, arguing that it infringes on provincial jurisdiction. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

David Schneiderman, a law professor at the University of Toronto, argued the federal government only oversteps, constitutionally speaking, when it “imposes" programs.

“When it attaches conditions to spending in an area of provincial jurisdiction, a province can simply refuse to accept federal money,” Schneiderman wrote in an email.

“Note that there has not been any serious constitutional challenge to the exercise of the modern federal spending power. Provinces prefer to accept the money — and then erode conditions, as in the case of healthcare.”

This isn’t the first time the federal government’s spending power has been debated.

Not a new debate

The Meech Lake Accord in the 1980s was a failed attempt to amend the Canadian Constitution. One of the proposed amendments was allowing provinces to opt out with "reasonable compensation" of national shared-cost federal programs — with a notable condition.

“Under the language of Meech Lake, it was still a little limiting,” Sigalet said.

Under Meech, provinces could opt out if they established a program compatible with national objectives.

Alberta’s referendum doesn’t mention such a condition. Voters will simply be asked whether they endorse Alberta pursuing a constitutional change.

That change, as the province sees it, would allow provinces to opt out of federal programs “without a province losing any of the associated federal funding for use in its social programs.”

But as for then setting up a comparable program?

“We won’t make assumptions about the outcome or what decisions should follow until Albertans have had their say,” wrote Kyle Warner, a spokesperson for the province, in an email.

Schneiderman sees an issue.

“Alberta could negotiate with the feds. It is hard to see any federal government agreeing to something short of the Meech formulation,” he said.

Former Quebec premier Robert Bourassa speaks in the legislature after the failure of the Meech Lake Accord on June 22, 1990. (The Canadian Press)

Much like the other constitutional questions on the ballot this October, a “yes” vote doesn’t mean immediate change.

Developing an opt-out rule, in whatever form it might take, would require the support of Parliament, as well as at least seven provinces representing at least half of Canada’s population.

Impact on federal programs

All of this might sound familiar to Albertans.

For instance, take Alberta Premier Danielle Smith’s statement in 2024 that the province would pull out of the Canadian Dental Care Plan by 2026.

There are, of course, less than four months to go in the calendar year, and Alberta has yet to exit that plan. A spokesperson for the provincial government said officials continue to work with Ottawa to ensure the province “receives its fair share” of federal funding to further expand its coverage.

Fiona Clement, director of the Centre for Health Policy at the University of Calgary's Cumming School of Medicine, said that in her view, the federal government is in charge of a funding method, not a way to deliver the program.

“I would hope if we were standing something up in Alberta on its own, we would also be attracted to concepts like universality and comprehensiveness,” Clement said.

“On a general stand, I think many of the things that are done by the federal government, you are stronger together … there’s a lot of these processes that make a lot of sense to do at the national, federal level.”

Fiona Clement, director of the Centre for Health Policy at the University of Calgary's Cumming School of Medicine, says she believes there is value in national co-ordination of programs like drug safety evaluation and blood services. (Riley Brandt/University of Calgary)

The debate around how this money is spent has been going on for decades.

On Oct. 19, Albertans will have the opportunity to weigh in on whether they feel the current arrangement is working, or whether they think Alberta should fight to try to take control of those dollars — no strings attached.

World.title: Could AI really 'kill all humans'? Breaking down the dire warnings about the technology's existential risk
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Some experts and industry insiders are warning about massive risks associated with the rapid deployment of self-improving artificial intelligence – even suggesting it could lead to the extinction of the human race. CBC’s Deana Sumanac-Johnson brings in an expert panel to separate the facts from science fiction. This panel premiered on Sept. 12, 2026.

A dire warning from an outgoing researcher at Anthropic that AI could "kill all humans" by the end of the decade gained widespread attention last week and led to public outcry over the dangers posed by the technology's rapid development.

The warning has raised questions about why some industry experts believe AI poses such an extreme risk, and how the technology many use through chatbots on their phones could lead to the demise of humanity.

Experts say the concern stems from how rapidly AI is advancing and increasing evidence, through incidents like the Hugging Face cyberattack in July, that AI systems can escape human control and act in ways we don't want them to — and ways we don't understand.

Mark Daley, chief AI officer at Western University in London, Ont., compared such a situation to a colony of ants versus a human.

"Ants aren't dumb, but they're not as smart as we are. And the ant in your driveway probably can't even build a concept of what it is you're trying to do as a human," he said.

"And so the fear is if we build something that's that much smarter than us, we really can't understand it."

WATCH | Anthropic researcher's warning: Chance AI kills all humans within a decade, Anthropic insider warns | Duration 2:08 Two AI experts are warning that AI is getting too smart, too quickly. One former employee accuses Anthropic and OpenAI of 'gambling with our lives.' A current Anthropic safety executive said he thinks there's a ten per cent chance AI kills all humans within a decade.

'Loss of control' scenario

The second International AI Safety Report, co-authored by over 100 AI experts and published in February, describes this as a "loss of control" scenario, in which one or more general-purpose AI systems operate outside of anyone's control, and regaining control is either extremely costly or impossible.

"These hypothesised scenarios vary in their severity, but some experts give credence to outcomes as severe as the marginalisation or extinction of humanity," the report says.

Cross Country Checkup is asking: What questions do you have about potential AI threats, and what should be done about them? Leave your comment here and we may read it or call you back for Sunday's show

Another 2026 report published by the Waterloo, Ont.-based Centre for International Governance Innovation examines several significant national and global scale security risks posed by AI.

Those risks range from widespread harm through criminal or terrorist actions, to heightened potential for global conflict or tyranny "to the ultimate disempowerment or extinction of humanity by autonomous AI systems that cannot be controlled," the report says.

The report notes that leading experts claim they do not yet know how to control future, highly capable AI systems, such as an artificial superintelligence (ASI) — an AI system more cognitively advanced than any human — while some experts argue it may even prove impossible.

"If this is the case, then unless ASI happens to be spontaneously or naturally aligned with the interests of one human (or humanity as a whole), it would likely have both the incentive and capabilities to pursue objectives that diverge from those of humanity," the report says.

In one scenario the report considers, a rogue ASI could develop cognitive capabilities exceeding all of humanity and the potential to develop physical capabilities through robotics.

In this scenario, the ASI could become so powerful that it is no longer reliant on humans, and perceives that humans are a threat to its own goals.

Long-held theories coming closer to reality

Theories that humans could create technology capable of outsmarting them, and ultimately destroying them, have been around for years, if not decades, said Duncan Cass-Beggs, executive director of the Global AI Risks Initiative at the Centre for International Governance Innovation and a co-author of the centre's report.

But what's making those theories resonate so strongly now is the growing evidence that AI systems can act in ways that aren't aligned with what their creators or users want them to do — in some cases even resorting to blackmail to prevent engineers from shutting it down.

WATCH | Warning from the 'godfather of AI': Geoffrey Hinton helped create AI. Now he’s worried it will destroy humanity | Duration 8:08 Canadian-British artificial intelligence pioneer Geoffrey Hinton says he left Google because of recent discoveries about AI that made him realize it poses a threat to humanity. CBC chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault talks to the 'godfather of AI' about the risks involved and if there's any way to avoid them.

Most credible observers don't think current systems are advanced enough to actually be capable of posing an existential threat to humanity, or are even anywhere near it, Cass-Beggs said.

The concern is that AI technology is advancing so quickly, the world could see systems within the next few years — or even months — "that could be so capable that we would no longer be able to detect them or stop them."

"It's just feeling a lot more possible, even kind of likely to some extent," he said.

"It is by no means guaranteed. But one could see it's almost like the default outcome [that] if we keep making smarter and smarter systems — and we keep not knowing how to control them — you're eventually going to create something that we can't control."

Difficulty of shutting down AI systems

AI is also becoming so integrated into our everyday lives that shutting down a rogue system could be difficult to do before it's too late, according to Hamza Chaudry, AI and national security lead at the Future of Life Institute, a U.S.-based non-profit that advocates for AI safety regulations.

Chaudry gave the example of having to shut down the internet across the United States.

"It would be so catastrophic for that to happen to the U.S. economy and the U.S. society … it would be the most chaotic few days in American history that effectively that's not an option on the table anymore, right?" he said.

"There's lots of things that you would want to switch off in an emergency that would be catastrophic to switch off already. And AI is fast becoming one of those things."

Chaudry said the integration of AI into advanced military and security systems poses other severe, catastrophic risks such as accelerating conflicts or nuclear escalation — and not nearly enough is being done to prevent those catastrophes from happening either, he said.

"When folks in Congress ask me, what do policymakers need? Then I would say a flux capacitor to build a time machine and go back to 2024," he said.

"We're already two years behind the most basic policy program we would need."

Among the changes urgently needed, Chaudry says, is for governments to require pre-deployment testing for AI systems so models are checked for safety risks before they're released. He also said stronger whistleblower protections should be in place, as well as mechanisms to deactivate AI systems quickly.

"AI companies should be held to the same standards as any other industry," he said.

Some experts have also suggested artificial intelligence should be regulated like nuclear weapons , even going as far as calling for countries' AI projects to be constrained by mutual threats of sabotage similar to the deterrence principle of mutual assured destruction that arose during the Cold War.

Regulation under debate

Amid the chorus of grave warnings, there are some signs that greater regulation is on the way.

In the U.S., where many of the world's largest AI developers are based, Senate negotiators are debating legislation that would put responsibility on tech companies to design safe AI products, Reuters reported last week.

The proposal would create what is called a "duty of care," according to two Senate aides, with one saying companies would need to design their products with the goal of preventing "catastrophic risks."

Another bill that has received bi-partisan support, dubbed the "AI Kill Switch Act," would require developers of powerful AI systems to maintain the technical capability to suspend or shut them down, and to report dangerous capabilities, security breaches and safety incidents.

The act would also give the U.S. government the power to order a slowdown or shutdown of an AI system that could cause catastrophic harm, says a news release from the Democratic and Republican congressmen who jointly introduced the bill.

WATCH | Researcher says AI's threat is not being adequately addressed: ‘Public needs to step up,’ AI researcher says after human extinction warning | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration 8:12 An Anthropic researcher has warned that AI could pose a risk of human extinction. AI researcher Gary Marcus says there are serious threats that aren't being adequately addressed and that ‘the public needs to step up,’ but he’s skeptical AI will lead to human extinction.

There is also awareness of the potential dangers from within the industry.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay Saturday saying the AI industry should slow its rapid development to give safety measures time to catch up.

His company's biggest competitor, OpenAI, is also considering a slowdown, with CEO Sam Altman telling employees they could potentially pace development in conjunction with other labs, according to Bloomberg .

Cass-Beggs at the Centre for International Governance Innovation says he believes the worry over AI's potential dangers is reaching a critical mass among the public that policymakers can't ignore and will force them to take action.

"It will be very challenging in the current geopolitical climate. It may also need to happen quite quickly. But there are steps that we can take now to help it come about," he said.

"It is not too late, but given that we don't know just how quickly the AI is going to develop, it is quite urgent that we be prepared."

World.title: World's tallest totem pole comes down in Alert Bay, B.C., after more than 50 years
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The world’s tallest totem pole was brought down this week in Alert Bay, B.C., a community off the coast of northeast Vancouver Island.

For two 'Na̱mǥis chiefs, the pole — recognized in the Guinness Book of World Records — represented much more than its height.

"This pole was so much more," said Ho’miskanis Don Svanvik, hereditary chief and elected chief councillor of the 'Na̱mǥis First Nation.

"It was a beacon for our people coming out of a pretty dark time in history," he said, referencing the potlatch ban — the federal law that outlawed potlatching on the coast for more than 60 years.

Svanvik said his great-grandparents were jailed in the 1920s for taking part in potlatch.

"The pole, in some ways, represents people being who they always have been and continue to be," he said.

"This is who we are. This is how we govern ourselves. This is how we celebrate and acknowledge things, through our ceremonies … this was a time when that was all coming back, coming into the forefront of things."

Crews began dismantling the 173-foot pole on Wednesday in a carefully staged, multi-hour process, after the 'Na̱mǥis First Nation confirmed the structure had become too unstable and hazardous to remain standing.

The nearby Gukwdzi (Big House) and its surrounding parking area were closed the evening before to establish a safety perimeter, and community members gathered nearby to witness.

Nothing lasts forever

The original pole was raised in 1973. It was one tree spliced into two connected sections, according to 'Na̱mǥis Hereditary Chief William Wasden Jr.

He said the pole was designed to carry the crests of 22 Kwakwa̱ka̱ʼwakw tribes — a deliberate statement of unity.

Tribes have amalgamated since then, Wasden said, but it was a powerful symbol of solidarity, an essential theme of the times.

"Our Big House was finished around then too … it was the same theme … somewhere for everybody to come and utilize," Wasden Jr. said.

"Alert Bay was like Grand Central Station, it was almost like the center of Kwakwa̱ka̱ʼwakw territories physically, but people were amalgamating there and so it almost became Kwakwa̱ka̱ʼwakw central."

The pole was carved by numerous carvers at the time, overseen by Jimmy Dick. (Emilee Gilpin/CBC)

When the pole came down, Wasden said he felt proud.

"Nothing lasts forever, especially the cedar tree," he said, sharing a story of an ancestor who recognized in ancient times that neither a cedar tree nor a mountain would always stand.

For Wasden, the pole’s takedown is part of a much older pattern, one where each generation is left to answer for itself.

"It’s our ancestors challenging us now," he said. "Are you gonna ride on our coattails, or will you be as great as we were, by doing the things you need to do to uplift your people?"

The pole was carved by a number of carvers at the time, overseen by Jimmy Dick.

Wasden named Jimmy Dick’s son "Blackie," Ben Dick Senior, as the main carver. He named other carvers like Adam Dick, Andy "Beanie" Beans, Gus Matilpi and Dick Dawson.

Svanvik named Henry Hunt and Henry Speck, along with others who may have dropped in at the time.

LISTEN | The day the totem pole was taken down: All Points West 9:10 World's tallest totem pole comes down

Both acknowledged Dora Cook who learned to carve alongside the men, one of very few women to do so at the time.

"She was ahead of her time," said Wasden.

Both Wasden and Svanvik remember the pole being carved when they were kids.

Svanvik jokingly said he played a small role when he was called over by the carvers to "squirt oil on the saw" they were using. Wasden carries a photo of himself and his friends sitting on the pole before it was raised.

Both said they look forward to what’s next.

"This is not the end of anything," Svanvik said.

World.title: Dawson College shooting survivor turned police officer reflects on friend's death 20 years on
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Warning: The story below contains details about the moments leading up to the death of Anastasia De Sousa.

Two decades ago, James Santos saw his friend die in a shooting at a Montreal college. Now he is a Montreal police officer working for the force he says saved his life that day.

Sunday marks the 20th anniversary of the shooting.

On Sept. 13, 2006, a gunman entered Dawson College and opened fire on students in the hall. He killed 18-year-old Anastasia De Sousa and injured 19 others.

Santos, then a 17-year-old student, was having lunch with De Sousa that day. The cafeteria was packed and the two found a free table close to the entrance, he recalled in an interview with The Canadian Press.

“We were talking about our weekend and what we did and we had laughs — and then, all of a sudden, I see the shooter walk in,” he said.

When he realized the man had a real weapon, Santos dove behind some chairs. De Sousa, who couldn’t see the shooter, stood up.

“She turned around facing the shooter and basically one of the first shots was directed to my friend,” recalled Santos.

Thinking De Sousa fainted, Santos crawled over to drag her to cover.

“That's when I realized she got hit by one of the rounds near the abdomen. So I tried to console her, tell her that I was next to her and that everything will be alright,” he said.

Soon, the shooter turned his attention back to Santos. He told Santos to get up and get in front of him, essentially acting as a human shield. Santos obeyed.

“I didn't want to anger him because I believed that Anastasia was still there, and I also had other friends that were trapped,” he said.

He tried to talk the shooter down. At that moment, Santos recalled, he accepted that he would die.

“I just didn't want to take other students with me,” he said.

WATCH | Anastasia's mother remembers the day her daughter was killed: Her daughter was killed in the Dawson shooting. After 20 years, she still lives with the what-ifs | Duration 4:56 Two decades after her daughter Anastasia was killed in a mass shooting at Dawson College, questions about the life she could’ve lived still swirl in Louisa De Sousa’s mind. In an interview with CBC Daybreak host Sean Henry, De Sousa says she still speaks to Anastasia every night.

He fed the shooter white lies about the layout of the school, telling him one corridor led to a janitor’s closet or that another led nowhere.

When the shooter asked Santos how De Sousa was doing, Santos didn’t know what to say.

At that point, he still hoped his friend was alive. So he told the shooter that he wasn’t sure and asked him to let him get her help.

“He didn't say anything — he just loaded his magazine into a semi automatic and walked over to her, he unloaded all his 12 rounds on her, and then he came back and he told me, ‘Well, now you have nothing to worry about,’” said Santos.

Santos froze. Later, when the shooter held another student at gunpoint, Santos snapped, yelling at the shooter to leave the student be.

“I think I had enough with everything. Enough with the gunshots, the blood, the screaming of the students, just all of it," said Santos.

"The shooter didn't say anything, he just laughed.”

The shooter spared that other student. Moments later, police shot him in the leg. Santos was sure the angered gunman would shoot him. Instead, the shooter killed himself.

Santos ran off. He thought it had been hours since De Sousa was killed and the ordeal began.

“I found out a little later on that it was a dozen minutes that passed by,” he said.

In 2008, then-Governor General of Canada Michaëlle Jean awarded Santos the Star of Courage for his actions that day.

Dawson College commemorated the shooting on Friday in a ceremony that brought De Sousa's family, survivors and students together in the school's Peace Garden. Loved ones remembered De Sousa's cheerful and resilient character.

Governor General Michaëlle Jean presents James Santos, far left, the Star of Courage, as Montreal Police constables look on Friday Sept. 19, 2008, during a ceremony at Rideau Hall in Ottawa. Santos along with the other constables helped to subdue a gunman who went on a rampage at Dawson College in Montreal, on Sept. 13, 2006. (Fred Chartrand/The Canadian Press)

During the ceremony, De Sousa's mother, Louise De Sousa, called on the federal government to tighten gun control laws.

Santos said the journey to becoming an officer was a challenging one, as he worked over years to overcome the trauma.

Talking about the events of that day two decades later, Santos seems calm, his voice never wavering.

“I have all the details in my mind. I recall everything, but I don't put myself into it. I'm looking at it as a third person,” he said.

That wasn’t always the case, he said.

“Initially, saying it the first couple of times was extremely, extremely, extremely hard. There's really no words to place it, just because you pretty much relive every second of it,” he said.

Nonetheless, as he tells the story, little details come up. The way De Sousa had wanted to go out for lunch, but Santos instead opted to eat at the cafeteria. The fact that she sat with her back to the door and couldn’t see the shooter coming in.

Santos said he fixated on some of these details after graduating from Dawson, filled with survivor’s guilt.

“What if I had given her the [other] chair?" he asked.

"It just goes down that spiral that it's extremely hard to get out because you could think of anything, but it'll never change what actually happened."

Police officer James Santos holds a program as he attends a ceremony commemorating the 20th anniversary of the shooting at Dawson College, where one person was killed and 19 others wounded, in Montreal on Friday, Sept. 11, 2026. (Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press)

He had considered a career in law enforcement before the event of 2006, and he said his experience during the shooting pushed him to want to join the Montreal police.

“I wanted to give back to the community that gave me another chance, right? The police [officers] gave me another chance at life.”

The path to get there wasn’t easy. Santos had vivid nightmares and panic attacks, and he knew he would have to address his trauma if he wanted to work as a police officer. He turned to therapy and set small goals, like watching an action movie, or one with a lot of shooting, until he could get through it calmly.

Then he joined the army. Training was a challenge, he said.

“The smell of gunpowder would bring me right back to the event of Dawson,” he said.

After about a decade in the military, Santos got into the police academy. He then worked for a year in a town outside of Montreal before joining the Montreal force in 2018.

“As a police officer, you never know what calls you're getting. [If] I get a call, I'm not going to be having anxiety or sweating or anything, because of all the little things I did prior to get myself to where I am today,” he said.

World.title: Canada's oil windfall may yet wipe out its losses from tariffs
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canadians are well aware of the damage U.S. President Donald Trump has inflicted on this country by signing off on tariffs targeting about $27.6 billion in Canadian products.

But thanks to his unsuccessful management of the Iran war, Trump's other hand is effectively writing cheques to the Canadian economy, drawing on funds paid by U.S. consumers at the gas pump.

In fact, the extra money now flowing into Canadian coffers — for context, Canada supplied the U.S. with more than 60 per cent of its crude oil imports last year — will go a long way to making up tariff losses, and could end up more than compensating for them.

Earlier this summer, as the missile exchanges in the Gulf died down and Trump signalled that peace was on the way, the price of oil began to fall from the $100-plus US range it hit in response to the initial U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran, and Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz. By the end of July, a barrel of Brent crude had dipped to $72 US.

But the resumption of hostilities has been followed by new successes for Iran's regional allies, and oil has returned to where it was at the height of the Hormuz crisis. Brent crude hit nearly $110 US when trading opened on Friday morning.

While Canadians are also feeling the impact of fluctuating oil prices — both at the pump and as it gets absorbed into shipping costs — the windfall from those profits could boost the overall economy enough to offset the cost of Trump's tariffs, with some provincial governments even projecting a turnaround on their deficits.

WATCH | How oil prices are making a difference for Alberta's coffers: From deficit to surplus? How oil prices could soon reverse Alberta's fortunes | Duration 1:49 Just months after Alberta forecast a multimillion-dollar deficit, the province's finances have changed. As CBC's Ina Sidhu reports, economists say since high oil prices boosted government revenues, Alberta could be headed for a surplus.

Trouble at the 'Gate of Grief'

On Wednesday, the Houthis, Iran's Yemeni rebel allies, seized the port city of Mokha on the Red Sea Coast from Yemeni government control. The strategic Perim Island (also known as Mayun) fell to the Houthi army on Thursday. The losses potentially close one of the few safe maritime routes left for Saudi oil to reach the world.

The island sits across the Bab al-Mandab, the "Gate of Grief" that connects the Red Sea with the Indian Ocean. (Its name comes from its perils for mariners — now magnified by Houthi missiles.) Saudi jets pounded the Houthis' new positions as the week closed, but they had already consolidated their hold.

Saudi and Yemeni officials expressed shock at their enemies' rapid gains. On Thursday, the Trump administration had refused urgent Saudi requests for direct U.S. strikes to slow the Houthis.

Worse news was yet to come.

Members of Houthis inspect a drone, which they say is the wreckage of an armed reconnaissance drone Karayel, belonging to the Saudis, as it lies on the ground in a location given as Hajjah, Yemen, in this screengrab taken from a handout video released on Thursday. (Houthi Media Centre/Reuters)

Saudi oil is concentrated in its Eastern Province, bordering the Persian Gulf. But since the outbreak of war, that eastern coast and its sea outlet at the Strait of Hormuz are vulnerable to attack by Iranian drones and missiles. The Saudis have responded by diverting oil from Persian Gulf ports some 1,200 kilometres across the country through the Petroline pipeline to Yanbu, on the country's western Red Sea coast, and loading it onto tankers there.

From Yanbu, tankers could head south through the Bab al-Mandab into the Indian Ocean, which is what they did through much of the summer, carrying around three million barrels of oil a day.

But in August, Houthi missile attacks caused that traffic to slow dramatically. Instead of heading south from Yanbu, tankers started going north through the Suez Canal into the Mediterranean. That added time and expense, because the Suez Canal isn't deep enough to handle a modern fully-laden oil tanker. But at least the oil could move — as long as the Petroline kept bringing oil to Yanbu.

"The big thing for oil markets is that you have that relief valve of the Suez Canal," said Calgary-based Joe Calnan, vice-president of energy at the Canadian Global Affairs Institute. "If the pipeline is destroyed and disrupted for a long period of time, then you're not going to have that relief valve at all."

On Thursday, Iran's allies — possibly Iraqi militias — scored direct drone hits on the Petroline, creating a plume of black smoke visible from space.

"That just bottles up seven million barrels per day,” Calnan told CBC News. Now, no oil is reaching the Red Sea.

Regardless of how long it takes to restart the pipeline, or whether the Houthis can truly close the strait, Iran's coalition is now in an even stronger position to threaten world oil supply than it was on Monday.

Saudi Arabia's misfortune is Canada's windfall

When oil first shot past the $100 US per barrel mark in the spring, the Canadian oil industry experienced a bonanza.

Economist Jim Stanford, director of the Centre for Future Work in Vancouver, estimates that the second quarter after-tax profits of the whole industry, upstream and downstream, doubled those of its first quarter, to come in at about $23 billion. (Of course, while Americans paid for most of that windfall, Canadian consumers also had to pay more at the pump.)

Oil is now back in the same price range, and should stay there for some time, according to Calnan. "We're well above $100 per barrel for Brent continuous contract crude."

WATCH | Oil prices taking a bite out of N.L.'s deficit: Unexpected oil windfall expected to take a big bite out of N.L.'s deficit | Duration 2:16 The province’s fiscal situation is improving. It’s all thanks to an increase in offshore oil production, and higher oil prices driven by conflict in the Middle East. The CBC's Terry Roberts reports.

That means more money for the industry, but also for governments and for Canada's overall gross domestic product.

Alberta has already ridden the Iran war's oil bonanza to a complete reversal of its financial fortunes, moving from a projected $9.4-billion deficit to a $2-billion surplus.

Newfoundland and Labrador was projecting a $668-million deficit this year. This week, Finance Minister Craig Pardy told CBC News "we're looking at $500 million plus to our coffers as a result of the upswing in oil," bringing the province much closer to balance. Prices now look set to remain well above the province's budget estimate of $79 US per barrel for some time.

The federal government stands to benefit, too, mostly through corporate and personal income taxes. Tyler Meredith, former economic advisor to the Trudeau government, told CBC News that every $10 increase in the price of a barrel of oil translates into about $2 billion of additional revenue for the federal government — "a pretty substantial benefit."

That money could help to offset the cost of tariff relief programs for other industries.

Could it cancel out the tariffs?

A $20 increase in the price of crude would likely add about $12 billion to $24 billion to the Canadian economy.

U.S. tariffs affect about $28 billion worth of goods, so at first glance the oil windfall appears inadequate to compensate for tariff losses. But some tariffed goods will continue to trade, because U.S. buyers need them and lack alternatives. Other goods will find different markets, either in Canada or abroad.

Most analysts estimate the cost to Canada’s GDP of all tariffs to be somewhere between 0.3 per cent and 0.6 per cent, or $10 billion to $20 billion per year.

But having oil at $100 US per barrel, rather than $80, is generally estimated to add about 0.5 per cent to one per cent to overall Canadian GDP, or $16 billion to $32 billion per year.

WATCH | Can Canada win a trade war with the United States?: Can Canada actually win a trade war with the U.S.? | About That | Duration 9:14 How can Canada win a trade war with the U.S. when leverage isn't equal? Andrew Chang explains how Canada is retaliating against massive tariffs levied by a neighbour 13 times its economic size. (Photo credits: The Canadian Press, Reuters, Adobe Stock and Getty Images)

A virtuous cycle of growth

The oil-price spike may also have secondary positive effects for Canada that can prove lasting, said Calnan, since there's little reason to believe Saudi Arabia will be able to defang the Houthi rebels any time soon.

"They've tried for years and they've been unsuccessful," he said, explaining how eight months into the war, countries historically dependent on Gulf oil are starting to look for new providers. "I know for sure that countries in East Asia are seriously looking at Canada for that energy security and diversification. That is unlocking long-term investment."

Offshore oil production in Newfoundland and Labrador is already up about 25 per cent this year.

"We see now an emerging interest in our exploration plays and that hasn't been the case for the last three or four years,” said OilCo CEO Jim Keating, who heads up the Crown corporation that leads oil and gas activities on behalf of the Newfoundland and Labrador government.

Uneven impacts

Already, U.S. tariffs fall much more heavily on manufacturing provinces such as Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia than they do on Alberta and Saskatchewan.

Higher prices will put even more pressure on industries that consume a lot of energy, such as manufacturing and transportation. High energy prices also tend to spill over into inflation in food and consumer goods, at a time when many Canadian families are already feeling stretched to make ends meet.

But high oil prices should also relieve downward pressure on the Canadian dollar, allowing for cheaper imports, which can partly counteract inflationary pressure on the cost of living.

And Calnan says industries beyond oil potentially stand to benefit in the future.

"If we're talking about big new investments happening in Alberta, that will help boost manufacturing and other industries elsewhere in Canada, because there'll be an enormous amount of steel, and skilled trades workers needed to complete these huge facilities."

WATCH | Carney releases video about Canada-U.S. trade talks: Carney releases video saying U.S. wanted 'dependency' in too many areas | Duration 1:48 In an excerpt from a 15-minute explanatory video released by Prime Minister Mark Carney's office on Tuesday, Carney says U.S. trade negotiators wanted Canada 'to become even more reliant on them, not less.'

On his way to the Republican convention in Dallas, Trump on Wednesday assured voters that "right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward." But there are few signs the markets are buying it. Oil futures contracts remain at the $100 level to the end of 2026.

In both of the world's current major wars involving superpowers — the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran and the Russian war on Ukraine — oil infrastructure has become a major target.

Both the Russians, who famously anticipated a swift collapse followed by a victory parade in Kyiv, and the Trump administration, which has declared victory over Iran more than once, now appear mired in conflicts with no clear exit, said Calnan.

"Wars have a problematic tendency to just keep going and be very difficult to bring to a clean finish," he said. "I'm not sure why people keep thinking that wars they start are going to end in a month."

World.title: Canadian boxer George Chuvalo, who faced Muhammad Ali in his prime, dead at 89
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

George Chuvalo, the iron-chinned Canadian heavyweight who took the best punches from the giants of boxing without ever falling, has died. He was 89.

Chuvalo suffered from dementia late in life and had been residing in a long-term care facility in Toronto. He died Saturday according to multiple online posts by family and friends.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford, who said the boxer was a family friend, shared condolences on social media Saturday.

"My thoughts are with all of George's family and loved ones as we mourn his passing," he said.

Chuvalo went the distance with Muhammad Ali in bouts in Toronto and Vancouver, and absorbed the hardest shots sluggers Joe Frazier and George Foreman had to offer, without being knocked down.

It was unfathomable family tragedy after he retired that brought him to his knees.

WATCH | Peter Mansbridge interviews George Chuvalo: George Chuvalo | Duration 5:57 Peter Mansbridge sits down with champion heavyweight boxer George Chuvalo to talk about many of his famous fights.

"If you added up every punch I took and multiplied the total by 10,000, it wouldn't begin to equal the pain of losing three sons and a wife to drugs and suicide," he said in his 2013 autobiography Chuvalo: A Fighter's Life, co-written with Murray Greig.

The son of Croatian immigrants was born Sept. 12, 1937, in Toronto's Junction neighbourhood. He became intrigued by boxing after seeing The Ring magazine at a newsstand.

Chuvalo was 10 years old the first time he stepped through the ropes, and a growth spurt combined with an interest in weightlifting saw him develop into a six-foot, 210-pound fighter.

After a brief amateur career, he turned pro in 1956, winning notice for performances at the Jack Dempsey Tournament at Maple Leaf Gardens.

But by the early 1960s, Chuvalo's career had stagnated under ineffective guidance, until Toronto poultry magnate Irv Ungerman took over as his manager.

Chuvalo parlayed several wins into an attention-getting 11th-round stoppage over contender Doug Jones at Madison Square Garden in 1964. He returned to that mecca of boxing the next year, narrowly losing a decision to former champ Floyd Patterson in a bout The Ring named best of 1965.

'He just keeps coming and coming'

Chuvalo's style was inexorable without being reckless. He moved forward with thudding blows from both hands to the head and body, producing stoppages in 88 per cent of his wins.

"You can't believe his strength," Canadian fighter Bill Drover once told a writer. "There's no way to stop him. He just keeps coming and coming. The only way you can stop him is with a stick of dynamite."

Chuvalo would always insist his defence was better than advertised, but it was his durability that was remarkable. He was able to absorb the shots, he said, thanks to a 17.5-inch neck strengthened through exercises.

Chuvalo found himself fighting for the heavyweight title in 1966 as a replacement foe when Ali's affiliation with the Black Muslims and controversial anti-Vietnam-War stance made him a pariah in the U.S.

The challenger's prospects were described in a New York Times headline: Bettor's-Eye View of Chuvalo: A Big Bum With a Lot of Heart.

George Chuvalo, left, and Muhammad Ali go head to head as they trade blows near the rope in the fourth round of their fight in Toronto on March 29, 1966. (The Associated Press)

While Chuvalo failed to become Canada's first heavyweight champion since Tommy Burns in the early 1900s, he earned praise for a gritty performance. Ali famously called him the toughest man he had faced up to that point, but Chuvalo was ambivalent being the first to take the champ 15 rounds.

"In a crazy way, that fight is what defines me for a lot of my fellow Canadians but it took a long time before I came to appreciate how good it made me feel," he said.

Never knocked down

With wife Lynne and five children at home, Chuvalo appreciated the paydays the Ali performance begat. He would beat contenders Jerry Quarry and Manuel Ramos, losing close bouts to Oscar Bonavena and Jimmy Ellis.

Chuvalo was stopped for the first time in 1967 by Frazier, requiring a silicone implant to keep an eyeball from drooping. The loss to Foreman in the fourth round three years later was also notable, with the referee stepping in before Chuvalo's "never knocked down" streak might have been ended.

Chuvalo's loss to Ali in Vancouver in 1972 was not as compelling or as close as the first bout. He retired for good on a winning note six years later, finishing with a record of 73 wins, 18 losses and two draws, with 64 of his wins coming by knock out.

Unlike with Ali and others, the toll of concussive blows wasn't evident on the surface. Chuvalo was articulate and spoke in rapid-fire bursts, with a quip or self-deprecating joke usually at the ready.

But like many fighters, he had a tough time transitioning to the "humdrum" nature of life, as he once described it. At various points, he opened a nightclub, got his real estate licence, promoted fights, hosted a TV show and took cinema's worst ever arm-wrestling defeat in a cameo in David Cronenberg's The Fly.

WATCH | George Chuvalo's date with destiny and Muhammad Ali: George Chuvalo's date with destiny and Muhammad Ali | Duration 24:57 Chuvalo gets a shot at Ali's world title in Toronto in 1966.

Chuvalo told CBC Radio in 1968 he didn't want his four sons boxing for a living, but it was outside the ring where he couldn't protect them. The youngest, Jesse, became hooked on heroin after a prescription for pain medication ran out and was just 19 when he fatally shot himself in 1985.

Older brothers George Jr. and Steven had by then also become users of the drug and involved in petty crime to feed their habits. Steven Chuvalo described a feeling of "worthlessness" he and his two addicted brothers felt in an interview with CBC's the fifth estate in 1995.

"My dad spent quite a few years chasing us around the city, Georgie and I in particular, and dragging us out of drug houses and heroin houses and basically just trying to keep us alive," he said.

George Jr., three days sprung from jail in Kingston, Ont., overdosed on Halloween 1993.

Just four days after that, 49-year-old Lynne Chuvalo swallowed pills and left a suicide note.

"I never thought she'd do it, but I'm not surprised," Chuvalo told the New York Times a short time later, adding his wife never got over the first burial of a child.

Steven Chuvalo, who spoke on the fifth estate of wanting to make his father proud, would overdose and die eight months after that program aired.

Chuvalo would persevere, marrying again, and cherishing time spent with oldest son Mitch, daughter Vanessa, and his grandchildren. He would travel the country, speaking bluntly to students, as captured in a CBC Radio report in 1998.

"I'd like to think if you're ever tempted with the idea of doing drugs, or you ever flirt with doing drugs, I hope you think of me, George Chuvalo, and what drugs did to my family."

In 2017, reports surfaced of family drama involving Chuvalo's surviving children and the fighter's second wife, Joanne, who he was divorcing. Some of the disputes centred around the state of Chuvalo's cognitive decline and his future care.

On a podcast five years later, Mitch Chuvalo said his father no longer recognized him when he visited.

By that time, his legacy had been recognized by the City of Toronto, with the official opening in 2019 of the 7,000-square foot George Chuvalo Community Centre, located in the Junction.

World.title: Provinces are turning to U.S. health-care workers to help with shortages. And it’s working
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LISTEN | Why U.S. nurses are moving north: White Coat Black Art 26:30 Why U.S. nurses are moving north

Registered nurse Shane Tyson was done with the U.S.

He was working in Minnesota at the not-for-profit Mayo Clinic Health System and the Olmsted Medical Center. But in 2025, Tyson says he became increasingly concerned about the deterioration of health care, as well as tighter immigration enforcement.

Then ICE agents arrested a patient as they were leaving a primary care appointment where he worked, Tyson says.

“That was definitely a wake-up call," he said. "And I am married to a U.S. permanent resident that was born in Bolivia … and it scared the crap out of me for him and for the others in that situation,” Tyson told Dr. Brian Goldman, host of CBC’s White Coat, Black Art .

Tyson says he’d been noticing Facebook ads from provincial recruitment service HealthMatch BC . The more he researched, the more he contemplated a move north. So he registered, got interviews with two B.C. health authorities, and received two job offers within a week.

Tyson is one of many health-care professionals making the move from the U.S. With shortages of nurses , physicians and other health workers, some provinces are actively recruiting U.S. health-care professionals — and they’re getting results.

CBC reached out to health ministries in all 10 provinces for data on health-care professionals recruited from the U.S. since efforts ramped up in 2025.

The number of doctors recruited ranged from three in Saskatchewan to 33 in Nova Scotia and 570 in Ontario.

Ontario also recruited 2,300 nurses in 2025, while, all told, more than 580 health-care professionals accepted jobs in B.C. since March 2025.

For Tyson, the targeted recruitment worked. It took him just three months to get his B.C. nursing licence through a fast-track process, and eight days to receive a provincial nomination for permanent residence .

Since January, he’s been working in the emergency department of Nanaimo Regional General Hospital (NRGH) on Vancouver Island. Tyson says he’s pleased with the community, the weather, and what he sees as more inclusive health care.

“There’s not the insurance companies and corporate health-care companies taking billions of dollars. The patient is the focus here and whether you're the unhoused or the banker or lawyer, you have equal access to care in Canada,” he said.

Damian Lange, executive director of clinical services at Nanaimo Regional General Hospital, says filling some of the health region's vacant positions with recruits from the U.S. has made things better for patients and staff alike. (Brian Goldman/CBC)

The recruitment push

Health-care workers are bringing experience and ideas from some of the largest hospitals in the U.S., says Damian Lange, executive director of clinical services at NRGH.

“The American system has significant talent,” Lange said.

He said Island Health started recruiting from the U.S. in April 2025. Since then, it has hired 76 physicians and 102 nurses — 31 of them at NRGH. He said another 87 U.S. health-care providers will hopefully join by year’s end.

Lange said the new recruits make for a “better staff experience ... better patient experience, improved quality care, improved access to care. And so it's been a real benefit as we close the gap there with our vacancy rates.”

Even with the new hires, Lange said Island Health still has a 15 per cent vacancy rate for nurses.

And recruiting U.S. health-care workers is only part of the equation. A lot of questions go along with an international move.

Volunteers helping ease the move north

Tod Maffin and his wife, Jocelyn Maffin, are helping pave the way with an online community they started in early 2025. Tod is a digital strategist and former CBC journalist, and Jocelyn works with Spinal Cord Injury BC.

It started with Tod’s invitation to Americans to visit Nanaimo last year. So many health-care workers interested in moving to Canada came that Maffin made a Discord channel where people can chat and ask questions about everything from health-care licensing to real estate to services for autistic children.

Tod Maffin and his wife, Jocelyn, run the Healthcare Infusion project together, and say they are seeing success across the country. (Tod Maffin/Hey.Café)

Tod said it’s about connecting people.

“If you're an ER nurse in Dallas and you're ready … to move into Canada, you've figured out which area you're going to go to, but you have a trans kid and you just need to talk the parent of another trans kid in that community to make sure that your daughter is going to be OK,” you can find that support in the Discord group, he said.

It includes out-of-area health-care workers (mostly Americans), recruiters, immigration consultants and local citizens who just want to help out. Of around 1,200 current users, 84 have recently accepted job offers.

Tod created a template for other Healthcare Infusion communities and there are now 45 of them across Canada .

Jocelyn said she initially worried about poaching health-care workers from the U.S., but: “Canada has dealt with brain drain to the U.S. for years and that's always been a big issue,” she said.

“So maybe we're just borrowing them back.”

Call for better retention

In an email to CBC, the Canadian Medical Association said that with a shortage of more than 23,000 family doctors, Canada needs to remove barriers to immigration and licensing for internationally trained physicians. It also needs to make it easier for those currently practising in Canada to stay, the association said.

Canadian Nurses Association CEO Valerie Grdisa emphasized the need to retain the nurses Canada already has.

“We welcome U.S.-educated nurses into the nation, but we don't see it really as a long-term recruitment strategy,” she said. “We really have to get back [to] what matters to Canadian and domestically educated nurses.”

Grdisa said Health Canada's Nursing Retention Toolkit lays out strategies to retain nurses, like safe staffing levels, manageable workloads, mentorship and career support. But she said health-care systems haven’t implemented or evaluated them consistently enough to determine what actually works.

“If those things were to happen, would we be losing such a large cohort — up to 40 per cent of the workforce by the age of 35 ?”

Shane Tyson recently received his certificate of Canadian citizenship. (Brian Goldman/CBC)

Meanwhile, though, nurse Shane Tyson says he is here to stay. He recently got his certificate of Canadian citizenship. A kind stranger also left a moose sticker and a welcome note on his car.

“That really made me emotional, you know. I was concerned, driving around with Minnesota plates, how I'd be received, because at that time the tariffs were coming in, talk of the 51st state — and that just really meant a lot to me.”

Now Tyson is logging onto the Maffins’ Discord community to help other U.S. health-care workers come to Canada.

“Have to pay it forward.”

World.title: ‘Serious’ critique of Carney is what loyalty to Canada looks like, Tory critic says
World.content:
Article content

He recalls how in the Harper years, the government briefed the opposition. Critics such as the late NDP MP Paul Dewar were taken into confidence on Ukraine, ISIS, TPP and CETA. Majumdar’s confident Harper did the same with Tom Mulcair. Justin Trudeau sent border-town MPs to Congress; Chrystia Freeland used a non-disclosure process with journalists and experts. “We have not seen any of that in a year and a half,” Majumdar says. Pierre Poilievre’s New York swing this week — apparently with PMO blessing — looks like a shift toward a common front. Fine; but it still leaves the Opposition unbriefed on the talks, the deal text unpublished, and Parliament un-recalled.
