World.title: From the archive: Are Mexicans really always late?
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in December 2024 — is a humorous look at a stereotype regarding Mexicans and punctuality.

Before we get into the nuts and bolts regarding Mexican punctuality — or lack thereof — it’s important to clarify one thing. Mexicans are not actually always late.

That said, all stereotypes have to come from somewhere, don’t they? But like everything in life, there’s nuance to it.

Just like people all over the world, there’s room for a great deal of variety. Some people are always on time, and some people never are. Most people are punctual for certain activities, and unpunctual for others.

My dad, for instance, has never been punctual; I remember my mother saying she was terrified he wouldn’t make it to their wedding on time. My ex-husband also has challenges with punctuality, as does one of my best friends; I’ve spent great chunks of my adult life waiting hours.

I’m always super duper on time for everything, though I might let myself get to a party up to an hour late. My kid is leaning unpunctual, but I’m doing my damnedest to lecture it out of her. Because if there’s one thing kids love and respond to, it’s a good lecture.

Linguistic flexibility

One of the problems about even defining “late” is the language around defining time. For a deep dive into this, check out Joseph Sorrentino’s excellent piece on this specific type of vocabulary. Ahorita, al ratito, mañana … None of these words specify an actual time, you see? So “ahorita” could mean right this minute, and it could mean in five hours, or never. Al ratito (in a while) might mean in a couple of hours, or it might mean in a few years, depending on who’s saying it. You get the idea.

And really, this kind of language is useful because it allows for flexibility. In this way at least, Mexico is a flexible country.

Really, it has to be. Things come up that need tending to. Public transportation can be unpredictable. The opportunity to have a meal or talk to a pretty girl might come up. Your mom tells you to go fetch some things from the store, and you don’t tell her, “Sorry, I have plans.” Really, you just never know what can happen!

Life is unpredictable, and Mexicans have a fairly high tolerance for it being unpredictable, which is lucky for all of us.

Sometimes, though, there are things you must be on time for. And a good indicator of what those things are is whether or not there’s a specific time attached to them.

The meaning of ‘tolerancia’

School is one of those things. At my daughter’s school, for example, 8 a.m. is the official time kids have to be in the door. As a courtesy to the perpetually-late parents, there’s a “tolerance” of 10 minutes. To me, this means my daughter must be there before 8 a.m. if we’re not to be seen as rude and irresponsible. To others, it means 8:10 or even 8:11 is the limit. If kids aren’t in by that time, they must wait to enter the 9 a.m. class.

It was like this when I taught school here, too; some things, I suppose, are non-negotiable.

The same goes for official appointment times, even if the official or doctor you’re meeting isn’t exactly on time. So if you have a meeting with, say, immigration, you’d better be there at your appointment time! Some places will let you know that they have a tolerancia (literally, tolerance) of 10-15 minutes. This means that if you’re more than that amount of time late, you lose the appointment!

For other things, usually involving celebrations, arrival and start times are more flexible. This is especially true of parties, to which you can show up rather late without causing a fuss. Unless you’ve promised to bring something essential for the party, they’re just glad to have you there at some point. This doesn’t mean they’ll wait for you to start in on the cake and piñatas, though, so beware!

Clocks vs. cultural norms

Concerts and plays typically start within 15 to 30 minutes of their “official” start time; rock concerts might start hours after they’re meant to. Oh, well!

And if you’re meeting friends, it might depend on the specific circumstances. Are you meeting someone busy who only has a few minutes? Are you meeting them alone? In my group of mom friends, we always know that things can come up. “I’ll text you when I leave” is a good, flexible bridge that keeps people updated but keeps plans flexible.

In my own conservative and somewhat strict view, being on time means showing respect for the other person. If you are not on time, then you do not care about them or their time. And if you are on time, not only are you showing respect for them, but you’re making things easier for yourself, avoiding fluster. My cultural chauvinism is showing, I know.

But for plenty of people here, that’s a ridiculous notion. Why stress so much about being on time when literally anything can happen to make you not on time? Perhaps there’s a message here too about avoiding blame and responsibility. “Se me durmió el gallo” (The rooster went to sleep on me; as in, the rooster didn’t wake me up).

But that’s for another article. For now, I’ll leave you with a cute little proverb, as well as its juxtaposed, more truthful meme:

“Al que madruga, Dios le ayuda.” (The one who rises early receives God’s help.) It rhymes!

“Al que madruga, encuentra todo cerrado.” (The one who rises early finds everything closed.)

Truer words were never spoken.

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, https://sarahedevries.substack.com/

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Exports and gas production hit record highs as patriotic spirit swells
World.content:
Listen to this article

Bilateral communications were front and center in Mexico the week of Sept. 7, with developments running the gamut from encouraging to combative. U.S. President Donald Trump’s remark that Mexico has “nothing” the United States needs beyond “hot tamales” and “tomatoes” caught fire over the weekend, unleashing a fresh round of provocations from Trump, Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio in the days that followed.

Mexico, however, continued to highlight trade and security collaboration with its northern neighbor, though the PISA test results and next year’s midterm elections sparked more conversations at home. Meanwhile, the annual inflation rate ticked up to 3.26% — as expected according to Banxico, which forecasts inflation of 3.5% by the end of 2026. President Claudia Sheinbaum remained optimistic through it all, especially as her administration makes its plans for 2027. Overhead, punishing heat baked Mexico’s northern border states even as monsoon rains drenched the Pacific coast and center of the country.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

2027 budget takes shape

On Monday, Finance Minister Édgar Amador Zamora submitted a 10.6-trillion-peso (US $627.8 billion) budget proposal for 2027 to Congress, an increase of about 1% in real terms over this year. Amador framed the package around “five pillars” — economic growth, protecting government priorities, strengthening revenue, more efficient spending and fiscal discipline. The government is banking on those pillars to shrink the budget deficit to 3.9% of GDP next year from an estimated 4.1% in 2026, even as public debt climbs to 55% of GDP. No new taxes or fuel-price hikes are planned.

Health care gets a 10.9% real-terms boost to 1.1 trillion pesos, largely for IMSS-Bienestar infrastructure and medicine supply, while education rises about 7% to 1.3 trillion pesos to fund new schools. Pension and welfare programs get just over 1 trillion pesos, and debt servicing alone eats up 1.6 trillion pesos — roughly one of every seven pesos the government spends. Security agencies see an 11.6% bump to 331.4 billion pesos, while Pemex funding falls 69.2% as the state oil company pushes toward self-sufficiency.

The National Electoral Institute (INE) is the biggest percentage winner of all, with an 87.5% real-terms increase ahead of 2027 midterm elections, while the Energy Ministry, the National Human Rights Commission and the Federal Electricity Commission absorb the steepest cuts. Sheinbaum said the following day that she is “very satisfied” with the package and that growth could exceed the official forecast of 1.5-2.5%, citing anticipated stability in trade relations with the U.S. and Canada.

Homicides continue to fall

Security officials reported this week that daily homicides fell 53% in August compared to September 2024, the final month of the López Obrador administration, making it the least violent August since 2015.

More than 67,000 people have been arrested for high-impact crimes since Sheinbaum took office, though Security Minister Omar García Harfuch cautioned that “the job is not done.” Days later, from Tuxtla Gutiérrez, the president highlighted a 63% drop in Chiapas’s homicide rate since Gov. Eduardo Ramírez Aguilar took office, alongside nearly 10,000 arrests in the southern state. The same briefing revealed the discovery of a clandestine hospital the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) used to treat injured members.

Olmeca Refinery notches record month

Pemex’s Olmeca Refinery in Tabasco posted its best month yet for fuel production in July, averaging 252,498 barrels per day, a 78.8% jump over June. Gasoline output rose even more sharply, up nearly 128% month-over-month, after equipment fires forced repairs earlier in the year. Despite the milestone, the plant — which began operating approximately two years ago — is still running at roughly two-thirds of its 340,000-bpd capacity.

Fox and PRI’s Alito Moreno join forces

In a striking political reunion, former President Vicente Fox met with PRI leader Alejandro “Alito” Moreno to discuss “the need to build a strong opposition” ahead of 2027 midterms — 26 years after Fox became the first opposition candidate to sweep the once-dominant PRI out of the presidency, and years after he called the party “black vipers, vermin and tadpoles.”

Morena, for its part, dismissed the pairing as “the reorganization of the power elite,” saying in a statement that “they change the names, they invent new organizations, but behind the facade, it’s the same old faces.” The PRI, which ruled Mexico for 71 years, now holds just two of the country’s 32 governorships — the same number as the much smaller Citizens Movement (MC) party.

At her Monday press conference, Sheinbaum branded the reunion “PRIAN” politics dating to the “neoliberal” era of former President Carlos Salinas de Gortari, and called Fox a “traitor of democracy” — a jab tied to his role in Mexico’s disputed 2006 election.

Bilateral high points

Trade and security cooperation produced some of the week’s more encouraging bilateral news. Mexico’s exports to the U.S. hit a monthly record in July: US $60.55 billion worth of goods were sent north, pushing Mexico’s share of the $332.92 billion U.S. import market above 18%.

Along the border, Mexican and U.S. forces carried out “High Eagle,” a binational operation to detect and disable drones cartels use to surveil authorities near Tijuana and San Diego. And though bad weather grounded Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s flight to Mexico City on Wednesday, he and Sheinbaum still held a video call on USMCA negotiations that Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard described as “cordial” and “very useful,” with talks on steel, aluminum and automotive tariffs continuing ahead of a fourth bilateral review round.

Bilateral low points

Other exchanges were considerably more combative. Over the weekend, Trump proposed to rename New Mexico “New America,” despite having no legal authority to rename a U.S. state, drawing pushback from the state’s Democratic leaders. Later in the week, from Ecuador, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio doubled down on claims that cartels control “vast territories” of Mexico, hinting the threat may eventually have to be “confronted one way or the other.” Sheinbaum shot back on Thursday morning, telling Rubio to keep Mexico out of U.S. midterm politics and calling his remarks electorally motivated. Rounding out the week, U.S. Vice President JD Vance labeled the Mexican flag “a symbol of the far left” after a protester interrupted his convention speech in Dallas, telling the man to “get your ass over there” if he loved Mexico so much.

Poor PISA scores spark a debate over screens

New results from the OECD’s Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), given to 7,843 students across 297 Mexican schools, showed that four in 10 15-year-olds — 41.8% — scored below the basic level in science, math and reading, more than double the 19.7% OECD average and Mexico’s worst showing since 2009.

Mexican students averaged 388 points in math, 408 in reading and 414 in science, all well below OECD averages of 463, 461 and 482, and the country has shed seven points in both math and reading since the 2022 test. The decline wasn’t unique to Mexico — the OECD’s education director called it part of a “dramatic” global drop, particularly in reading — and Mexican students still reported unusually high curiosity (80%, versus a 24% global average who called school “a waste of time”). Education International, the global teachers’ federation, pinned the broader slide on shrinking attention spans, heavy AI use and a worldwide teacher shortage. China, Singapore, South Korea, Estonia and Canada topped the rankings.

Education Minister Mario Delgado blamed excessive screen use for the drop in reading comprehension — arguing that “screens make it easy to ‘read’ or consume images” — while defending the New Mexican School curriculum model and promoting traditional games like yo-yos, marbles and spinning tops as a substitute for phone time. He conceded the PISA sample was “statistically representative” even as he questioned whether the test amounts to a comprehensive evaluation of Mexican education. Sheinbaum later told reporters Mexico will roll out new math and reading textbooks next year, including poems and short stories, and push a “return to pencil and paper,” tying the effort to new national guidelines already restricting cellphone use in schools.

Education Ministry, UNESCO team up on AI in schools

Also this week, Mexico’s Education Ministry signed a letter of intent with UNESCO to guide the “responsible” rollout of artificial intelligence in classrooms, with the U.N. body offering technical assistance, teacher training and research support. Officials said the goal is to ensure AI supports, rather than substitutes for, teaching and critical thinking, and the deal also opens the door to new rules on cellphone use in schools.

Mexico prepares for El Grito and Independence Day

With the country’s 216th independence anniversary approaching, more than 18,000 members of Mexico’s armed forces are readying for the Sept. 16 military parade through Mexico City, featuring drones, horses, dogs and a float marking the country’s World Cup hosting duties this past June and July. The holiday kicks off the night before, with Sheinbaum leading the Grito de Independencia from the National Palace balcony and Tejano band Intocable headlining a concert in the Zócalo.

Festivities and gritos will ring out from cities across the country, including in Sinaloa, whose capital city of Culicán will hold a public celebration of Independence Day for the first time in two years.

Points of 🇲🇽 pride

A 20-year-old engineering student from a Chihuahua farming family, Luis Ángel Robles Morales, won a national innovation award for an irrigation filter that is already helping 500 drought-stricken farmers use water more efficiently.

Forward Julián Quiñones and Club América’s Scarlett Camberos earned historic Ballon d’Or nominations, marking the first time two Mexican players — and a Mexican club — have featured on the shortlist for world soccer’s top individual honor.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Witnessing the explosive sledgehammer ritual in San Juan de la Vega, Guanajuato
World.content:
A door in the street cracked open just enough for a hand to slip through. A kid, maybe 15, curled his fingers toward himself: come here, come here, then pulled back into the dark. I looked around the street. Nobody. I stepped inside.

The house looked like a drug kitchen. Two folding tables stretched across the room, their surfaces dusted white and yellow. On one side, a bucket of potassium chlorate. On the other, sulfur. Three kids stood around the tables, working the powders together with their bare hands. One kid looked up at me and grinned, then went back to scooping powder into small plastic bags.

Josué was the one who had waved me in from the doorway. One of the boys had no hands. Both arms ended at the wrists. I didn’t want to ask. I asked anyway. He told me it happened during the explosions, a few years back. He said it the way someone tells you about a stolen bicycle, part of life.

Don Juan David, Josué’s father, walked into the room. He greeted me with a handshake and a smile, glanced at the tables of explosive powder where their children worked, and walked back out.

A dangerous tradition

Every year, on Shrove Tuesday, the townspeople of San Juan de la Vega pack homemade explosives onto sledgehammers, carry them to the streets and open fields, and slam them against the ground. People lose limbs. This time, something was different. For the first time in the town’s history, authorities had banned the use of explosives during the carnival.

Families wanted to talk. Each family insisted theirs was the true story. The carnival, they all agreed, celebrates San Juan de la Vega, a saint who saved the town from gold robbers centuries ago. The explosives reenact the gunshots from his battles.

Every family also wanted to make sure we knew that the big explosions, the ones the town is famous for, are not the real tradition. The real tradition is small. Modest. A respectful crack of gunpowder in honor of the saint. Kids started making bigger and bigger explosives, destroying city piping. Everything breaks, they said, shaking their own heads. This is not what we are.

A man named Aquino de la Vega was moving silver shipments by mule along the Camino Real when bandits started robbing him. He prayed to San Juan Bautista. The robbers stopped. Aquino vowed he would honor the saint every year, forever, and so would his sons.

Six families still carry that vow. Each one is tied to a barrio. The families fund the music, the food, the processions. They keep the image of the saint in their home for a year.

Adrenaline and danger

The word I heard more than any other was adrenalina. The afternoon before the carnival, I found Josué sitting on a curb outside a corner store, rolling a cigarette. He was quiet.

“I’m always scared before I do it,” he told me. “But once I blow up one, I can’t stop. The adrenaline is too strong. I want to keep going.”

I asked about the dangers, and stories came easily: a man who burned, another who was paralyzed, people who lost fingers, hands, arms, legs. Accidents happen because the explosives are powerful enough to send 25-kilogram sledgehammers flying through the air. A hammer goes up, a hammer comes down, and sometimes there is a head in the way.

“Police always try to take them away,” one man said, sitting in a plastic chair outside his house, two kids playing in the dirt beside him. “But they will never stop the tradition. Nothing will change.”

On the afternoon before the main event, the streets were empty. Doors closed. No music. No voices.

Boom. The first hammer hit the ground as soon as night fell.

The sound moved through me. The ground shook under my feet. My ears whistled, even from 100 meters away. My chest vibrated. Windows cracked. The pipes beneath the street groaned and split.

Then came another. And another.

Parades took the streets. Villagers singing, dancing, playing instruments, carrying the image of San Juanito through the town. Following them in the back, kids dressed as soldiers, some in boots and gas masks, others with no gloves, no protection of any kind. Everyone carried sledgehammers and backpacks stuffed with explosives.

Defying the ban

I found Josué in the crowd. Face covered in soot, eyes wide. He swung a hammer down and the detonation threw him sideways. He got up laughing and loaded another charge.

Around midnight, the first police cars appeared.

The crowd froze. About 10 men climbed out with SWAT gear, assault rifles and bulletproof vests. They walked toward the kids with the backpacks. The boys scattered.

I saw a grandmother crack her front door open. She let the kids shove their backpacks full of explosives through the gap; she closed the door, and she stood in front of it. When the police asked to enter, she stood immobile like a statue until they were gone.

The police confiscated what they could, caught a few guys, and left. Within minutes, the parades reformed. The hammers came back out. The explosions picked up where they had stopped.

At around 3 a.m., we walked back toward town to catch some sleep. I did not sleep. The bed shook after every boom. Even with earplugs, my ears hurt. It went on until 7 a.m.

We walked outside. Over 10 police cars patrolled the town. They had shut everything down. But beyond the edge of town, we could hear it. Boom. Boom.

We followed the sound.

Moving to the tracks

The townspeople had moved to the train tracks. Flat, open land, sand, rocks and gravel, not a piece of shade anywhere. They placed explosives on the rails and waited for trains to roll over them. Between trains, they took turns blowing up hammers on steel bars laid flat against the ground.

There, away from the police, the hammers got bigger.

It was noon. The sun was directly overhead. People packed more and more powder onto the sledgehammers and took turns. Huge hammers flew tens of meters into the air.

I watched a kid swing a hammer down. The explosion threw him back onto the ground. The hammer launched upward, spinning, and came down on his head. The ring of steel on skull. He tried to stand. Blood ran from his scalp, down his face, into his eyes. His friend pulled off his own shirt, wrapped it tight around the kid’s head, and hauled him onto the back of a motorcycle. They disappeared down the road.

Nobody stopped. The next person stepped up.

The next morning, the market opened in the square as always. People walked slowly, said good morning to each other. A dog slept in a doorway. The church bell rang at 8.

Here was Josué, down the road. He waved.

I went to say goodbye to Don Juan David. He pulled me into a hug that lasted a long time. He held on. We had barely talked. When he finally let go, his eyes were wet. He thanked me. He begged me to come back next year.

“Sí, San Juanito permite,” he said. If San Juanito allows it.

Mattia Astori and Daniele Colucci make Sacratos, a documentary project on extreme rituals with photos, interviews, articles and videos. They’ve worked in Mexico, India, Bolivia, Thailand and Italy.

World.title: Turtle power: Volunteer to protect Mexico’s sea turtles
World.content:
Turtle camps can be found all over Mexico’s coastline, including the Gulf Coast, allowing volunteers to liberate baby turtles.

With the fifth-longest coastline in all of Mexico — a country that is internationally known and beloved for its beach offerings — Veracruz is certainly a sea-loving state, boasting some 450 miles of Gulf Coast access. For the record, Baja California Sur, a peninsula surrounded by water on three sides, has the longest total coastline at more than 1,350 miles of beach.

Historically, Veracruz is celebrated for its seafood and coastal tropics, as well as being the site of Mexico’s largest and oldest port with access to the Atlantic Ocean.

But what has been lost in the greater narrative is that, as part of its cultural significance along the Gulf Coast, Veracruz has also become one of Mexico’s leading states for turtle conservation.

The legacy of turtle conservationism in Mexico

The earliest federal efforts to focus on sea turtle nesting in Mexico began in 1962, led by the National Institute of Biological and Fisheries Research on both of Mexico’s ample coasts. In 1963, the Center for Turtle Culture opened on Isla Mujeres, Quintana Roo.

Shortly after, in 1966, Rancho Nuevo — located in Tamaulipas, just north of Veracruz — was among the first turtle conservation camps to formally open in Mexico. The National Commission of Protected Natural Areas outlined the importance of these efforts from the mid-1960s; the investments significantly helped to maintain the growth of Mexico’s turtle populations by increasing local awareness and participation. During that time, the National Sea Turtles Conservation Program was founded as a result.

Rancho Nuevo, along with the other turtle conservation camps that would spring up all over Mexico’s beaches — from the Gulf to the Pacific — has become a crucial element of turtle protection efforts since then, utilizing a mix of dedicated turtle conservationists and public volunteers. Responsibilities include the protection of nesting sites via monitoring and safeguarding turtle nests, and assisting (or “liberating”) fresh turtle hatchlings to ensure they make it to the sea.

Milestones in national protection rights

Since the 1960s, Mexico has become a global leader in turtle conservancy; in 2025, Mexico was recognized as an exemplar for its turtle protection efforts. Currently, Mexico federally operates 26 turtle conservation centers, in addition to various independent organizations and nonprofits extending across 13 coastal states. Officials announced a record of more than 34 million newborn olive ridley turtles that reached the ocean in a single season, in Oaxaca’s Morro Ayuta region alone.

In 1990, federally backed turtle protection rights gained further ground when then-President Carlos Salinas de Gortari decreed an end to the commercial harvesting of all sea turtles and related products. The landmark move shifted former turtle hunting communities — such as areas in Mazunte, which had among the highest rates of turtle slaughter — into epicenters of turtle conservation. Mazunte opened the Mexican Turtle Center in 1991, aiding the area’s turtle population and ecotourism alike.

Mexico’s role as a sanctuary for sea turtles

According to a 2008 report from the Secretariat of Environment and Natural Resources (Semarnat), “Mexico is the country with the largest number of sea-turtle species worldwide. Seven of the eight species known … nest in Mexican beaches, both in the Pacific and in the Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean littorals: loggerhead turtle, white or green turtle, black turtle, hawksbill turtle, Kemp’s ridley, olive ridley and leatherback turtle. Two of them, Kemp’s ridley and black sea turtle, nest exclusively in Mexican beaches.”

A more recent investigation from 2023, published in Revista Mexicana de Biodiversidad, revealed that southeastern Mexico, including Veracruz, is the most diverse region for turtle conservation in the country: “According to our results, southeastern Mexico supports three-fourths of the families — and more than half of the genera — found nationwide in Mexico. These findings highlight southeastern Mexico as a region of high importance for the composition of land and freshwater turtles at the national level … Oaxaca, Chiapas and Veracruz stand out as the states with the highest species richness and endemism, respectively. These three states are located within the region considered the richest in total herpetofauna, a result of complex orography, diverse habitats and environments, and the biogeographic history of Mexico.”

An afternoon with turtle conservationists in Veracruz

Jeanne A. Mortimer, a world-renowned marine biologist known as “Madame Torti” who specializes in sea turtle conservationism, once wrote that “The importance of the central coast of Veracruz (for turtle nesting) may be attributed to the fact that the beaches are easily accessible from the ocean without great obstacles like rocks, pronounced slopes or coastal developments that prevent the movement of the adult females along the length and breadth of the beaches.”

It partially explains why Veracruz has been able to cultivate a long-lasting ethos and engagement around turtle protection, with civic initiatives like Fundación Yépez and the Veracruzano Center for Research and Conservation of the Sea Turtle having launched decades ago. Additionally, Veracruz boasts Veracruz Reef System National Park, which played a role in a major environmental ruling by Mexico’s Supreme Court to conserve sea turtle habitats by restricting the construction of industrial ports in endangered areas (although reports that the ruling hasn’t been properly enforced have been published).

Vida Millenaria is among Veracruz’s most prominent turtle conservation groups. The project began in Tecolutla in 1974 as a personal mission for Fernando Manzano, whom locals began to call “Papá Tortuga,” or Turtle Father. Over half a century later, his efforts have expanded to include other members.

To date, the nonprofit has protected and released thousands of baby turtles each year. Visitors arrive year-round to receive public education and help to release newborn turtles into the water along the beaches on the city’s northern outskirts, about a 20-minute drive from the town’s center, along a mostly deserted dirt path.

Camping under the stars in Tecolutla

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Kate Levasseur (@katelevass)

I personally drove out to experience it for myself. Depending on your budget, you can rent a group-sized or personal tent near the beach at a campsite that includes outdoor showers, bathrooms and a common area for campers and volunteers who arrive at different hours of the day to participate in the turtle release. The camp area is shaded by palm trees and is relatively cool due to the strong coastal breeze.

The camping experience adds a layer of memory-making, as you sleep beneath the moonlight on a private, mostly isolated beach while the waves wash ashore in the near distance. A rotation of Vida Millenaria workers takes turns patrolling the area on ATVs around the clock, mostly to keep an eye on the turtles and their nests. (Note: If you decide to camp overnight, be sure to bring plenty of supplies, water and food, as a one-way trip back into town requires more than 20 minutes of off-roading to reach the edge of Tecolutla). There, you can enjoy a paradisiacal beach to yourself, undisturbed, until the next day.

A volunteer brigade assembles

Early in the morning, around 7:30 a.m., volunteers of all ages begin to arrive and assemble at the center of camp. A local expert introduces the nonprofit’s history, and a musician plays music dedicated to sea turtles. Maps and visuals are used to show and explain a brief history of turtle conservation in the state, and an adult-sized turtle replica stands in as a faux mascot for guests to take pictures with.

Afterwards, participants are escorted to the nearby souvenir shop, where everything is turtle-related (of course) and handmade. Each purchase grants a set of baby turtles for group liberation — so the more things you buy, the more turtles you’re able to liberate (prices start around 150 pesos and include turtle plushies, stuffed animals, mugs, shirts, etc.). For breakfast, a local volovanero (a savory pastry vendor common in Veracruz) brings a freshly baked batch for about 50 pesos each.

Releasing hatchlings into the wild

Then, the finale: Everyone strolls down to the beach together, lines up, and is given baby turtles to release into the ocean together. It’s a spectacular sight to see upwards of 50 small creatures — more or less, depending on the volunteer group’s size that day — crawling their way into the waves for the first time. They are swept away, their tiny heads occasionally poking out from the shimmering waters before completely disappearing into the distance by the dozens.

Of course, if you’re nowhere near Veracruz, you can search for your nearest beach. You’ll likely discover a turtle conservation group awaiting your participation. It makes a memorable weekend trip — and most importantly, it helps to keep an essential part of Mexico’s ecosystem intact.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: Anuel AA Monterrey Concert Postponed: Mexico Show Moves From 17 September to 8 April 2027
World.content:
MEXICO · MUSIC

Key Facts — What happened The Anuel AA Monterrey concert set for 17 September 2026 has been postponed to 8 April 2027.

— How big Estadio Borregos holds about 10,057 people and sits on the Tecnológico de Monterrey campus.

— What it means Ticket holders now wait almost seven months, or claim a refund through Ticketmaster instead.

— The catch The stadium is an open-air football ground, so there is no roof over the seats.

— Who it affects Local fans, plus visitors who booked flights or hotels around the September date.

— What comes next The show returns on 8 April 2027, and the Guadalajara date moved to 15 April 2027.

The Anuel AA Monterrey show at Estadio Borregos is not happening this week. Promoter OCESA has moved the Mexico date to Thursday 8 April 2027.

The Estadio Borregos in Monterrey. The stadium has no roof, which is why an April date changes what you should pack. (Photo: “Estadio Borregos, 2019.” by Diegonyc, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

If you hold a ticket for the Anuel AA Monterrey concert on 17 September, do not go to the stadium. The Puerto Rican singer’s Mexico date has been pushed to April 2027.

What changed, and when

Anuel AA was booked to play Estadio Borregos on Thursday 17 September 2026. The show was billed as a stop on his Real Hasta La Muerte tour.

On 27 August the promoter OCESA said the date was off. It gave the reason as causas de fuerza mayor, a Spanish legal phrase for events outside a company’s control.

OCESA did not explain further. Its Guadalajara date of 19 September moved to 15 April 2027, at the Coliseo GNP Seguros.

The Monterrey show now sits on Thursday 8 April 2027. The venue stays the same.

Tickets, prices and refunds

OCESA said every ticket already bought stays valid for the new date. You do not need to swap it or print a new one.

If April does not work for you, you can ask for your money back. Box office refunds opened on 31 August 2026.

Online buyers use the help button inside their Ticketmaster México account. People who paid at a counter go back to that same counter.

Original prices ran from 1,066 pesos (about US$63) in the Plata tier to 2,914 pesos (about US$172) in Platino. Floor tickets were listed at 1,761 pesos (about US$104) and 2,468 pesos (about US$146).

Currency conversions use the 13 September 2026 rate of 16.96 pesos to the US dollar, from er-api.com. Prices for the April date have not been confirmed.

Who Anuel AA is

Anuel AA is a Puerto Rican singer and rapper born Emmanuel Gazmey Santiago. He works in trap and reggaeton, two Latin urban styles built on heavy bass.

He broke through in 2018 with the album Real Hasta la Muerte. The phrase means real until death, and it now names both his brand and this tour.

His songs are fixtures on Spanish-language streaming playlists across Latin America. Crowds at his stadium shows sing along rather than listen quietly.

Tickets for his Latin American dates are sold city by city. A ticket bought for one country does not transfer to another.

The Rio Times reported earlier on his December dates in Santiago de Chile. Those are indoor arena nights, and they are listed separately from the Mexican leg.

What Estadio Borregos is

Estadio Borregos belongs to the Tecnológico de Monterrey, a large private university. Its home team is the Borregos Salvajes, the university’s American football side.

It sits in Distrito Tec, the neighbourhood wrapped around the campus in southern Monterrey. The address is Avenida Ricardo Covarrubias, in Nuevo León, the northern Mexican state whose capital is Monterrey.

The ground opened in April 2019 and holds about 10,057 people. That makes it small for a stadium show.

Signs at the ground may read Estadio Banorte, a sponsor name added in 2021. Ticket listings still call it Estadio Borregos, where Dua Lipa, Muse and Imagine Dragons have played.

Distrito Tec has hotels, cafes and student bars within walking distance of the gates. That makes it easy to arrive early and wait nearby.

The open-air catch

This is a football field, not an indoor arena. There is no roof over the pitch and none over most of the seating.

Monterrey sits in a dry basin ringed by mountains, and it runs hot. April afternoons often reach about 30C (86F), with little shade at the gates.

September, the original slot, is the wetter end of the year here. The move to April lowers the rain risk but raises the sun risk.

Plan for the queue, not just the concert. A hat, sunscreen and water before you go in will matter more than they would indoors.

Getting to Distrito Tec

Metrorrey is the city metro, and its published station lists show no stop inside Distrito Tec. You will finish the trip by bus, taxi or ride-hailing app.

Uber and DiDi both operate in Monterrey. Drivers know the campus well, because it is one of the city’s landmarks.

The campus sits beside Avenida Eugenio Garza Sada, a busy road into the centre. Traffic around the gates builds for hours before a stadium show.

Organisers have not published dedicated parking for the April date. If you drive, plan on private lots in the surrounding streets.

Agree a pickup point a few streets away for the ride home. Phone signal near the exits is often poor when everyone leaves at once.

Entry rules and what to bring

Gates at Mexican stadiums usually open one to two hours before the music starts. Songkick lists doors for the April 2027 date at 9:00 pm.

Security is airport-style. Expect small bags only, no professional cameras, and no outside food or drink.

Bring photo identification and the card you paid with. Listings note that staff may ask for both at the door.

Keep your original booking email even after the date change. It is the proof that links your old ticket to the new night.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Anuel AA concert in Monterrey still happening?

Not in September. OCESA postponed it, and the show is now set for 8 April 2027 at Estadio Borregos.

What is the new date for Anuel AA at Estadio Borregos?

Thursday 8 April 2027, at the same venue in Distrito Tec. The Guadalajara show moved to 15 April 2027.

Are tickets bought for 17 September 2026 still valid?

Yes. OCESA said all tickets bought for the original date stay valid for April, with no exchange needed.

How do I get a refund for the postponed Monterrey show?

Online buyers use the help button in their Ticketmaster México account. Counter buyers go back to the original point of sale, which began refunds on 31 August 2026.

World.title: wave to earth Mexico City: Korean Band Plays Pepsi Center WTC on 15 September, Mexico’s Grito Night
World.content:
MEXICO · MUSIC

Key Facts — What happened South Korean indie band wave to earth play the Pepsi Center WTC on 15 September.

— How big The hall is an indoor venue, far smaller than the stadiums used by touring pop acts.

— What it means Quiet Korean indie music now fills mid-sized Mexican rooms, not only the big arena tours.

— The catch The concert falls on El Grito night, when independence crowds and road closures grip the city.

— Who it affects Anyone heading to Colonia Nápoles that evening, including drivers, Metrobús riders and ticket holders.

— What comes next Tickets are sold through Ticketmaster México, and the show is listed to start near 20:00.

The wave to earth Mexico City show falls on El Grito night, the biggest street party in Mexico. Here is what that means for tickets, transport and timing.

The World Trade Center tower in Mexico City. The Pepsi Center WTC sits in the same complex, on the edge of the Napoles district. (Photo: “Aerial view World Trade Center Mexico 03 2014 MEX 7842” by Mariordo (Mario Roberto Durán Ortiz), via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.)

The wave to earth Mexico City concert lands at the Pepsi Center WTC on Tuesday 15 September. The South Korean indie band is bringing The Pieces Tour to Mexico for one night only.

What is happening at the Pepsi Center WTC

wave to earth are an indie and alternative band from Seoul, South Korea. They play soft, jazz-tinged guitar songs, and they sing in both Korean and English.

The Mexican capital is one stop on The Pieces Tour. It is the only Latin American date announced on that run.

The show is set for Tuesday 15 September at the Pepsi Center WTC. Mexican listings put the start at 20:00 local time, so plan on a late finish.

One international listing shows 19:00 instead, and Songkick puts doors at 20:15. Check the time printed on your own ticket before you leave.

Tickets are sold through Ticketmaster México, the country’s main ticketing platform. Resale sites also carry seats, usually well above the original counter price.

The band has not announced a second Mexican date. Treat this as a single visit rather than the start of a short residency in the capital.

Where the venue sits, and how to reach it

The Pepsi Center WTC is not a stadium. It is an indoor hall attached to the World Trade Center complex in Colonia Nápoles.

Nápoles lies in the Benito Juárez borough, south-west of the historic centre. It is a calm grid of offices, taquerías and mid-century apartment blocks.

The Metrobús is the closest link. Metrobús CDMX names Poliforum on Line 1 as the nearest station to the World Trade Center.

The nearest Metro station is San Pedro de los Pinos on Line 7, about 15 to 20 minutes on foot. Metrobús Line 1 runs along Insurgentes Sur from Roma, Condesa and Del Valle.

There is paid parking beneath the World Trade Center. It fills early on event nights, so public transport is the simpler choice for most visitors.

El Grito falls on the very same night

Here is the part the concert listing does not mention. The night of 15 September is El Grito, the country’s independence celebration.

El Grito means the cry, and it recalls the 1810 call to arms against Spanish rule. President Claudia Sheinbaum gives it from the National Palace at 11 pm.

Every borough stages its own version, with live music, fireworks and street food. Crowds fill the plazas, and many streets close to traffic for the night.

That matters for your travel plans. Ride-hailing prices climb sharply, the historic centre gets sealed off, and stations near celebrations get very busy.

The concert should finish well before the main Zócalo ceremony begins. Even so, give yourself a generous buffer in both directions.

What the ticket categories actually mean

Ticketmaster México lists seven price tiers for this show. The published prices already include the ticketing service charge.

General B is the cheapest at MXN 930 (about US$55). Sección C follows at MXN 1,240 (about US$73), then Box Superior at MXN 1,860 (about US$110).

Sección A costs MXN 2,356 (about US$139), and the accessible zone is priced the same. Platino is MXN 2,728 (about US$161).

Corona Lounge is the dearest tier at MXN 2,852 (about US$168). Listings do not say where each block sits, so open the seat map before you buy.

Currency conversions use the 13 September 2026 rate of 16.96 pesos to the US dollar. That rate comes from the exchange data service er-api.com.

How Korean indie music found a Mexican audience

Korean pop has had a solid base in Mexico for a long time. What is newer is the quiet, indie side of that scene selling real tickets here.

wave to earth grew mostly through streaming playlists and short video clips. Their songs travel well because the mood carries more than the words do.

The city has leaned into Korean culture in other ways too. Our report on the free K-Expo festival at the same venue covers that side of it.

Bigger Korean acts are touring the region this season as well. We covered aespa opening their Latin American run in São Paulo this month.

The Pepsi Center WTC sits neatly in the middle of that shift. It is small enough for a cult act and central enough for a weeknight crowd to fill.

Staying nearby on a holiday night

If you are visiting, sleeping close to the venue saves you the worst of the traffic. Nápoles and Del Valle both sit within walking distance.

Roma and Condesa are the usual expat picks, and they are a short ride north. Both neighbourhoods throw their own independence parties in the street.

The historic centre is the wrong base for this particular night. Access tightens around the Zócalo, and getting back in after a concert is slow.

Book a room early if you still need one. Domestic travellers fill the capital’s hotels around the independence holiday every single year.

Banks and government offices close on 16 September, the public holiday that follows. Some shops and restaurants keep short hours, so plan an early flight carefully.

Practical tips for a busy Tuesday night

Arrive earlier than you normally would. Security lines move slowly when a holiday crowd is already out on the streets around the venue.

Dress for a warm hall and a cool street. September nights in the capital often turn chilly, and heavy rain is common after dark.

Eat before the show, or eat in Nápoles. The neighbourhood has plenty of taquerías and small restaurants within a few blocks of the hall.

Plan how you get home before the encore. Do not book anything that depends on a quiet road, because this is not a quiet night in the city.

If you want the independence party too, head out afterwards. Local celebrations in Nápoles and Del Valle run well past midnight.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is wave to earth playing in Mexico City?

The concert is on Tuesday 15 September 2026 at the Pepsi Center WTC in Colonia Nápoles. Listings show the music starting around 20:00 local time.

How much do wave to earth tickets cost in Mexico?

Ticketmaster México lists seven tiers, from MXN 930 (about US$55) to MXN 2,852 (about US$168). Those prices include the service charge.

How do I get to the Pepsi Center WTC by public transport?

The Metrobús Line 1 stop Poliforum is the closest station to the World Trade Center. The nearest Metro is San Pedro de los Pinos on Line 7, 15 to 20 minutes on foot.

Does the concert clash with El Grito in Mexico City?

It falls on the same night as the independence celebration. The main Zócalo ceremony runs late in the evening, after the concert should already be over.

World.title: Myke Towers Guadalajara: September 18 Show Is Missing From the Auditorio Telmex Calendar in Mexico
World.content:
MEXICO · MUSIC

Key Facts — What happened The Myke Towers Guadalajara concert set for 18 September is gone from the Auditorio Telmex calendar.

— How big The hall seats 8,712 people and is owned by the Universidad de Guadalajara.

— What it means Ticket sites still sell a night that the venue itself no longer lists for September.

— The catch Nobody has announced a cancellation, so holders have no refund window and no new date.

— Who it affects Ticket holders in the metro area, plus visitors who booked travel around 18 September.

— What comes next The booking already moved once from 27 May 2026, and no third date has been announced.

The Myke Towers Guadalajara concert was listed for Friday 18 September at the Auditorio Telmex. The venue’s own September calendar no longer shows it.

The Auditorio Telmex in Zapopan. The University of Guadalajara hall no longer lists the 18 September booking. (Photo: “Auditorio telmex” by Jorge Blanco dragon, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

The Myke Towers Guadalajara show was booked for Friday 18 September 2026 in western Mexico. The Auditorio Telmex no longer lists that concert on its published calendar.

What the venue calendar shows

The Auditorio Telmex publishes its own month-by-month programme. Its September 2026 page lists eight shows, and none of them is this concert.

That page still carries dates from earlier this month. The 18 September slot is simply not on it.

The venue’s event page for the booking now returns an error. It no longer loads the listing that search results still point to.

Cancelled shows at this hall usually stay online with the word CANCELADO in the title. This one was taken down instead.

The hall’s calendar can be filtered by month and by year. The September 2026 view is the one that omits the booking.

Our roundup of the Auditorio Telmex September lineup covers the rest of the month at the same hall.

What the ticket listings still say

Songkick still shows the concert for Friday 18 September 2026 and marks it on sale. It gives both doors and start time as 21:00, or nine at night.

Two local event sites, Conciertos Guadalajara and Tudu, also still carry the date. All three put the venue at Avenida Obreros de Cananea 747 in Zapopan.

Listing sites often lag behind a venue by weeks. A hall’s own calendar is the better guide when the two disagree.

StubHub México shows no event for this artist at this venue. Ticketmaster México is the seller named on the listings that remain.

How the date got to September

The booking was first set for Wednesday 27 May 2026. Songkick still prints the line ‘Fecha original: 27 de mayo de 2026’.

TV Azteca reported the move on 8 May 2026. The artist wanted more time to prepare new music and a bigger stage show.

That report said May tickets stayed valid for the new night. It also said refunds opened on 15 May 2026.

So 18 September was already the second date printed for this booking. No third date has been announced.

The rest of the Mexico run

The tour was billed as the Myke Towers Gira México 2026. Other stops on it have since fallen away.

On 27 August local outlets reported three cancellations. Veracruz on 17 September, Cancún on 19 September and Torreón on 2 October were all dropped.

The Veracruz date had been booked at the Auditorio Benito Juárez. The Cancún show was set for the Plaza de Toros there.

Refunds for those dates run through Boletea and SuperBoletos. No public reason was given for the cancellations.

El Gráfico reported in August that some fans had waited months for their money. Those complaints concern earlier cancelled dates, not this one.

What the Auditorio Telmex is

The Auditorio Telmex is a concert hall owned by the Universidad de Guadalajara, the state’s public university. It opened on 1 September 2007.

The room seats 8,712 people. It is widely described as the main show venue in western Mexico.

It stands on the university’s Los Belenes campus in Zapopan, not in central Guadalajara. Zapopan is a separate city, joined to Guadalajara by an unbroken stretch of streets.

The hall is roofed and seated throughout. Ride-hailing apps such as Uber and DiDi reach it from anywhere in the metro area.

Our Guadalajara cost of living guide explains what taxis and nights out normally cost here. It is worth a look if the city is new to you.

Who the artist is

Myke Towers is a rapper and singer from Puerto Rico. He works mainly in reggaeton and Latin trap, two Spanish-language styles built over heavy beats.

Reggaeton grew out of Panama and Puerto Rico in the 1990s. Latin trap is its slower, darker cousin, borrowed from the southern United States.

He has played this city before. A local music site reported a show by him at this same hall in August 2025.

His North American dates run under the name La Pantera Negra Tour. The Mexican leg was billed separately, under its own name.

What ticket holders should do now

Do not book flights or hotels around this date yet. Ask Ticketmaster México in writing whether your ticket is still valid.

Keep your original booking email and your card statement. Both are proof of purchase if a refund window opens.

Public listings do not show a ticket price for this date. Treat neat round figures on resale pages with suspicion.

Check the venue’s own programme page before you travel. It is the first place a restored date would appear.

Organisers have not announced a cancellation for this night. They have also not confirmed that it is going ahead.

More: Mexico news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Myke Towers still playing in Guadalajara on 18 September 2026?

That is unclear. Ticket sites still list the show, but the Auditorio Telmex no longer has it on its own September calendar.

Has the concert at the Auditorio Telmex been cancelled?

No cancellation has been announced. The venue’s event page has been taken offline, which is not the same as a public cancellation.

Was this date moved before?

Yes. The booking was first set for 27 May 2026 and moved to 18 September, with May tickets kept valid.

What should I do with my ticket?

Ask Ticketmaster México in writing before you travel. Keep the original booking email and your card statement as proof of purchase.

World.title: Merida El Grito 2026: Free La Adictiva Concert on the Plaza Grande in Mérida, Mexico, 15 September
World.content:
MEXICO · CULTURE

Key Facts — What happened Mérida marks Mexican independence with a cry at 11 pm on 15 September on the Plaza Grande.

— How big More than 200 municipal police will cover the historic centre across 15 and 16 September.

— What it means The free La Adictiva concert starts about 11:15 pm and the centre closes to traffic.

— The catch September 16 is the holiday, yet the celebration runs the night before, so arriving on the 16th means missing it.

— Who it affects Anyone in Mérida can attend free, including the city’s large United States and Canadian communities.

— What comes next A civic and military parade starts at 8 am on 16 September at Paseo de Montejo.

Merida El Grito happens on the night of 15 September 2026, not on the public holiday itself. Here is how the evening runs in Mérida, Yucatán, and where to stand.

An ordinary evening on the Plaza Grande in Mérida. On 15 September the same square fills for the cry of independence at 11 pm and the concert that follows. (Photo: “Inflatable toys and plaza grande at night Merida Mexico” by amanderson2, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.)

Merida El Grito is the high point of Mexico’s independence night, and it falls at 11 pm on Tuesday 15 September. The cry comes from the Palacio de Gobierno on the Plaza Grande, and a free concert follows.

What the Grito is, and why it happens at night

El Grito is short for the Grito de Independencia, the cry of independence. It is a short ceremony, not a speech.

It recalls Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla, a parish priest in Dolores, Guanajuato. Before dawn on 16 September 1810 he rang his church bell and called his parish to revolt.

That call began the war that ended in Mexican independence. The date on the calendar is the 16th, but the bell rang in the small hours.

So the re-enactment is held late on the evening of the 15th. The president does it in Mexico City, and state governors do it in their own capitals.

In Yucatán the governor leads it. Reports name Joaquín Díaz Mena for the 2026 ceremony in Mérida.

The 15 September programme on the Plaza Grande

A cultural programme opens the night on the Plaza Grande at 8 pm. That is three hours before the ceremony itself.

The cry is given at 11 pm from the Palacio de Gobierno, the state government building on the square. It takes only a few minutes.

A free concert by La Adictiva follows at about 11:15 pm on the same square. There is no ticket and no seating plan.

Nothing on the night costs money. You pay only for food, drink and your ride home.

The square is open to everyone, with no ticket and no reserved seating area. Families come early and stay late.

Who La Adictiva are

The full name is La Adictiva Banda San José de Mesillas. The band comes from Mesillas, in the municipality of Concordia in the state of Sinaloa.

They play banda sinaloense, a brass and percussion style from Mexico’s northwest. Think tubas, clarinets, trombones and a very loud drum line.

The group formed in 1990 and is one of the better known names in regional Mexican music. Hits include “Después de ti” and “Peligro de extinción”.

This is stadium-volume music played outdoors after midnight. If you want an early night, leave once the short ceremony ends.

Organisers have not published how long the set will run. Dress for a late night outdoors in the September heat.

Where to stand and when to arrive

The Plaza Grande is Mérida’s main square, framed by the cathedral and the colonial arcades. The Palacio de Gobierno faces it, and the cry comes from its balcony.

Get there well before 10 pm if you want a view of that balcony. The square fills from the cultural programme onwards.

Police will run security filters and access control at the entry points. Last year the state banned large bags, glass bottles and alcohol, so travel light.

Agree a meeting point with your group before you go in. Mobile signal gets patchy once the square is packed.

Our expat guide to El Grito in Mexico City covers how the same night runs in the capital.

Closures, transport and staying safe

More than 200 officers of the Mérida Municipal Police, or PMM, will work the historic centre on 15 and 16 September. The state public security force backs them up.

Streets around the square close to traffic for both nights. The municipal police chief said the plan was almost final and would follow last year’s scheme.

Do not try to drive to the Plaza Grande. Walk in, or have a taxi or app car drop you several blocks away.

Buses thin out badly after midnight. Plan the trip home before the concert starts, not after it.

Last year the state set up breath-test points across the city on these nights. Nothing is confirmed for 2026, so check local notices and leave the car at home.

Why 16 September is the real holiday

16 September is Mexico’s Independence Day and a federal day of obligatory rest. Banks and government offices close, and many shops keep short hours.

Sort out any paperwork, transfers or bank errands before the 15th. Nothing official moves on the Wednesday.

The civic and military parade starts at 8 am on 16 September. It sets off from the Remate de Paseo de Montejo and finishes at the Parque de San Juan.

Shade along that route is thin and the morning heats up fast. Bring water, a hat and sunscreen, and stake out a spot early.

Mérida has a well-established foreign community, with many residents from the United States and Canada. If you are new here, our guide to things to do in Yucatán is a good next stop.

More: Mexico news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What time is El Grito in Mérida in 2026?

The cry is set for 11 pm on Tuesday 15 September, from the Palacio de Gobierno on the Plaza Grande. The cultural programme opens at 8 pm.

Is the La Adictiva concert in Mérida free?

Yes. The concert on the Plaza Grande is free and open to all, starting at about 11:15 pm once the ceremony ends.

Is Mexican Independence Day on 15 or 16 September?

The holiday is 16 September. The Merida El Grito ceremony is held late on the 15th, because Hidalgo made his call before dawn in 1810.

What is closed in Mérida on 16 September?

It is a federal day of obligatory rest, so banks and government offices close. Streets in the historic centre also close for the 8 am parade.

Sunday on the northern half of this continent is a trade war that has moved from the podium to the pantry. Washington is scheduling bans, Ottawa is collecting tariffs, and Canadian shoppers have started enforcing their own sanctions at eye level. Two days after the twenty-fifth anniversary of September 11, the neighbourly psychogram has a new texture: the relationship is not broken, but it is being itemised.

Read in English and French, across both countries’ largest outlets and our own North America desk. Domestic only: no sport, no foreign wars.

The Trade War Comes To The Supermarket

Reuters reports that Canada’s consumer boycott — buy Canadian, boycott American — is reshaping supermarket shelves, forcing grocers to improve labelling and find new suppliers. A boycott that changes shelf layout has crossed from sentiment into infrastructure; it is the difference between being angry and being organised.

Washington’s answer is a calendar. Dairy, most alcohol and motorcycles from Canada face a ban from 29 September; a fifty per cent tariff on goods including mattresses, motorboats and golf carts takes effect on 15 September. Canada’s counter-tariffs — a multi-billion-dollar package of duties at varying rates — are already in force. Both governments now speak in dates and percentages, which is what trade wars do when they intend to stay.

Ottawa: Hardening, Politely

Prime Minister Carney says Canada will move faster to reduce its economic reliance on the United States now that the retaliatory tariffs are in effect — a sentence that would have been unthinkable in an election speech and is now a governing programme. In Quebec, Premier Christine Fréchette is already working the politics of the rupture, which in Canada means the rupture is real enough to campaign on.

The Guardian finds Canadians simply angry — at the tariffs, at the 51st-state talk, at the tone. Canada’s temperament this Sunday is the coldest kind: not outrage, but reorientation. A neighbour that stops expecting the relationship to recover stops building for it, and Ottawa is quietly reordering a century of assumptions into a spreadsheet marked “alternatives”.

Washington: The Deal That Is Always Coming

Trump said again this week that a deal with Canada is coming “fairly soon”, in remarks carried by Canadian outlets — the same phrase, a week older, against a backdrop of newly scheduled bans. The promise and the escalation are not a contradiction in this White House; they are the two handles of the same lever.

Underneath the theatre, the domestic number of the week is three point four. Consumer prices rose at that annual pace in August, matching July and firming expectations of a rate move — inflation that refuses to fall is the one opponent the tariff strategy cannot ban. Washington’s psychogram is confidence with a sore tooth: performing strength, quietly testing the molar.

The Anniversary, Two Days On

Friday marked twenty-five years since September 11, and the weekend’s reflective coverage in both countries — CBC’s national package among it — carried the shared memory the trade war has been trampling. A quarter-century ago the border thickened overnight in the name of security; this month it thickens again in the name of tariffs, and the anniversary made the echo audible.

Public life otherwise goes on at full domestic volume: the lettuce parasite outbreak was declared over after nearly thirteen thousand cases across twenty-one states and two deaths, and Washington’s culture skirmishes — artificial intelligence anxieties, pressure on the Smithsonian — continue in the background. A country’s ordinary news does not stop for a trade war; it merely files it under “also”.

What This Means From Latin America

Mexico is the silent third party at this table. Canada and Mexico have both signalled they want the continental trade pact renewed; Washington has not joined them — and every tariff Washington schedules against Ottawa is a clause Mexico City reads twice. Latin America’s largest lesson from this weekend is that the pact is no longer a floor — it is a negotiating position, and positions move.

The Canadian boycott deserves Latin America’s closer attention. A consumer movement that relabels shelves is doing what no communiqué could: making the tariff visible at the checkout. From the Mexican boycotts of past decades to Chile’s consumer politics, the region knows that when shoppers join a diplomatic dispute, the dispute has found its longest-lasting weapon.

What We Are Watching

15 September: the fifty per cent tariff on mattresses, motorboats and golf carts — applied, or postponed at the last hour.

29 September: the dairy, alcohol and motorcycle bans — and Canada’s counter-calendar.

Any named round of renewed pact negotiations with Mexico at the table.

The next inflation print after August’s three point four per cent, and the rate path it implies.

Whether the boycott’s shelf changes persist into the holiday quarter, when margins are decided.

Carney’s first concrete “reliance reduction” measure — the programme behind the sentence.

The Bigger Picture The continent’s two closest economies are learning to fight like strangers while still living like neighbours. The tariffs are dated, the boycott is shelved in, the deal is always coming. What to watch is not the next ban but the first retreat — whoever blinks after 15 September will have priced the whole quarrel.

Frequently Asked Questions

What new measures did Washington schedule this weekend?

A ban on Canadian dairy, most alcohol and motorcycles from 29 September, and a fifty per cent tariff from 15 September on goods including mattresses, motorboats and golf carts. Canada’s multi-billion-dollar package of counter-tariffs on American goods is already in force.

Is the Canadian boycott actually changing anything?

Yes, visibly. Reuters reports supermarkets relabelling products and re-sourcing suppliers as shoppers reject American goods. A boycott that reorganises shelves has moved from mood to mechanism.

Where does the promised US–Canada deal stand?

Trump said again this week that a deal is coming “fairly soon”. Nothing has been signed, and the tariff calendars on both sides are running meanwhile — treat the phrase as leverage, not as a date.

What did the August inflation number say?

American consumer prices rose three point four per cent year on year, matching July. That steadiness at an elevated level is what firms up expectations of a rate move — and what makes the tariff fight expensive at home.

Sources: Reuters, CTV News, CBC, The Guardian, WTOP, SCMP, The New York Times, Congress.gov, and the Rio Times North America desk. Figures carried with their outlets and dates.

Sunday in Europe is an election day stacked on the morning after an election nobody finished talking about. Sweden votes with the far right at the door; Germany is a week into its Saxony-Anhalt shock and discovering that the aftershock is the story. Around them, the continent is doing quieter arithmetic: Paris counting the cost of an apology, London counting a crypto billionaire’s money, Madrid counting cubic metres of gas. The register is unease administered by spreadsheet.

Read in English, German, French, Spanish, Italian and Polish, across the continent’s largest outlets and our own Europe desk.

Stockholm: Voting With The Door Open

Sweden votes all day in a general election that could put the Sweden Democrats — a party with neo-Nazi roots — inside a government for the first time, Al Jazeera and Reuters report; polls close at 20:00. Friday’s Ekot poll read the left bloc at 50.8 per cent against the right’s 47.6, and Prime Minister Kristersson has already promised the hard right cabinet jobs if his bloc holds — which turns entry from surprise into contract.

Whatever the count says by midnight, the quarantine loses. Either the Sweden Democrats take ministries, or every coalition conversation runs through them. A week after Saxony-Anhalt, Europe is holding two referendums on the same question in two countries — and tonight’s answer arrives first.

Germany: The Week After The Earthquake

Forty-three point eight per cent. The AfD’s Saxony-Anhalt result of 7 September — thirty-nine of eighty-three seats, three short of governing alone — has had a week to settle, and it has not settled. Merz, whose party fell to seventeen point two per cent in the state, spent the week warning that parts of the economy are in a very critical condition, which is a chancellor naming the fuse and the dynamite in one sentence.

Berlin’s own forecasters have now signed the diagnosis, in the government’s updated projections reported this weekend. Growth this year is projected at zero point five per cent, halved from one per cent; next year was cut to zero point nine; inflation ran at two point nine per cent in August. Germany’s psychogram is a specific one: a country that believes its virtues are procedural, confronting a result that procedures did not prevent. The question in Berlin this Sunday is no longer whether the firewall holds, but what it was protecting.

Paris: An Apology, Precisely Worded

France has issued the United States a statement of regret over their diplomatic spat — well received in Washington, France 24 reports — as the frozen approval of its incoming ambassador, Aurélien Lechevallier, comes up for release. The gesture costs Paris a headline and buys it an ambassador; the Élysée has always known the exchange rate.

At home, the louder row is cultural. Radio France staff are striking over the appointment of a far-right weekly’s editor, and the state broadcaster’s corridors are arguing about who French public speech belongs to. Between an apology abroad and a strike at home, Paris this weekend is conducting both halves of its national debate at once — how to face Washington, and who faces France.

London: Thirty-Six Million Pounds Of Momentum

Reform UK has been given a record donation of thirty-six million pounds by a British crypto billionaire, The Guardian reports; other tallies count seventy-two million pounds in total recent donations to the party, and both figures are carried here as reported. Either way, Britain’s insurgent right is no longer running on grievance alone — it is capitalised.

The government’s Sunday counterweight is administrative: clearer guidance on student loans after a repayment row. A party funded like a hedge fund against a state answering with guidance notes is the whole of British politics in one contrast. Westminster’s temperament is the anxiety of incumbents who have noticed that the money has stopped being embarrassed.

Madrid: Counting Cubic Metres

Spain is entering the final stretch to meet the gas-storage target set by Brussels, EFE reports, against an energy market in which the Iran war is driving fossil-fuel prices upward. Storage targets are the least visible form of national security, and the most honest — a tank either fills or it does not.

Madrid’s mood is disciplined worry: a country that has done this before, doing it again with worse weather. The filling of the tanks will not make a front page unless it fails, which is precisely why it belongs in this brief.

What This Means From Latin America

The week’s quietly Latin American scene is a French-Canadian one: Macron and Canada’s prime minister will visit France’s North Atlantic islands after a Trump map post redrew a border in pixels. Two middle powers affirming a rock in the ocean is a reminder that territory in this decade is defended by visits as much as by fleets — a logic Latin America knows from the Malvinas to the Essequibo.

The German lesson travels further south. A model economy that halves its growth forecast while its far right more than doubles its vote is the exact sequence Latin America has lived through in several capitals — and the region’s experience says the economics is settled first and the politics is settled second, never the reverse. Brasilia and Buenos Aires will read Berlin’s zero point five per cent as a forecast about more than Germany.

What We Are Watching

Sweden’s count from 20:00 — entry, arithmetic or relief, and what Berlin reads into each.

Berlin’s next procedural move on Saxony-Anhalt — coalition arithmetic, legal review, or studied silence.

Whether the German forecast cuts land as a budget argument or as a campaign gift.

The new French ambassador’s arrival date in Washington, and the price tag attached.

Radio France’s strike: settled by retreat, or by escalation into a wider media fight.

Reform UK’s next accounts filing — whether the crypto money is a moment or a pipeline.

Spain’s storage percentage at the next reporting date, against the Brussels target.

The Bigger Picture Europe’s Sunday is a continent auditing itself: its votes, its money, its gas, its manners. The audits all rhyme — each capital is discovering that a thing it assumed was settled is merely current. Putin’s “system errors” heckle from Friday is only the rude version of the continent’s own question this weekend: which of these systems is still working as designed?

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is a state election from 7 September still the lead?

Because its consequences are still arriving. Forty-three point eight per cent for the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt, three seats from an absolute majority, is being absorbed this week by Berlin’s coalition arithmetic, the chancellor’s economic warnings, and now the forecasters’ cuts — the result was an event, the aftermath is the story.

How bad are Germany’s new forecasts?

Growth this year was cut to zero point five per cent from one per cent, next year to zero point nine from one point three, with August inflation at two point nine per cent. Not a collapse — a stall, which for Europe’s largest economy is its own kind of emergency.

Did France really apologise to the United States?

Paris issued a statement of regret that Washington received well, per France 24, as the frozen approval of ambassador-designate Aurélien Lechevallier comes up for release. The substance of the original spat matters less than the form of the settlement: Paris decided the embassy mattered more than the point.

How much money did Reform UK actually get?

The Guardian reports a record single donation of thirty-six million pounds from a British crypto billionaire; other coverage counts seventy-two million pounds across the party’s recent donations. This brief carries both figures as reported rather than merging them.

Sources: Reuters, Al Jazeera, Deutsche Welle, France 24, The Guardian, EFE, CNBC, ABC, Ekot, and the Rio Times Europe desk. Figures carried with their outlets and dates; conflicting tallies are printed as conflicts.
