World.title: Piastri hit twice on first lap, Antonelli wins thanks to safety car luck
World.content:
Oscar Piastri and George Russell made contact with each other twice before the first corner, as Kimi Antonelli took full advantage of a fortunate safety car to win the Formula 1 Spanish Grand Prix.

Piastri finished eighth in the maiden grand prix at the brand-new Madring circuit, driving most of the race with a damaged front wing.

The Australian started seventh on the grid and got a fair start off the line. Russell, starting sixth, cut across Piastri and made contact with the Australian's front wing.

The pair made contact again while braking for the first corner, with Piastri's front left colliding with the rear of Russell's car.

Part of Piastri's damaged wing flapped in the breeze as the Australian tried to finish as high as he could.

Piastri went deep into the race before pitting, emerging back on track in 11th.

The Australian battled back in the final laps to climb back up to eighth.

Norris cruelled by safety car, Antonelli tightens grip on title with win

An ill-timed safety car cost reigning world champion Lando Norris the chance of victory in Spain, as Kimi Antonelli's win gave the young Italian an 81-point lead in the drivers' championship.

Kimi Antonelli has now won eight grands prix this season. (Reuters: Albert Gea)

Norris, who started on pole, had a healthy lead over Antonelli on lap 14 of 57 when misfortune struck the McLaren driver.

Aston Martin's Lance Stroll went off the track, leading to a virtual safety car being called.

Norris had passed the entrance to the pit lane moments before the VSC was deployed, meaning he had to drive at 40 per cent speed while others behind him, including Antoenlli and Max Verstappen, took a cheap pit stop.

As Norris approached the pit entrance on lap 15 the VSC ended and he pitted while his rivals were able to race at full speed.

McLaren also had a slow stop thanks to an issue with changing the front right tyre, meaning he dropped from first to sixth.

"Tough race, one that just got away from us," Norris said.

"I felt like we deserved it today, but that's racing. We'll take it on the chin and try again next time."

Ferrari's Charles Leclerc did not pit and led the race from Antonelli.

Leclerc stayed out until lap 48 of 57, and with the Madring proving hard to pass on, Antonelli, Max Verstappen and Norris were bunched up behind him, setting up a tense finish.

Once Leclerc pitted, Antonelli was able to drive in clean air and pulled away from Verstappen, who was able to hold off Norris for second place.

"It was a very difficult race, not straightforward at all," Antonelli said post-race.

" It's good to win, but it doesn't feel as good because I think Lando deserved the win. "

While Antonelli claimed his eighth grand prix win of the season, his nearest rivals in the championship were off the podium.

Mercedes teammate Russell placed fifth, while Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton retired early with a brake failure.

Antonelli's lead in the drivers' championship is a big 81 to Russell, and 101 points to Hamilton with either eight or nine race weekends remaining, depending on whether F1 can race in the Middle East at the end of the year.

World.title: 'Put them together': Trump reiterates call for unified Ireland after UK dismissal
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has reiterated his support for Northern Ireland to break from the United Kingdom and unify with the Republic of Ireland, but said he would not talk about Scotland becoming independent "yet".

"You have Northern Ireland and you have Ireland and it would seem to me that one of the naturals of all time is to put them together," Mr Trump told reporters on Sunday during a visit to the Irish Open golf tournament.

"You asked about Scotland. That one I won't talk about yet. I'll save that for another day," he added.

The president's fresh comments on Ireland double down on a statement made in Dublin on Saturday.

Donald Trump spoke to reporters on Sunday during his visit to the Irish Open golf tournament. (Reuters: Kylie Cooper)

"Well, I don't want to cause any problems, but I will tell you, I'd love to see it unified," Mr Trump told reporters after a meeting with Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin in Dublin.

" The way I look at it, it's going to happen eventually ... I think it would be a fantastic thing. "

The UK prime minister's office responded that its position on Irish unity was unchanged.

Turning his attention to US domestic issues, Mr Trump told reporters the United States can easily afford his promise to send US adults a $US5,000 "dividend" if his Republican Party keeps control of Congress after midterm elections.

He announced the plan earlier this week, drawing skepticism from legal experts, opponents and even some Republicans.

US President Donald Trump gestures during the Amgen Irish Open 2026, at Trump International Golf Links in Doonbeg, County Clare, Ireland, September 13, 2026. (Reuters: Cathal McNaughton)

"I don't know but it's easy if the Republicans win," he said on Sunday.

"Five thousand dollars to all adults in the country and we can easily handle that because we're taking in so much money," Mr Trump told reporters when asked if Congress would need to approve the pledge.

"The Democrats can't make that pledge because it would all go to hell right away, we'd go into a depression.

"I made that pledge, I always keep my pledge."

Reuters

World.title: Russian strike on Ukraine-Poland border shows war at Europe's 'doorstep'
World.content:
Fresh Russian strikes in close proximity to NATO sites have stoked fears among some European leaders that the war between Ukraine and Russia is spilling across borders.

A Russian attack on a truck near Ukraine's border with Poland was confirmed by Polish and Ukranian officials on Sunday.

The attack marks the latest strike to hit areas near NATO nations as Moscow and Kyiv intensify their long-distance strikes to try to shift momentum in the war.

A Russian drone struck near the Ukrainian-Polish border in the small town of Yahodyn, Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said, which is only 2km from Poland.

"Russia's barbaric strikes at the Ukraine-Poland border in Yahodyn are not just a continuation of its attacks on our state borders," Mr Sybiha said on X.

"This is Putin's terror 'knocking' directly on the doors of the EU and NATO. Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners," he added.

Polish border guards said that the Dorohusk-Yahodyn crossing point had briefly stopped working after the attack around 800 metres from Poland, but that the crossing had since resumed operations.

Fears the Russia-Ukraine war is expanding

Lithuania also briefly closed Vilnius airport on Sunday, local time, in response to a possible sighting of a drone, prompting NATO to summon at least one fighter jet, the National Crisis Management Centre said.

Lithuania later said the sighting turned out to be a flock of birds.

Russia resumes strikes on Kyiv after weekend ceasefire It came as Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin held an hour-long phone conversation about talks between their envoys in recent days.

The air alert was lifted and the airport reopened within 38 minutes, after the NATO jet made a visual identification, Lithuania's National Crisis Management Centre said.

"On initial radar readings, marks left by birds and drones can be similar," it added in a statement.

Military drones straying into the airspace of Finland, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania are stoking concerns that the war in Ukraine is spilling over into NATO's northern borders with Russia.

Transport sites near Ukraine-Poland border targeted

In a separate statement, Ukrainian Railways said that in Volyn — another region bordering Poland, — a drone attacked the locomotive of a passenger train just 2km from the Polish border.

The company said no-one was injured.

A passenger train in Lutsk was also hit in a Russian drone strike over the weekend. (Reuters: supplied )

Ukraine operates several border crossings with Poland, through which a significant proportion of the military and humanitarian aid from its allies is delivered to the country.

Russia's Defence Ministry said it had targeted infrastructure facilitating military cargoes from Europe in Western Ukraine.

Ukraine is dependent on trade and arms shipments from across the Polish, Romanian and Moldovan borders.

Russia has begun targeting Ukraine's border crossings with its Western allies in recent weeks, as part of a growing campaign by both sides to erode the other's economic infrastructure more than four years into Russia's invasion.

Putin told the war in Ukraine must end

In India, where Russian President Vladimir Putin had been attending the BRICS summit, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that both Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping had offered help brokering a peace settlement, Russian state news agency TASS reported.

Last month, at a summit in Kyrgyzstan, Mr Modi told Mr Putin that the war must end, one of several calls for peace by leaders of nations that have traditionally strong relations with Russia.

Narendra Modi (left) has told Vladimir Putin that the war must end. (Pyotr Kovalyov via Reuters)

Last month, Kazakhstan's President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev publicly told Mr Putin that he should halt the conflict along the front line, which has remained largely static this year.

Russia has ruled that out, saying Ukraine should pull back to leave the industrialised eastern Donbas region in Moscow's hands, something Kyiv has said it will never do.

Both Brazil and China, themselves founding BRICS members, have called for a resumption of peace talks.

TASS cited Mr Peskov as saying that Mr Putin had informed Mr Modi of the situation "on the ground" in Ukraine, and that Russia had not ruled out resuming three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States in October.

Ukraine strike nuclear power plant in Russian-held territories

Overnight, hostilities showed no signs of letting up.

In the Russian-held part of Ukraine's southeastern Zaporizhzhia region, the head of Russia's state nuclear energy company Rosatom accused Ukraine of striking fuel trucks close to the Zaporizhzhia nuclear power station, Europe's largest.

Russia currently controls the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant in southern Ukraine. (Reuters: Alina Smutko)

The Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant has been controlled by Russia since March 2022, and remains close to the front line.

A Ukrainian military spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Russia, Ukraine to halt strikes on capitals during peace talks Vladimir Putin and Volodymyr Zelenskyy have agreed to halt strikes on their respective capitals.

In Russia itself, the mayor of the city of Nizhnekamsk, in the Volga River region of Tatarstan, said that "civilian and industrial" targets in the city had been struck by Ukrainian drones, causing at least two deaths and several more injuries.

Mayor Radmir Belyaev did not clarify which targets had been struck, but the city hosts a major oil refinery which has been attacked in the past.

Ukrainian authorities did not immediately comment on the strike on Nizhekamsk, but did say they had struck another refinery in the southern Krasnodar region.

ABC/Reuters

World.title: Cowboys back in the saddle as Alice Springs Rodeo returns
World.content:
The dust was flying and cowboys were hitting the dirt as the Alice Springs Rodeo returned after a year out of the saddle.

More than 2,000 spectators in total visited the arena at Blatherskite Park on Saturday, watching competitors take on bucking bulls and horses, while some of the youngest riders tried their luck on poddy calves.



For Aileron Bush Club secretary James Christian, the response showed how much the event had been missed.

"It's electric," he said.

"People are really glad to have a rodeo back on here in town.

"There's people from all different parts of society here, all cheering … they're enjoying the spectacle."

James Christian says the rodeo brought the community together. (ABC News: Chris Murrkarany Fitzpatrick)

Mr Christian said the event drew organisers and competitors from across a huge stretch of the Territory.

"The committee comes from probably a diameter of about 1,000 kilometres," he said.

"We've all converged on Alice Springs to put on this show.





[ Young competitors took part in horse and poddy calf events. (ABC News: Chris Murrkarany Fitzpatrick) "But it takes the whole community to help make that happen."

Young riders take their turn

Among those preparing to enter the arena was 10-year-old Lucy Muenstr, who was competing on the poddy calves.

She said she was more excited than nervous about getting into the arena.

"It's pretty fun," she said.

"You can just watch everyone fall off, and that, and it's just funny sometimes — but it's not funny if someone hurts themselves."

Ten-year-old Lucy Muenstr was excited to take on the poddy calves. (ABC: Chris Murrkarany Fitzpatrick)

Another young rider, 12-year-old Ollie McKay, had travelled 300 kilometres and was also hoping to leave with a buckle.

"I enjoy it, and it's just, like, the fun and the feel," he said.

"I just like riding and just like the cattle and all that."

For a cowboy veteran, 41-year-old rider Garyshane James, who has competed in rodeos for about 25 years, seeing another generation taking part was an important part of the event.

"Kids that get here — amazing young fellas getting in and having a go and keeping the cowboy spirit going," he said.

"Rodeo was our key to get out and see our mates."

Garyshane James has competed in rodeos for about 25 years. (ABC: Chris Murrkarany Fitzpatrick)

Three competitors taken to hospital

The dangers of the sport were also on display.

Three competitors were taken to hospital after being injured during the rodeo and were reported to be in a stable condition and recovering.

Three competitors were taken to hospital after being injured during the 2026 Alice Springs rodeo. (ABC: Chris Murrkarany Fitzpatrick)

Rodeo announcer Ricky J. Morrison said injuries were an accepted risk for many competitors.

"The cliché saying for rodeo is it's not if you get hurt, it's when," he said.

"If you do it long enough, you're going to get hurt."

He said the difference in size between riders and bulls made the risks clear.

"When a cowboy weighs anywhere from 50 to 100 kilos, and the bulls weigh anywhere from 450 to 600 kilos … you're probably going to come out second best sometimes," he said.

Rodeo announcer Ricky Morrison (right) says getting hurt is an accepted risk of the sport. (ABC: Chris Murrkarany Fitzpatrick)

Animal welfare concerns remain

While the crowd cheered on the competitors, not everyone was tipping their hat to the rodeo.





Di Evans has written numerous papers on rodeo for the RSPCA (Supplied: RSPCA) RSPCA Australia senior scientific officer Di Evans said the organisation remained opposed to rodeos because of concerns about the animals involved.

"We oppose rodeos on animal welfare grounds because of the high risk of pain, injury, fear [and] stress," she said.

Dr Evans said behaviours including head tossing, showing the whites of the eyes and excessive salivation could indicate distress in bucking animals.

" Great for a spectacle, but not so good for the animals. "

She acknowledged rodeos could provide social connections and contribute to the identity and economy of regional communities, but argued those benefits could be achieved in other ways.





Sam Webb pocketed $3,000 after winning the Open Bull Ride and shoot-out. (ABC: Chris Murrkarany Fitzpatrick) "If there's other ways that people can … connect with this culture and this focus without harming animals [and] display these skills through another way," she said.

Sam Webb cleans house

In the end, the competition produced a clear winner.

Territory cowboy Sam Webb, 38, won the Open Bull Ride before taking out the final shoot-out, earning $1,500 for each victory and pocketing $3,000 in total.

Mr Webb said there was no secret to his success.

"It's just like a hard day at work," he said.

"You work hard, you get the results.

"I was due for a bit of money."

He said he was never worried about taking on the bull that ultimately delivered his win.

"That's the fella I wanted, the big red fella," he said.

Mr Webb said beyond the competition, the rodeo offered something less tangible but no less valuable.

"It just brings the community together, brings everybody together," he said.

"It's a time to meet and greet and have a good time."

After the hiatus in 2025, organisers have described the rodeo as a "peak success" and hope to get back in the saddle again next year.

World.title: Kangaroos survive Blues scare to keep AFLW record alive
World.content:
Ash Riddell racked up 39 disposals as North Melbourne survived a scare to keep its record AFLW winning run rolling with a 10-point victory over Carlton.

In other results on Sunday, Melbourne defeated Port Adelaide 11.8 (74) to 2.11 (23) at Casey Fields, Richmond beat St Kilda 9.4 (58) to 6.7 (43) at Windy Hill, Sydney got past cross-town rivals GWS 13.9 (87) to 8.8 (56) at Henson Park, and Fremantle downed Essendon 5.7 (37) to 3.4 (22).

In front of more than 3,500 supporters at Arden Street, a boilover was on the cards after the Blues kicked back-to-back goals against the breeze in the second quarter to take a three-point lead.

The match was still in the balance in the dying minutes, with Carlton's Lily Goss having the chance to close a 10-point deficit to four after taking a mark 35 metres out.

But not realising there was a player behind her, Goss played on and was immediately tackled, with the moment proving Carlton's last chance to fire a shot as the Kangaroos held on to win, 4.9 (33) to 3.5 (23).

Riddell was unstoppable throughout, while Jasmine Garner (30 disposals, five clearances, one goal) was also a significant contributor for the victors.

The Kangaroos have a 5-0 win-loss return this season.

They have won a record 32 straight matches since drawing with Geelong in round two of 2024.

Riddell said her team embraced the challenge thrown down by the Blues.

"We love it, and we had that against Brisbane a couple of weeks ago," Riddell told the Seven Network.

"We get excited by that. You could see the girls smiling as they came in at three-quarter time. We want that challenge, so it's great."

Although Carlton dropped to a 4-1 win-loss record, the strong display against the Kangaroos has fuelled their belief.

"We would have loved to have won, so we're a little bit disappointed, but also super proud," said Blues captain Abbie McKay following her 27-disposal, five-clearance effort.

"We lost by [53 points] last year, so it shows we're really growing as a team.

"We're here to win, and we're here to win a grand final. Although we lost, it shows we're improving."

Riddell was everywhere in the first term on the way to 15 disposals and four inside 50s.

Goals against the breeze to Nell Morris-Dalton and Lila Keck thrust Carlton into a shock lead early in the second term, but a 40-metre set-shot from Tahlia Randall followed by Blaithin Bogue's goal on the run ensured the Kangaroos entered the long break with a nine-point advantage.

Randall suffered a scary moment in the third quarter when she hyperextended her left elbow, but she was able to return after receiving treatment.

The stand-out moment of the third quarter was a two-bounce, tackle-busting effort from Carlton speedster Goss that helped set up a goal to Erone Fitzpatrick.

Garner's late major ensured the Kangaroos headed into three-quarter time with an eight-point lead, and there were no goals scored in a frantic final term.

AAP

World.title: Screen time to be capped for NSW students to improve results
World.content:
Students in NSW public schools will be limited to as little as 15 minutes of screen time per day, under guidelines announced by the state government.

The 15-minute limit will apply to students from kindergarten to year 2.

Students in years 3 and 4 will have up to 30 minutes of daily classroom screen time, increasing to 45 minutes for years 5 and 6.

The guidelines will become mandatory from 2028. (ABC News)

The guidelines will be introduced next year, but will not become mandatory until 2028.

Education Minister Prue Car said children needed to get back to basics, including using pens and paper.

"There's just too much screen time for our young people in our school system," she said.

"We want to make sure that at school it's not the default, that the default is pen and paper."

Screen time limits will be more relaxed for high-schoolers, with digital learning allowed to make up 25 per cent of a subject's coursework for years 7 to 10.

Students in years 11 and 12 will be able to spend half their class time on digital devices like laptops and tablets.

Ms Car says there is too much screen time in schools. (ABC News: Nick Dole)

Raising standards

The state government said the screen time limits were designed to arrest a "worrying trend" of falling academic results.

Ms Car said according to the OECD's Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), Australian students were nearly twice as likely to spend more than two hours a day learning using digital devices than the OECD average.

Global results show Aussie students' struggles Australian students have recorded their lowest-ever scores in maths and reading in international testing, but improved on their science results.

Last week, PISA data also showed reading and mathematics scores for15 year olds in NSW were going backwards.

"There's no doubt the two are linked, and they're linked around the world," Ms Car said.

Education secretary Murat Dizdar said while technology would continue to play an important role in classrooms, imposing screen time limits would help students concentrate.

"It's about backing in the research and evidence that our own students and our teachers are telling us around avoiding distractions in the learning process."

Digital detox a 'relief' for students

While mobile phones have been banned in all NSW classrooms for several years, some schools have recently been trialling their own limits on other forms of screen time.



Chatswood High School principal, Robin Chand, said since paring back the use of digital devices, staff had noticed an improvement in students' handwriting and engagement.

"I know that this will be welcomed by students because students directly tell me that they feel relieved at times when they are working directly with pen and paper and their course books," Mr Chand said.

"When screens go down, relationships go up.

"And the relationships that are the most important in our classroom are relationships between the students and their teachers," he said.

Mr Chand says that "when screens go down, relationships go up". (ABC News)

Seventeen-year-old student, Archie Newman, said learning with hard copy books, pens and paper had allowed him to slow down and think more deeply, without the temptations of a laptop or tablet.

"I was someone who could get distracted so easily with digital technology," he said.

"And [now] the emphasis on handwriting is allowing me and my learning experience to be maximised."

World.title: 71yo motorcyclist dies after hitting pothole on highway
World.content:
A motorcyclist has died after hitting a pothole on the Western Highway in Victoria's south-west this afternoon.

Victoria Police said emergency services were called to the Western Highway in Trawalla after reports that a motorcycle had struck a pothole and lost control at around 12:50pm.

The rider, a 71-year-old Ballarat man, died at the scene.

"The exact circumstances surrounding the crash are yet to be determined and will be investigated," a Victoria Police spokesperson said.

All westbound lanes were closed on the Western Freeway between Windermere and Beaufort.

It comes just days after a new report from Victoria's auditor-general found almost half of Victoria's road network is in poor condition and crumbling faster than the government can repair it.

Victoria Police has urged anyone with dashcam footage to contact Crime Stoppers.

World.title: 'Can't get boy's face out of my head': Witness retells Sydney carjacking
World.content:
A bystander who attempted to protect two children during a pursuit and carjacking in Sydney's south-west, described the moment a man allegedly lunged at him with a knife.

About 3pm on Saturday, police were called to carry out a welfare check on a 36-year-old man in Lakemba, but he fled in a vehicle with two children, who police confirmed were his sons.

Officers engaged in a short pursuit through the Campsie area, which they said was called off due to the "manner of the man's driving".

The car crashed in Lidcombe at the intersection of Parramatta Road and Bombay Street. (ABC News)

The car crashed at the intersection of Parramatta Road and Bombay Street at Lidcombe, about nine kilometres away, where members of the public attempted to intervene after the father got out of the car with the boys.

Nicholas Karagiannis was driving along Parramatta Road when he came across the crash scene.

While rendering assistance to the driver, the 46-year-old said he heard bystanders yell, "He's getting away" and "He's got children".

Mr Karagiannis said he chased after the man, who was allegedly attempting to enter other vehicles while armed with a knife.

Witness Nicolas Karagiannis. (ABC News)

Instinctively, Mr Karagiannis said he wanted to make sure the two boys were okay, but "everything happened so fast".

"He had a knife in his hand, he did not look well," he said.

" I can't get that boy's face out my head. "

Video shows Mr Karagiannis and several other men attempting to subdue the father in the middle of a busy road.

At one point Mr Karagiannis managed to grab one of the young boys "but the boy wanted to go back".

"They were just crying …in shock, my heart bleeds for those kids," he said.

Mr Karagiannis said he pleaded with the father to let the children go to no avail.

A woman was thrown out of a black Cerato. (ABC News)

In the video, the man appeared to bundle the boys into a black Kia Cerato, and moments later the female driver is forcibly thrown from the car.

Police said he allegedly threatened the woman with what they described as "a small black knife".

"I just did what I think anyone else would do in that situation [when] you see a guy with a knife and two young boys," Mr Karagiannis said.

The children, aged between five and seven, suffered minor injuries and were expected to be released from hospital on Sunday.

Second altercation

Inspector Mark Wakeham said a member of the public had unsuccessfully tried to remove the keys from the Cerato's ignition, sustaining a laceration to his hand as the father sped off with the two children inside.

The vehicle came to a stop on the M4 near the overpass of Greystaynes Road before being approached by members of the public, including an off-duty police officer, Inspector Wakeham added.

Bystanders this time managed to restrain him before police arrived.

Police praised the actions of bystanders who tried to help. (Supplied)

Inspector Wakeham described their actions as "incredibly brave".

" They did a wonderful job and we'd like to thank members of the public for assisting us with this case. "

He ruled out the incident as an act of kidnapping.

The man remained under police guard in hospital on Sunday where he was charged with three offences, including aggravated robbery with wounding, police pursuit and reckless wounding.

In the afternoon he appeared in court from hospital via a video link.

He did not apply for bail with the matter adjourned until September 24.

World.title: The specialists charging eye-watering mark-ups on medical fees
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalHealthcare The specialists charging eye-watering mark-ups on medical fees Brittany Busch September 14, 2026 — 4:08am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australians paid more than five times the benchmark price for a visit to a specialist doctor on more than a million occasions last year, the Department of Health has found. Health Minister Mark Butler has put “excessive” specialist fees in his sights as Labor attempts to ease persistent cost of living pressures on Australians. But his department has also uncovered a broader affordability problem: specialist out-of-pocket costs have been rising at twice the rate of inflation over the past decade. Health Minister Mark Butler has vowed to crack down on price-gouging doctors. Alex Ellinghausen Australians paying for out-of-pocket, out-of-hospital specialist fees last year were charged $458 more than they were in 2019, according to a department consultation paper into specialist affordability released this week. That’s a more than 75 per cent jump, to $4.17 billion.



In-hospital gap fees for those with private health insurance rose almost as sharply over the same period, the paper found. Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare ‘Out of control’ specialist fees will be Labor’s next health priority The department acknowledged the “significant community concern” over the rising cost of healthcare, and it said the government was concerned about the pace with which specialist fees were increasing. But it said its paper was primarily focused on excessive fees charged by a “small minority of providers on top of these general fee increases”. Specialist healthcare cost more than five times the benchmark price on 1.24 million occasions last year. Another 6 million services were billed at between three to five times the schedule fee. The government determines the benchmark schedule fee for services, and providers can set their own prices on top.



Dermatologists charged the most above the benchmark for out-of-hospital services, and had the highest proportion of patients paying five times the schedule fee. Obstetricians, gynaecologists and sports and exercise specialists followed. In hospital, anaesthetists charged the most above the benchmark. The department said many providers recognised their ethical obligations to ensure fees for healthcare were reasonable. “However, analysis of the fees charged by providers indicates there are providers who are charging fees that are significantly higher than their peers,” its paper said. The department said limited transparency over how costs were set, the imbalance of power between the provider and patient, and excessive fees were compromising access to specialist services. Those with chronic health conditions or in need of ongoing psychiatric care faced a greater financial burden when returning to the same high-fee provider, the paper said.



Private Healthcare Australia chief executive Dr Rachel David called for Labor to do more to tackle rising costs as the Australian Bureau of Statistics reports millions of Australians are delaying or going without healthcare due to the cost. Related Article Disability As Labor’s NDIS overhaul passes, Mark Butler says states have more work to do “The government should not stop at the most extreme outliers. Excessive fees are the sharpest edge of a much broader affordability problem: specialist fees and gaps across the market have been creeping up much faster than inflation for years,” David said. She said the organisation supported the measures the government was considering through a parliamentary inquiry, including fee caps, incentives to encourage more bulk billing, and consequences for unreasonable pricing. David said one in three people referred to a specialist doctor were not attending, according to Private Healthcare Australia surveys.



“This is causing delayed diagnoses, avoidable complications and people to need invasive, expensive hospital care that could have been prevented,” she said. “That undermines the value of health cover and adds pressure across the entire health system.” The organisation has also found some patients paying thousands of dollars more for procedures that cost others nothing. Its data show the median fee for a knee replacement in 2024-25 was $1080, but 10 per cent of patients had been charged more than $5300. “Private health insurance cannot protect patients from every medical bill. Health funds are legally limited in what they can cover outside hospital, and no-gap and known-gap arrangements depend on doctors choosing to participate. When specialists charge well above those arrangements, the extra cost falls directly on patients,” David said. Butler said Labor had made improving specialist affordability a priority for its second term.



“I’ve asked my department for advice on options to start to get this huge growth in out-of-pocket costs back under control,” he said, pointing to the inquiry into specialist fees, which is taking submissions until October. He said Labor was also fixing the former government’s Medical Costs Finder by publishing information about specialists and their billing. “Australians deserve transparency, fair pricing and confidence their premiums are being directed where they are needed most,” he said. “I expect private health insurers and hospitals to work hard to bring down costs and keep future price increases to a minimum.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Forget the Cleary chaos. These Panthers moments tell the true tale of another epic
World.content:
Analysis SportNRLNRL 2026 Forget the Cleary chaos. These Panthers moments tell the true tale of another epic Dan Walsh September 14, 2026 — 4:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Penrith can enjoy a beer and a lie down. The Roosters, the same, with the knowledge they’ve revived the form of a month ago that was feared lost. But they go again in six days’ time, because as good as they were in Sunday’s epic 19-12 east-west showdown, the Panthers were that tiny bit better, not necessarily in the moments that mattered most. Loading But in the moments in between. The moments that truly make premiership-winners, and those that Penrith have made their own for a dynasty and more. The Panthers started Sunday on fire. Liam Martin screamed four-letter sweet nothings as he scored his opening try and they should have had more to show for their early dominance.



But when Rob Toia iced the Roosters first attacking opportunity of the afternoon, and Mark Nawaqanitawase reeled in a Cirque du Soleil intercept that only he could have pulled off, the Tricolours held a shock 10-6 lead. They’d nailed the big, juicy moments and deserved every bit of it. “There is a theory,” Phil Gould ruminated in Channel Nine commentary, “that if you get them behind on the scoreboard, they do become a different sort of team and you can bustle them.” True. But the Panthers can hustle themselves. They did just that throughout the seven minutes of ball-in-play that stretched out either side of the half-hour mark. The Roosters gamely went with them. Until they didn’t. Victor Radley, who had already clocked 26 tackles in a busy opening 35 minutes, threw a tired forward pass that brought a break in play and Panthers attacking scrum. A few plays later, Nathan Cleary swung play back through the middle, sending Dylan Edwards screaming past an exhausted Radley and into the in-goal for Penrith’s second try.



One of the moments in between and the moment that matters collided rather nicely right there. Minutes later came the ugly collision that had Cleary running right through Hugo Savala’s kicking leg. Knowing exactly what he had done, Cleary grimaced, scolded himself and looked ready to keep on running right on through the suburb of Parramatta. Rugby league’s voracious media will spend the next 48 hours analysing that from every possible angle, from every possible grassy knoll.



As far as moments go, it was as big and juicy as they get. But the 10 minutes Cleary spent cooling his heels, agonising away his time in the Commbank naughty corner? Penrith didn’t concede a point. Only once did they look like doing so. It was Savala who almost stole his way over from a scrum straight after halftime. Isaiah Papalii and Edwards scrambled their way across to stop him on the tryline. The Bunker got involved in dubious fashion, prompting Gould to blow up over the way momentum is governed in tryscoring situations and replays are used in slow-motion and real-time. It’s a valid and worthy debate, but not one we’re having here. Once the replays were run and done though, Penrith played their way through their one-man deficit deftly, and never let the Roosters back down their own for another moment more.



When Cleary did return, he did so to an impromptu countdown from the Commbank crowd. Mark it down as another moment in the little black book, because not even Spencer Leniu can work the masses like that. Related Article Analysis

NRL 2026 Roosters go down but Nawaqanitawase magic breathes life into their season The Roosters, gallant to the end, had their chances throughout an enthralling second half and they know it. None more than Daly Cherry-Evans – it’s hard to recall him shanking too many field goals quite like he did like in the 73rd minute, just minutes after Cleary had nailed home his own wonky one-pointer. Big, juicy moments. They matter most after all. Along with of course, how Cleary clattered into Savala’s right leg. Not to mention the champion No.7’s own hobbled right foot.



But the moments in between all that, those chunky, six and 10 minute stretches when you know you’re really, well and truly alive, and trying to stay that way in a game of rugby league – they’re still what Penrith treasure just as much after all these years.

World.title: Kimi Antonelli wins the Spanish GP; Early collision costs Piastri dearly
World.content:
Oscar Piastri’s increasingly underwhelming and unlucky 2026 season has taken another hit, finishing eighth after an early contact in the opening lap of the Spanish Grand Prix.

In a race marred by botched pitstops and ill-timed safety cars, Kimi Antonelli came out on top piloting his Mercedes to victory to strengthen his championship lead.

Kimi Antonelli has won the Spanish Grand Prix AP Photo/Bernat Armangue

Dutchman Max Verstappen finished in second, with pole sitter Lando Norris in third.

“It was a very difficult race - not straightforward at all, especially trying to manage tyres,” Antonelli said in a post-race interview.

“I think today it’s good to win but it doesn’t feel as good because I think Lando today deserved the win but overall, we [will] take it.”

It was an unfortunate day for McLaren, with Piastri suffering early contact on the opening lap and Lando Norris losing the lead of the race after missing the pitstop window during a virtual safety car.

Lando Norris had a horrifically slow pitstop. AP Photo/Manu Fernandez

Norris then weathered an agonisingly slow 7 second pitstop – a mixture of human error and a wheel gun problem. The reigning world champion still managed to salvage his race to secure a podium position.

Meanwhile Piastri– who started in seventh after a self-described “pretty shocking qualifying session” – had a solid start, but was hit twice by George Russell in the opening lap, before the first corner.

The Mercedes cut it in front of Piastri and the impact sent debris flying. It left Piastri with damage to his left front wing and marooned him back to 11th place.

McLaren CEO Zak Brown summarised the situation perfectly, noting the racing gods “were cruel today”.

Piastri still produced a commendable drive, showcasing stunning overtakes on Arvid Lindblad and had a great battle with Franco Colapinto.

He managed to get back into the points and clinch eighth place.

Speaking after the race, Piastri said: “It was pretty, pretty painful from Lap 1. And not much I could’ve done from there.“

“The timing of the VSC (virtual safety car) was certainly not ideal for us, starting on the hard… It was just a difficult afternoon.”

This weekend marks the first time F1 has raced at the Madring – the first track to debut on the F1 calendar since Las Vegas was added in 2023

The 57-lap circuit is 5.44km long and has incredibly fast corners and basically no margin for error, with limited overtaking opportunities.

The Spanish GP in Madrid is a hybrid street circuit. AP Photo/Manu Fernandez

Turn eight – “El Bunker” – is named after La Mata Espesa, two bunkers built in 1936 by the Republican forces to protect the eastern flank Madrid from attack during the Spanish Civil War.

The new hybrid street circuit has been one of the most highly anticipated tracks this year, with George Russell describing it as the “the most risky” track on the calendar and Lewis Hamilton characterising it as “massively challenging circuit”.

Meanwhile, Alpine driver Pierre joked that he’d hit the wall multiple times during his simulation trials for the new track.

Overall, most of the drivers fared reasonably well – excluding Lewis Hamilton and Lance Stroll who both retired from the race.

The next race will be the Azerbaijan Grand Prix in Baku on September 26.

Kimi Antonelli leads the 2026 Formula 1 Drivers’ Championship by 81 points.

World.title: WA teacher sentenced over trespass, threats to kill neighbour’s dogs
World.content:
Exclusive NationalWACourts WA teacher sentenced over trespass, threats to kill neighbour’s dogs Holly Thompson September 14, 2026 — 3:35am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A man in his 60s, currently working as a teacher at a northern suburbs high school in Perth, has been found guilty of threatening to kill his neighbour’s dogs, in addition to trespassing on and damaging their property, following a lengthy court process. Stephen Elford was sentenced in Joondalup Magistrates Court on Friday after a two-year process, including a trial following not-guilty pleas to three charges, with the magistrate stating he had “self-evidently lied to police” to avoid consequences. The man was sentenced following a lengthy court process. In October 2024, Elford broke into a neighbouring property in Carabooda by damaging an electric security gate, before threatening to kill the homeowner’s dogs and refusing to leave when asked. In court on Friday, Elford’s lawyer Rachel Robson said in the lead up to the incident there had been “months of tension and previous arguments” over the erection of an adjoining fence.



Elford had two rottweilers and a “bully breed” on his property when one of them was attacked, allegedly by the neighbour’s dogs, leading to a severe injury to its abdomen. The neighbours maintained it was not their dogs who attacked, saying it was not possible due to the fact they were secured in the shed and behind the security gate at the time. Robson said her client “acted in anger” due to what had occurred and the fact his daughter had been extremely upset over the incident. “It’s a case of responding poorly to trauma,” she said. Robson submitted he was a person of prior good character, and was a respected member of the community as both a teacher and a person who regularly fostered dogs, asking for a spent conviction.



She also requested a violence restraining order against Elford was not granted, as there had been no contact between him and his neighbours for more than a year. Both requests were denied, with Magistrate Andrew Maughan making it clear he did not believe Elford was of prior good character given he had deliberately lied to police, in a recorded interview and in court, and had dragged the proceedings out. “I think you will agree that these offences are not trivial,” he said. “And … he lied to avoid the consequences of his own actions.” Maughan said he found Elford had “wilfully and intentionally destroyed” his neighbour’s property and made threats.



“I accept it was a stressful situation, but your response was totally inappropriate. With some hindsight, you should have taken a deep breath,” he said. A restraining order was granted for a period of two years. Maughan said the WA Department of Education would find out about the proceedings regardless of a spent conviction, and the case was in the public interest given his position. “In my view you don’t meet the criteria (for a spent conviction), given the way this trial was conducted … the Education Department should be made aware of the circumstances,” he said. A compensation order for thousands of dollars worth of damage was also requested, which Elford said he would not pay. The fence has not yet been repaired.



“If he wants to get involved in another court case, in the civil courts, that’s up to him,” Maughan said. In a statement, an education department spokesperson said, “without commenting on the particular circumstances of this case, where a teacher is convicted with offences not related to their job, it can still have implications for their employment and registration as a teacher”.

World.title: ‘Humans make mistakes’: Insurer offers discount to self-driving car owners
World.content:
BusinessConsumer affairsGeneral insurance ‘Humans make mistakes’: Insurer offers discount to self-driving car owners Elias Visontay September 14, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Self-driving cars have successfully developed to a point where a major insurer believes they reduce the risk of collision enough to warrant offering some owners using the technology cheaper insurance premiums. Most Australians may not realise they’re already sharing the road with self-driving cars or have full confidence in their safety, but on Monday Zurich Insurance said it will offer discounted premiums to drivers who insure a Tesla that uses Full Self-Driving (FSD) Supervised mode. Tesla’s self-driving in action. Janie Barrett/Cormac Lally The Tesla drivers will be deemed less risky policyholders after early-stage data reviewed by Zurich’s underwriters showed there was lower accident frequency for drivers using the futuristic technology. The underwriters formed the view that the automated trips using FSD were safer than human-driven journeys. FSD mode – which requires a human’s constant supervision to legally operate – became available for owners of certain newer Model 3 and Y Teslas in Australia about 12 months ago, allowing those who pay a $149 per month fee to let their vehicles drive them around.



The technology relies on eight cameras fixed on the car that provides a 360-degree view, which feeds information into a neural network navigation software that processes more than one million pixels of visual data every millisecond to determine how to steer, accelerate, brake and change lanes to navigate to a user’s pre-entered destination. If no destination has been set, the car continues driving straight ahead, while sticking to its lane. Drivers using FSD must be paying attention to the road, with an internal camera monitoring their retinas to ensure they are not distracted and are ready to intervene and take over control should the car make an error. If the car detects that the supervising driver’s eyes are distracted or their hands are holding anything and not otherwise ready to grab the wheel at any moment, a warning will be issued. The car will automatically pull over and deactivate the self-driving option for the rest of a trip if a supervising driver is repeatedly caught failing to pay attention or have their hands free. By requiring supervision to operate, Tesla’s FSD is classified as a Level 2 Advanced Driver Assistance System under Australia’s road rules, with the human behind the wheel considered legally in control of the vehicle. Supervising drivers can intervene to re-take control at any time, whether by choice to redirect or pull over, or if prompted due to issues with the car’s sensors.





During a test drive conducted by this masthead this week, FSD’s handling of roundabouts was smooth, with the car swiftly slowing to respond to hazards and pedestrians during a drive across Sydney. However, the car’s navigation system became confused at times, including when driving through recently updated lane changes off Sydney’s Harbour Bridge. At one point, it attempted to exit using a bus-only lane, and another time it did not recognise a school zone 40 km/h speed limit. Tesla’s Full Self-Driving (Supervised) mode in action. Janie Barrett The inclusion of FSD as a risk rating factor is a first in Australia. Zurich believes it is just the second globally to take the step. Zurich would not specify the exact discount would be in price terms for FSD users. The offer of cheaper insurance comes at a time of surging costs for motorists, with premiums jumping by about 50 per cent between 2019 and 2025.



“As vehicle technology and driver behaviour continues to evolve at an extraordinary pace, it is critical that we continue to innovate alongside this change”, said Alex Morgan, Zurich’s head of general insurance. Related Article Driverless cars ‘You can tell I’m not steering’: Self-driving Teslas hit Australian roads “Humans make mistakes. They get tired. They can be distracted. It’s not that the machine is perfect, but it does appear to be true that on average, across the population and over time, it makes fewer of the mistakes that humans do,” Morgan said. “It should be noted that self-driving technology helps to solve a lot of problems associated with driver error. It does not, however, do much to solve the problem of a tree branch falling on your roof in a storm, a shopping trolley being pushed into your passenger door, hail smashing your windscreen, or your vehicle being stolen,” he said. Thom Drew, Tesla’s Australia director, said the company was pleased to see insurers beginning to recognise the safety benefits of automated driving. “FSD [Supervised] is making driving significantly safer, and it’s encouraging to see ... this [insurance] benefit and reflecting the reduced risk for Tesla owners.”



The reporter tested FSD on a vehicle loaned by Tesla. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: Crows call in police, AFL after ‘disgusting’ message sent to Jordan Dawson
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Crows call in police, AFL after ‘disgusting’ message sent to Jordan Dawson Roy Ward September 13, 2026 — 9:24pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Adelaide Crows have reported a “disgusting” troll attack on captain Jordan Dawson to South Australian Police and the AFL integrity unit. On Sunday, Dawson took to social media, calling out a direct message sent to his Instagram account that had made a self-harm reference towards him following the Crows’ loss to the Brisbane Lions in a semi-final at the Gabba on Saturday night. “There is absolutely no place for this in the world, be better,” Dawson wrote. Adelaide captain Jordan Dawson leads his side out during a game in August. Getty Images The Crows skipper last month won the AFLPA’s Robert Rose Most Courageous Player Award after playing out the season following the tragic death of his eldest brother Jaryd in April. SA Police said at the time that there were no suspicious circumstances surrounding the 35-year-old’s death.



Adelaide has reported the message sent to Jordan Dawson to police. Instagram An emotional Dawson, who was also named vice captain of the All-Australian team, made an inspiring address about mental health at the awards night. “The mental health space is something that’s pretty new and pretty raw to me at the moment, but it’s definitely something that I want to learn a bit more about,” Dawson said on the night. “I just want to wish anyone who’s struggling with mental health to know that you are definitely loved and the world is a better place with you in it. “You are enough, and we all love you, and you have beautiful family and friends around you.”



The Age has chosen not to show the name of the account or repeat the message. The account was set as private on Sunday night. Related Article AFL 2026 Gawn makes All-Australian history, but Dawson’s moving speech steals the show Crows chief executive Tim Silvers spoke up for Dawson and teammate Callum Ah Chee, who also faced post-game abuse on social media. “Unfortunately, this disgusting and disturbing behaviour is becoming more common,” Silvers said on Sunday. “It’s simply not good enough, and it has to stop. There’s no place for it in our community.



“We will provide Jordan and Cal with the appropriate support, as is the case when any of our people are subjected to online attacks and abuse. “We will also be reporting these latest incidents to SA Police and the AFL’s integrity unit.” If you or anyone you know needs support, call Lifeline on 13 11 14, or Beyond Blue on 1300 224 636.

World.title: Blues fail to capitalise on key moments, ruthless Roos extend AFLW unbeaten streak
World.content:
All dynasties eventually have to end. But North Melbourne’s AFLW team are clearly steadfast on remaining immortal for, well, for as long as possible.

On Sunday afternoon 4048 fans packed into a wind-whipped Arden Street Oval, to watch the all-conquering Kangaroos’ reign continue with a tight 10-point win over Carlton – their third-lowest winning margin since their unbeaten streak began after the 2023 grand final defeat.

North have continued their winning streak but other teams are closing in. Getty Images

The ever-dominant Kangaroos also played a draw early in their 2024 premiership season.

North have advanced to a record-extending 32st-consecutive victory. They faced a tough onslaught from Carlton defenders who dimmed the Roos’ typical fast attacking style and managed to keep the margin largely to about one goal.

Carlton’s Harriet Cordner. Getty Images

North coach Darren Crocker conceded the winning margin – the closest a team has come to the Kangaroos all year – was nail-bitingly tight, and said Carlton “threw everything at us”.

“There were lots of almost moments in that game where I thought that we were going to break the game open, but we... to Carlton’s credit, we just couldn’t,” he said.

“They made it, very hard for us to score, we were able to still get there, which was really pleasing.”

Irishwoman Erika O’Shea said the reigning premiers knew “Carlton was going to give it to us”, praising the Blues’ pressure and physicality.

“They’re a young team... they’re fast, and I suppose it was an exhausting game. It was very hot, but I suppose we love the challenge,” she said with a grin.

Carlton announced their intention to challenge the Roos within the opening seconds of the first quarter. The Blues defenders brought a high level of pressure and capitalised on some relieving marks, with Harriet Cordner leading the charge with four intercepts and one intercept mark by the end of the first quarter.

The Blues’ pressure limited Talia Randall to two behinds in the opening term but couldn’t stop Alice O’Loughlin from booting North’s first goal. But two consecutive goals from Nell Morris-Dalton and Lila Keck put Carlton in front during the second quarter, earning a wild cheer from the smattering of Blues supporters in the crowd.

But Randall quickly snatched the lead back with a perfect goal from 45m out, followed by another from Blaithin Bouge.

Carlton Lilly Goss had the job on last year’s best and fairest winner Ash Riddell, dulling the midfielder’s impact briefly. Goss and teammate Erone Fitzpatrick were also at the centre at one of the game’s best moments.

In the third term Goss swooped on the Sherrin and sprinted down the field, dodging a fierce tackle from O’Shea and booting the ball towards the goal. Fitzpatrick almost did a 360-degree turn, scooping the ball up and snapping arguably the best goal of the week in AFLW.

By three-quarter time, the rowdy North Melbourne crowd were noticeably quiet as Carlton sensed a rare opportunity to unseat the Roos. The Blues were within a goal and an animated Carlton coach Matthew Buck came down from the coach’s box to shout instructions from the boundary line.

Ultimately, it was a goalless final quarter with Carlton holding North to only two behinds. But Carlton failed to capitalise on key moments and North held on to win 4.9 (33) to 3.5 (23).

Post-match Buck said his message to the group at three-quarter time was about “continued belief”.

“We felt like we took a good step forward today in the way we want to play, and the way we want to play against a really strong team,” he said.

“You love playing against the best side, and clearly the Kangaroos being the best in the competition for a long time, and they were great against today. You have to beat them, like you have to beat them in all different areas of the ground.”

North Melbourne face Hawthorn next week and the week after have a highly anticipated clash against Melbourne – a match up that could be their biggest test.

Under the stewardship of new coach Tim Wilson, Melbourne remain undefeated in 2026 and are second on the ladder. The Demons face Carlton next week – a match up Crocker said he would be tuning in to.

World.title: The specialists charging eye-watering mark-ups on medical fees
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalHealthcare The specialists charging eye-watering mark-ups on medical fees Brittany Busch September 14, 2026 — 4:08am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australians paid more than five times the benchmark price for a visit to a specialist doctor on more than a million occasions last year, the Department of Health has found. Health Minister Mark Butler has put “excessive” specialist fees in his sights as Labor attempts to ease persistent cost of living pressures on Australians. But his department has also uncovered a broader affordability problem: specialist out-of-pocket costs have been rising at twice the rate of inflation over the past decade. Health Minister Mark Butler has vowed to crack down on price-gouging doctors. Alex Ellinghausen Australians paying for out-of-pocket, out-of-hospital specialist fees last year were charged $458 more than they were in 2019, according to a department consultation paper into specialist affordability released this week. That’s a more than 75 per cent jump, to $4.17 billion.



In-hospital gap fees for those with private health insurance rose almost as sharply over the same period, the paper found. Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare ‘Out of control’ specialist fees will be Labor’s next health priority The department acknowledged the “significant community concern” over the rising cost of healthcare, and it said the government was concerned about the pace with which specialist fees were increasing. But it said its paper was primarily focused on excessive fees charged by a “small minority of providers on top of these general fee increases”. Specialist healthcare cost more than five times the benchmark price on 1.24 million occasions last year. Another 6 million services were billed at between three to five times the schedule fee. The government determines the benchmark schedule fee for services, and providers can set their own prices on top.



Dermatologists charged the most above the benchmark for out-of-hospital services, and had the highest proportion of patients paying five times the schedule fee. Obstetricians, gynaecologists and sports and exercise specialists followed. In hospital, anaesthetists charged the most above the benchmark. The department said many providers recognised their ethical obligations to ensure fees for healthcare were reasonable. “However, analysis of the fees charged by providers indicates there are providers who are charging fees that are significantly higher than their peers,” its paper said. The department said limited transparency over how costs were set, the imbalance of power between the provider and patient, and excessive fees were compromising access to specialist services. Those with chronic health conditions or in need of ongoing psychiatric care faced a greater financial burden when returning to the same high-fee provider, the paper said.



Private Healthcare Australia chief executive Dr Rachel David called for Labor to do more to tackle rising costs as the Australian Bureau of Statistics reports millions of Australians are delaying or going without healthcare due to the cost. Related Article Disability As Labor’s NDIS overhaul passes, Mark Butler says states have more work to do “The government should not stop at the most extreme outliers. Excessive fees are the sharpest edge of a much broader affordability problem: specialist fees and gaps across the market have been creeping up much faster than inflation for years,” David said. She said the organisation supported the measures the government was considering through a parliamentary inquiry, including fee caps, incentives to encourage more bulk billing, and consequences for unreasonable pricing. David said one in three people referred to a specialist doctor were not attending, according to Private Healthcare Australia surveys.



“This is causing delayed diagnoses, avoidable complications and people to need invasive, expensive hospital care that could have been prevented,” she said. “That undermines the value of health cover and adds pressure across the entire health system.” The organisation has also found some patients paying thousands of dollars more for procedures that cost others nothing. Its data show the median fee for a knee replacement in 2024-25 was $1080, but 10 per cent of patients had been charged more than $5300. “Private health insurance cannot protect patients from every medical bill. Health funds are legally limited in what they can cover outside hospital, and no-gap and known-gap arrangements depend on doctors choosing to participate. When specialists charge well above those arrangements, the extra cost falls directly on patients,” David said. Butler said Labor had made improving specialist affordability a priority for its second term.



“I’ve asked my department for advice on options to start to get this huge growth in out-of-pocket costs back under control,” he said, pointing to the inquiry into specialist fees, which is taking submissions until October. He said Labor was also fixing the former government’s Medical Costs Finder by publishing information about specialists and their billing. “Australians deserve transparency, fair pricing and confidence their premiums are being directed where they are needed most,” he said. “I expect private health insurers and hospitals to work hard to bring down costs and keep future price increases to a minimum.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: Forget the Cleary chaos. These Panthers moments tell the true tale of another epic
World.content:
Analysis SportNRLNRL 2026 Forget the Cleary chaos. These Panthers moments tell the true tale of another epic Dan Walsh September 14, 2026 — 4:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Penrith can enjoy a beer and a lie down. The Roosters, the same, with the knowledge they’ve revived the form of a month ago that was feared lost. But they go again in six days’ time, because as good as they were in Sunday’s epic 19-12 east-west showdown, the Panthers were that tiny bit better, not necessarily in the moments that mattered most. Loading But in the moments in between. The moments that truly make premiership-winners, and those that Penrith have made their own for a dynasty and more. The Panthers started Sunday on fire. Liam Martin screamed four-letter sweet nothings as he scored his opening try and they should have had more to show for their early dominance.



But when Rob Toia iced the Roosters first attacking opportunity of the afternoon, and Mark Nawaqanitawase reeled in a Cirque du Soleil intercept that only he could have pulled off, the Tricolours held a shock 10-6 lead. They’d nailed the big, juicy moments and deserved every bit of it. “There is a theory,” Phil Gould ruminated in Channel Nine commentary, “that if you get them behind on the scoreboard, they do become a different sort of team and you can bustle them.” True. But the Panthers can hustle themselves. They did just that throughout the seven minutes of ball-in-play that stretched out either side of the half-hour mark. The Roosters gamely went with them. Until they didn’t. Victor Radley, who had already clocked 26 tackles in a busy opening 35 minutes, threw a tired forward pass that brought a break in play and Panthers attacking scrum. A few plays later, Nathan Cleary swung play back through the middle, sending Dylan Edwards screaming past an exhausted Radley and into the in-goal for Penrith’s second try.



One of the moments in between and the moment that matters collided rather nicely right there. Minutes later came the ugly collision that had Cleary running right through Hugo Savala’s kicking leg. Knowing exactly what he had done, Cleary grimaced, scolded himself and looked ready to keep on running right on through the suburb of Parramatta. Rugby league’s voracious media will spend the next 48 hours analysing that from every possible angle, from every possible grassy knoll.



As far as moments go, it was as big and juicy as they get. But the 10 minutes Cleary spent cooling his heels, agonising away his time in the Commbank naughty corner? Penrith didn’t concede a point. Only once did they look like doing so. It was Savala who almost stole his way over from a scrum straight after halftime. Isaiah Papalii and Edwards scrambled their way across to stop him on the tryline. The Bunker got involved in dubious fashion, prompting Gould to blow up over the way momentum is governed in tryscoring situations and replays are used in slow-motion and real-time. It’s a valid and worthy debate, but not one we’re having here. Once the replays were run and done though, Penrith played their way through their one-man deficit deftly, and never let the Roosters back down their own for another moment more.



When Cleary did return, he did so to an impromptu countdown from the Commbank crowd. Mark it down as another moment in the little black book, because not even Spencer Leniu can work the masses like that. Related Article Analysis

NRL 2026 Roosters go down but Nawaqanitawase magic breathes life into their season The Roosters, gallant to the end, had their chances throughout an enthralling second half and they know it. None more than Daly Cherry-Evans – it’s hard to recall him shanking too many field goals quite like he did like in the 73rd minute, just minutes after Cleary had nailed home his own wonky one-pointer. Big, juicy moments. They matter most after all. Along with of course, how Cleary clattered into Savala’s right leg. Not to mention the champion No.7’s own hobbled right foot.



But the moments in between all that, those chunky, six and 10 minute stretches when you know you’re really, well and truly alive, and trying to stay that way in a game of rugby league – they’re still what Penrith treasure just as much after all these years.

World.title: Kimi Antonelli wins the Spanish GP; Early collision costs Piastri dearly
World.content:
Oscar Piastri’s increasingly underwhelming and unlucky 2026 season has taken another hit, finishing eighth after an early contact in the opening lap of the Spanish Grand Prix.

In a race marred by botched pitstops and ill-timed safety cars, Kimi Antonelli came out on top piloting his Mercedes to victory to strengthen his championship lead.

Kimi Antonelli has won the Spanish Grand Prix AP Photo/Bernat Armangue

Dutchman Max Verstappen finished in second, with pole sitter Lando Norris in third.

“It was a very difficult race - not straightforward at all, especially trying to manage tyres,” Antonelli said in a post-race interview.

“I think today it’s good to win but it doesn’t feel as good because I think Lando today deserved the win but overall, we [will] take it.”

It was an unfortunate day for McLaren, with Piastri suffering early contact on the opening lap and Lando Norris losing the lead of the race after missing the pitstop window during a virtual safety car.

Lando Norris had a horrifically slow pitstop. AP Photo/Manu Fernandez

Norris then weathered an agonisingly slow 7 second pitstop – a mixture of human error and a wheel gun problem. The reigning world champion still managed to salvage his race to secure a podium position.

Meanwhile Piastri– who started in seventh after a self-described “pretty shocking qualifying session” – had a solid start, but was hit twice by George Russell in the opening lap, before the first corner.

The Mercedes cut it in front of Piastri and the impact sent debris flying. It left Piastri with damage to his left front wing and marooned him back to 11th place.

McLaren CEO Zak Brown summarised the situation perfectly, noting the racing gods “were cruel today”.

Piastri still produced a commendable drive, showcasing stunning overtakes on Arvid Lindblad and had a great battle with Franco Colapinto.

He managed to get back into the points and clinch eighth place.

Speaking after the race, Piastri said: “It was pretty, pretty painful from Lap 1. And not much I could’ve done from there.“

“The timing of the VSC (virtual safety car) was certainly not ideal for us, starting on the hard… It was just a difficult afternoon.”

This weekend marks the first time F1 has raced at the Madring – the first track to debut on the F1 calendar since Las Vegas was added in 2023

The 57-lap circuit is 5.44km long and has incredibly fast corners and basically no margin for error, with limited overtaking opportunities.

The Spanish GP in Madrid is a hybrid street circuit. AP Photo/Manu Fernandez

Turn eight – “El Bunker” – is named after La Mata Espesa, two bunkers built in 1936 by the Republican forces to protect the eastern flank Madrid from attack during the Spanish Civil War.

The new hybrid street circuit has been one of the most highly anticipated tracks this year, with George Russell describing it as the “the most risky” track on the calendar and Lewis Hamilton characterising it as “massively challenging circuit”.

Meanwhile, Alpine driver Pierre joked that he’d hit the wall multiple times during his simulation trials for the new track.

Overall, most of the drivers fared reasonably well – excluding Lewis Hamilton and Lance Stroll who both retired from the race.

The next race will be the Azerbaijan Grand Prix in Baku on September 26.

Kimi Antonelli leads the 2026 Formula 1 Drivers’ Championship by 81 points.

Anything can happen in F1. But so far, the Italian is on track to be the youngest world champion in history.

The underwriters formed the view that the automated trips using FSD were safer than human-driven journeys. FSD mode – which requires a human’s constant supervision to legally operate – became available for owners of certain newer Model 3 and Y Teslas in Australia about 12 months ago, allowing those who pay a $149 per month fee to let their vehicles drive them around.



The technology relies on eight cameras fixed on the car that provides a 360-degree view, which feeds information into a neural network navigation software that processes more than one million pixels of visual data every millisecond to determine how to steer, accelerate, brake and change lanes to navigate to a user’s pre-entered destination. If no destination has been set, the car continues driving straight ahead, while sticking to its lane. Drivers using FSD must be paying attention to the road, with an internal camera monitoring their retinas to ensure they are not distracted and are ready to intervene and take over control should the car make an error. If the car detects that the supervising driver’s eyes are distracted or their hands are holding anything and not otherwise ready to grab the wheel at any moment, a warning will be issued. The car will automatically pull over and deactivate the self-driving option for the rest of a trip if a supervising driver is repeatedly caught failing to pay attention or have their hands free. By requiring supervision to operate, Tesla’s FSD is classified as a Level 2 Advanced Driver Assistance System under Australia’s road rules, with the human behind the wheel considered legally in control of the vehicle. Supervising drivers can intervene to re-take control at any time, whether by choice to redirect or pull over, or if prompted due to issues with the car’s sensors.





During a test drive conducted by this masthead this week, FSD’s handling of roundabouts was smooth, with the car swiftly slowing to respond to hazards and pedestrians during a drive across Sydney. However, the car’s navigation system became confused at times, including when driving through recently updated lane changes off Sydney’s Harbour Bridge. At one point, it attempted to exit using a bus-only lane, and another time it did not recognise a school zone 40 km/h speed limit. Tesla’s Full Self-Driving (Supervised) mode in action. Janie Barrett The inclusion of FSD as a risk rating factor is a first in Australia. Zurich believes it is just the second globally to take the step. Zurich would not specify the exact discount would be in price terms for FSD users. The offer of cheaper insurance comes at a time of surging costs for motorists, with premiums jumping by about 50 per cent between 2019 and 2025.



“As vehicle technology and driver behaviour continues to evolve at an extraordinary pace, it is critical that we continue to innovate alongside this change”, said Alex Morgan, Zurich’s head of general insurance. Related Article Driverless cars ‘You can tell I’m not steering’: Self-driving Teslas hit Australian roads “Humans make mistakes. They get tired. They can be distracted. It’s not that the machine is perfect, but it does appear to be true that on average, across the population and over time, it makes fewer of the mistakes that humans do,” Morgan said. “It should be noted that self-driving technology helps to solve a lot of problems associated with driver error. It does not, however, do much to solve the problem of a tree branch falling on your roof in a storm, a shopping trolley being pushed into your passenger door, hail smashing your windscreen, or your vehicle being stolen,” he said. Thom Drew, Tesla’s Australia director, said the company was pleased to see insurers beginning to recognise the safety benefits of automated driving. “FSD [Supervised] is making driving significantly safer, and it’s encouraging to see ... this [insurance] benefit and reflecting the reduced risk for Tesla owners.”



The reporter tested FSD on a vehicle loaned by Tesla. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.
